column121: After an uneventful approach; landing; and taxi to the gate; we approached the J-line for our gate. While verifying that the safety zone was clear; we noticed that a provisioning truck was servicing the forward galley of the aircraft at the adjacent gate. The lower tailgate of the truck was very close to the edge of the safety zone but we determined that it was outside the line and continued. I taxied very slowly because the box of the truck looked close from my angle of sight. We did not receive any signal to stop and parked without incident. However; the wing walker came up to the cockpit to talk to us afterwards and mentioned that he noticed me looking at the wingtip; and he had the same concerns I did. He stated that the wingtip and the truck box seemed very close; approximately one foot in his estimation. He also was wondering if I could see his wand because; at that point; he and the Marshaler had no line of sight with each other due to the jetbridge. My concern is that if I am looking at the Marshaler and he cannot see the left Wing Walker in this situation; then we are essentially blind. Even though nothing happened; I feel like I should have stopped and waited for the truck to move. The Wing Walker and the rest of the Ground Crew did an excellent job getting us parked without incident but that seems like a situation with a high potential for a negative outcome. Although a negative outcome was avoided; it may be beneficial to have a note in the SIP to let Crews know that the Marshaler and Wing Walker cannot see each other at a certain point in the parking process. I don't know if this is a common issue at every gate; but I always thought they could see each other the entire time.

column123: I was the flying pilot. We were arriving on the RNAV STAR into ZZZ. At the time of the incident we were between the ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 waypoints; very close to the ZZZZZ waypoint. ATC instructed us to descend. The autopilot was engaged. I pushed the MCP FLCH button to start the decent. Immediately afterward I expected the aircraft to pull the power back and start a descent via the FLCH mode. Immediately the aircraft showed an 'autopilot mode' caution message on the ECAIS. Both the captain and I then realized that the aircraft was not descending as per the selected mode. We did not get a horn or a red autopilot warning message. Also the PFD showed that the autopilot was still engaged via the A/P FMA but the aircraft was not descending. We weren't sure if the aircraft was connected to the autopilot or not as per the conflicting information the aircraft was indicating. We then noticed that the aircraft airspeed was slowing and wasn't descending. I disconnected the autopilot and pushed the throttles forward to correct the low airspeed and pushed the yoke forward to start the aircraft descent. We also disconnected and reengaged the flight directors. We then noticed that the yellow 'autopilot mode' caution message had disappeared. Since we believed that the problem had been resolved I reengaged the autopilot. At that time the aircraft continued to descend and fly at the correct assigned airspeed. We didn't however notice that LNAV had not reengaged since we had just reengaged the autopilot and believed that all the modes had been reengaged correctly via the autopilot. At this time; only about 10 seconds later; we noticed that the aircraft was not tracking the arrival course correctly and immediately turned to the left towards the FMC arrival course to intercept. About 5 seconds later ATC said 'it appears that you missed your turn'; and the gave us a 090 heading. The captain told ATC that we were having autopilot issues and were already correcting back to the STAR arrival course. We were then given two more heading changes. We followed ATC directions for the remainder of the approach and landing to a safe landing with no further incident. I'm not certain; but I may have accidentally pushed the autopilot disengage bar while I was reaching for the FLCH button to start the descent.

column121: In the logbook and on our flight plan we had MEL 27-88-02 which was suppose to deactivate the Kruger flap system. The logbook was reviewed and the MEL was discussed between the First Officer and myself. All the placards were in place and signed off by maintenance that the DMP was accomplished. We started the aircraft and taxied out to the runway. I did notice a Kruger light on the SFPI; which was in the MEL that it might be displayed. We took off and climbed out. As we retracted the slats we received an ECAM warning and a single chime. The First Office was flying so I handled the ECAM. The ECAM message showed a Kruger not retracted and a notation of MAX SPD 300KIAS/.65. We did our after takeoff flows and checklist and I told the First Officer to fly the airplane and to not exceed the speed shown in the notation on ECAM. I did remember that besides getting the Kruger light that you could also get an ECAM message saying Kruger Fault. This was not the message we received after bringing up the flaps. I decided to get Maintenance Control on the line with Dispatch. I queried the maintenance people about our situation. I explained what we were showing and that it did not correspond with the MEL we had in the log book. We both concluded that if we could we would continue .65/300 knots. Maintenance was sure that the MEL was complied with and that it was probably an erroneous message; but to be safe we would comply with the speeds on the ECAM. After a discussion with dispatch about extra fuel burn and a longer duration flight we decided we were safe even if the Kruger Flap was extended. The dispatcher did run the numbers for fuel burn with Kruger Flap extended. The flight was uneventful and we landed with no further problems. I did make a comment in the logbook about what had transpired during the flight so if this was an anomaly maintenance could add this message to the MEL. We exited the aircraft where I noticed the Kruger Flap on the left side of the aircraft was partially extended. I immediately got the mechanics involved and told them of the situation. We headed to hotel for a 3 hour layover where we were to return to fly later. After returning to the gateway; and heading to the same aircraft we noticed the gear doors down and a panel on the wing root open. I met up with the maintenance people and asked if there was a problem. He told me that the aircraft was out of service. I asked him what was going on and we were told that the DMP for the KRUGER Flap MEL had not been complied with even though it had been stated so in the log book. Our flight was eventually cancelled as they were having some issues with the log book and could not do the DMP for this MEL.
column123: The aircraft had MEL 27-88-02. During initial climb we received an ECAM for kruger flap not retracted. The MEL did not mention this warning so we complied with the restrictions and called dispatch and maintenance to see if they had any additional information for us and if they preferred us to come back or continue to our destination. column121: Throughout the arrival ATC requested best forward speed; comply at ZZZZZ: 230kts; 10;000 ft. After ZZZZZ; we were vectored for the approach to XXL. We called the airport in sight and ATC cleared us for the approach. We were also requested to slow to 160kts for spacing with an aircraft in front of us for the same runway. At this point I had flaps 8; and requested flaps 20. [Another] flight was also being vectored for XXL; coming from the west. ATC then asked us to slow to final approach speed and if we had the aircraft ahead insight. We did not have it insight; so were quickly told to turn left to a heading of 270. I believe the [other] flight was then cleared for the approach ahead of us; behind the first aircraft we were following. They then gave us a right turn back to the East and told us to intercept the localizer for XXL; but we were 90 degrees to the course and wouldn't have been able to make it and we weren't configured. I think I remember the controller stating that 'this isn't going to work' and asked if we could accept runway XXR. We said yes; and ATC began vectoring us for XXR. At this point I was very task saturated and should've done a go around. I was very concerned that the aircraft was set up for XXR and verbalized this. He said it was. In hindsight; I should have just disconnected the autopilot. We were configured by the FAF and a stable approach was completed. A go around should have been executed before this situation got so far. We did not have time to find the original aircraft in front of us; and then the [other] flight was thrown into the situation. When ATC switched us to XXR; a localizer frequency should have been offered. The Captain called the tower after we landed to discuss what happened with the supervisor. He said they were happy he called; and the supervisor was watching the whole situation. He also agreed a report should be completed.
column123: After being vectored on to final for runway XXL from the west at on approach control frequency; I called the airport in sight after we descended below the clouds; approximately 3;000 ft. AGL; ATC cleared us for the visual approach and instructed a speed reduction to 160 KIAS. There was another aircraft on final about 4 miles ahead of us. I offered to slow to approach speed and the controller immediately requested for us to do so while asking if we could also see the aircraft ahead of us. I indicated that I was unable to see an aircraft ahead. First Officer already had flaps 8 and called for flaps 20 to start slowing when I replied that I was unable to see the other aircraft. Suddenly ATC issued instructions for us to turn left to a heading of 270. At the same time; [another] flight was cleared to join the localizer ahead from the opposite direction; from the east; and midway between us and the previous aircraft. As we rolled out on the 270 heading; we were instructed to turn back to the right to a heading of 090 to intercept the localizer. As we rolled through 360 I could clearly see the [other] aircraft; rolling onto final about 2 miles ahead of us. By then it appeared as if the controller was going to want us to join the LOC on almost a 90 degree angle; not fully configured on a 3 mile final. I was about to ask for re-sequence when the controller asked if I could take runway XXR. I responded that we could; without taking the time to consult the flying pilot. As we crossed the approach path for XXL I was quickly pulling up the LOC frequency for XXR and trying to get the frequencies retuned. [Pilot Flying] asked if I was sure it was XXR and not XXC. I followed procedure and got verification from ATC prior to tuning it on the RTU (Radio Tuning Unit). This seemed to take longer than [Pilot Flying] had expected and I was not yet fully aware of his level of stress over the sudden unnecessary changes. We were then vectored through the XXR LOC and given right turns back towards the airport and cleared for a visual to XXR. The approach and landing was stabilized and without further incident. In retrospect; I think not giving [Pilot Flying] time to give his input about accepting a different runway; understandably added to his stress. While I may not have been uncomfortable with what I saw outside the window; I could have made my fellow pilot less comfortable by not asking him what he was thinking. Other contributory factors were compounded when the controller did not offer a LOC frequency whilst changing runways after getting us to less than optimal airspeed and giving us an impromptu tour of his airspace. Our company procedures require us to use an ILS as a backup whenever available; even in visual conditions. This meant that our crew had to simultaneously deal with clarification of communications; following ATC instructions; practice slow flight; and setting up navigation for a late runway change. To add to the equation; there were 80 souls in the main cabin who were certainly wondering why we were zig-zagging around the airport. I think most pilots don't like being loaded up that much in the simulator. Even less do we enjoy such practice in a real airplane at low altitude; and in the most critical phase of flight. Once at the gate; I asked the tower for a phone number to Approach and was given the number that connected me immediately to the supervisor who had been standing behind the controller during the entire ordeal. ATC stated first that he was glad I called. He then explained to me that he had told the controller to re-sequence us and not try to save the situation after his first mistake had put us in a position for an unstable approach. He apologized for the inconvenience and indicated that the [other] aircraft should not have been squeezed into the line. He should have sent the [other] aircraft to runway XXR to begin with. But by the time the situation had developed; it was better for us to break off of the approach than toattempt to turn the other aircraft around. [The supervisor] was professional and wanted to reassure me that such traffic management is not acceptable and that the controller at the helm during the situation was made well aware of that fact. He and I agreed that a report should be filed if it has the potential prevent at least some similar situations from occurring. I can't speak for the ATC practices and procedures; but from my perspective; there are a few variables at play here that should receive a little more focus in the near future. This applies several large class B airports facilities as well warrants adequate and candid discussion. I can't speak for the ATC practices and procedures; but from my perspective; there are a few variables at play here that should receive a little more focus in the near future. This applies several large class B airports facilities as well warrants adequate and candid discussion. RNAV arrivals have been created to help reduce controller and pilot work load as well as simplify clearance delivery. Issue them; let us all fly them as published; line us up; and watch us keep the line moving as you switch us to the next sector. Trust us to do our part as pilots. TCAS tells us how far behind the next aircraft we are. You want separation; ask us to keep 4 to 5 miles and we will do it. We will be far less confused and take up less time on frequency getting clarification of what you actually need us to do. Keeping the frequency more clear will also allow for us confused pilots to actually ask for the help we need when we don't understand something rather than have to wait for a lengthy exchange while a potentially adverse situation gets worse. It would also be nice if there were some regularly scheduled meetings between professional pilot groups and ATC groups. Before 9/11; it was as easy as asking on the radio if we could come visit the tower in between flights. But after all the bureaucrats got involved; common sense seemed to get tossed right out the window and now we have a generation of pilots who have never been to an ATC facility; seen a radar screen; or had the chance to ask questions directly to a controller and vice versa! I would love to see that decision get more attention.

column121: During boarding Flight Attendant B let me know there was a passenger who was speaking on her cell phone while not wearing a mask. Flight Attendant B asked her to put the mask on and the passenger said she can't talk on the phone through a mask. Flight Attendant B insisted and the woman begrudgingly put the mask on. As I passed by the passenger she was again not wearing the mask and speaking on her phone. I stood by the seat in front of her waiting for a good break in the conversation for a time to talk with her and she wrapped up the conversation and said sorry and put the phone away. I told her it wasn't an issue with the phone; but the health and safety of those around her. She put her mask on. Shortly thereafter as we were preparing the cabin for departure I noticed her mask was below her nose. She was wearing her headphones and did not hear me; but when she saw me she pulled the mask up over her nose. Based on the attitude she gave Flight Attendant B and the fact that the mask was off again when I came by; and then not properly worn a third time Flight Attendant B and I concurred that if we had to speak with her again it would merit a disciplinary action. We also told the flight deck this; so that they would be aware. Throughout the flight we did have close eyes on her; as one does when a passenger has already exhibited behavior that is against the rules; but I tried not to hound on her. During service I saw her and some others wearing their mask below their nose or off in the long times between sips and I made a PA asking everyone to be compliant (in no way singling her out).Once it came time for final compliance for landing I came back through and again her mask was fully below her nose. I stopped and kneeled down and told her that we had already spoken with her about the mask and that wearing it under the nose does not comply. During the conversation that followed she did not pull her mask over her nose until after I had walked away.She told me that she has a medical condition that makes her light headed and that she has been doing her best with the mask. I told her that while for several months we had mask exemptions for medical cases for the last month it has been mandatory regardless of individual. She asked me for my full name and asked if she could take a picture of my name tag. I told her I was not comfortable giving my last name but if she reached out to the company they would know who I was. She said that I was rude for hounding her and briefly said the word 'Nazi' in reference to my strict adherence to the mask policy and 'targeting' of her.The specifics of timing between what was said during this conversation and what was said in the conversation after I brought disciplinary action and later during final compliance all kind of meld; but these things were said.She said that it was wrong to single out people who have medical conditions and that they don't have to share what the condition is. I reminded her that at no point did I ask her what her condition is and that she only shared that she had a condition at the end of the flight after things came to a head. I also explained again that regardless of condition the mask policy is for anyone who wants to fly.Some guests in the nearby rows thanked me for sticking to the policy as they had had concerns with the passenger in question not wearing her mask throughout the flight. I did my best to thank them for their support; but also to not rile up the non-compliant passenger nor the woman across the aisle who seemed to have befriended and come to the passenger's side (however this woman never spoke up to me or in my earshot). I did not want to put passengers against each other or cause more disruption.Passenger also said that she was not planning on flying [Airline] ever again. We let the Captain know [of the situation] and he called ahead to have a Supervisor meet passenger. During deplaning several of the other passengers that were in surrounding seats and had spoken up again thanked me for the way I handled the situation and said they'd be writing in to the company.
column123: Passenger was sitting in seat XX1. When securing the cabin before door closure she was on phone and had mask looped on one ear and hanging down and I asked her to put it on she said 'but I can't talk on the phone with it' and I said 'I apologize but it has to be worn over your nose and mouth at all times it is our policy' then she just looked at me with an attitude and then I asked her again if she could please put it on to which she said 'sssuurrreeee' and put it on. Then I informed another FA and told him to keep an eye on her and then he immediately walked through the cabin and she had it off again; not even one minute later. So he also asked her to put it on. After safety demo passenger had mask on but not covering her nose FA A asked her to pull it up and make sure it is covering both her nose and mouth.Inflight there were times she took exaggerated time to eat and drink. As were others in the cabin so we made a PA; (overall I bet we made 20 mask policy PAs during the entire flight).Then during descent FA A observed her with it off again. I seen him having a conversation with her so I approached and he mentioned to her the policy and the reasons and the procedure and then told her he would be back.He said she said she knows the policy. And around that time she mentioned to him that she was trying her best but she has a medical condition. She continued to argue with him and ask for his name to file a complaint. Passengers in front of and behind her gave thanks to FA A for enforcing the policy and said he handled it well. I do believe she overheard them praising him. We notified Captain and he informed [the] arrival station.

column121: During vectors to ICN we got a delay due to unauthorized drone activity. Approach Control was unable to predict the length of the delay. We were at least the 6th aircraft in line being delay vectored. We evaluated our fuel and the number of aircraft ahead of us being delayed and transmitted Pan Pan to Approach Control for vectors to land at ICN. Approach Control would not vector us to ICN. They asked for our alternate airport which was ZZZZ1. We reported to Dispatch of our diversion and followed another flight diverting to ZZZZ1. We landed; parked and later departed again to complete the flight to ICN. This diversion was due to the unauthorized drone activity. No one had the ability to predict the length of the delay. The only known and the safest course of action was to divert to our alternate airport.
column123: Upon switching approach control we could here holding instructions being given to aircraft.  We immediately began evaluating options for fuel and landing.  After being vectored for around 10-15 minutes Captain made the decision to declare minimum fuel.  The approach controller  responded that we were number 7 for landing at Incheon and requested our alternate airport.  We informed him that Gimpo (RKSS) was the alternate given a vector for approach.  Landing was uneventful.  Apparently there was drone activity near RKSI which prevented aircraft from landing.  Without any clear time frame as to when we would be landing and being number 7 for landing we made the decision to divert.  Don't really have any.  Can't control rogue drone activity.

column121: I was conducting a visual approach to [Runway] XXR backed up by the RNAV Y XXR. I was the Pilot Flying and the Captain was the Pilot Monitoring. We had briefed all the threats and the approach per the AOM prior to the TOD and were planning flaps full for the landing configuration. We were being vectored onto a base leg to join the final visually. I was faster than I should have been on the base for the distance we were out (180 selected speed I think) and so I had to delay calling for the flaps. I think the last altitude we were given was 8;000 feet on the base before we reported the field in sight and were cleared for the visual. The approach had been activated and I went to managed speed. We then set a lower altitude just above the altitude for the next fix after the one just ahead of us on the approach so I could use vertical speed to start down and stay on the path since the approach was not quite captured. I had armed the approach and it annunciated FINAL APP as we were joining the final and the aircraft continued descending on the path. I was using the auto pilot for lateral and vertical NAV until established on final. We extended the gear prior to joining the final to help with slowing the aircraft to flap deployment speeds. The vector had put us in closer than I had anticipated and I had also started slowing later than I should have. The speed did not come back very quickly; possibly because of a tailwind shifting to a headwind as were turning final; so I had to disconnect the autopilot and arrest the descent to get the aircraft slowed for flap deployment and also to prevent an overspeed. Both the Captain and I noticed the RA was close to 1;000 [feet] as we deployed final flaps; and our speed was still well above approach speed; but we were VMC and our assessment was that we had been in final configuration prior to 1;000 AGL. We continued the approach and were stable at 500 [feet] so we landed out of the approach within the required criteria. We were at the gate when the ACARS printed a Self-Assessment Flight Report. We weren't surprised to see Y for speed and descent; but we were surprised to see a Y for flap change. We discussed it; and although we were unstable at 1;000 [feet]; we felt that we had been configured and thought the report generated a flap change Y at 0974 RA because the terrain rises to the north and the spot elevations are around 300-600 feet higher than the airport elevation near where we selected final configuration. Regardless; the final configuration selection was closer to 1;000 AGL than it should have been and we decided we would file an report just in case. Normally; I call for gear down and managed speed at 2;000 AGL so as to have plenty of time to reach final configuration prior to 1;000 AGL; but I missed that cue because I was in the yellow due to being tighter and faster than I had anticipated; and I didn't realize it because I was busy trying to get back in the green slowing and turning final and descending to stay on the path. This is also a case where my experience exceeded my performance due to being new to being back in the right seat and not flying much in September. I also didn't say anything about being in the yellow; and so I didn't get as much help as I could have used. I also failed to brief that we may need to be configured on base depending on where the base leg is and to say something if I don't ask for the gear down by 2;000 AGL. The other factor was conducting a visual approach to a high-altitude airport where AGL altitudes happen at much higher MSL altitudes than were are used to and neither I nor the Captain had been into ZZZ in a long time. I will more thoroughly brief visual approaches regarding the gates I want for configuration and speed changes that provide plenty of margin for a stabilized approach.
column123: As we turned to intercept final and configure for landing with a near 0 VSI; a hill on final gave us an unexpected 1;000 ft. radio alt call. We where visual and comfortable with continuing the approach due to distance. I recall being fully configuration when the second 1;000 foot reading on final and on speed at 500 ft. We failed to slow down in time on base leg not taking into effect high alt difference and ground speed. We did not brief the ground speed difference and the delayed slow down or terrain around the base turn. Haven't been to ZZZ in years.

column121: The FA (Flight Attendant) came up about 30 minutes prior to departure and said there was a smell; similar to when a gas stove is turned on but not lit; around the exit row. I was eating and asked the FO (First Officer) to go check it out. He came back and said the report was accurate; so I called Maintenance. I was busy eating and asked MX (Maintenance) if he wanted me to write it up; and he said no. He came on and said he had smelled something outside approaching the plane. Once I was done eating; I went back and smelled for myself. It was just as described. The confusing thing was that I had never smelled anything like it before; nor could myself; any passengers; Maintenance or the flight attendants determine what it could be. We continued trying to solve the problem; going up and down the cabin seeing if it was stronger one place versus the other; and seeing if it was dissipating. We did have a family of four leave the flight; English was not their first language so I am unsure if they understood my briefings. As we were dealing with that; we called OPS to notify them of the delay. Shortly after; our mechanic came up and said they noticed a ramp sweeping machine that runs on propane nearby. Then Operations called and said it was a tug nearby that was leaking fuel. With this information; we decided we would pushback and see if it goes away after we left the gate area. We did and checked with the flight attendant twice during taxi to get an update. The first time she said it was dissipating; and on the before takeoff check to the line; she said it was gone. During descent; in the mid-teens; we got a call saying the smell was back. It wasn't busy so we asked for a quicker route to the airport; which was granted and we landed uneventfully. I have no good answer as to why I didn't write this up. I have thought about it since I got off the phone with Maintenance in ZZZ1; and I cannot think of a reason why I decided to not write this up. Referring to [the] manual. Mechanical Irregularities; D. Reporting Mechanical Irregularities; it does not specifically state to write anything in the MX Log. It simply states if the item is notice prior to block out; to contact Maintenance and they will determine the action required to correct or defer the irregularity. I will re-write to read that any time Maintenance is contacted; a write muse ensue.
column123: As we were doing preflight duties a FA (Flight Attendant) reported an odd smell in the cabin while passengers were boarding around the exit row. The Captain (CA) asked me to go back and see what I smelled and I did. It was like a natural gas smell mixed with garbage. Nothing I could place a finger on. I reported it to the CA and he went back to check it out. I continued preflight work and he called Mx (Maintenance) out. I didn't hear his and Mx conversation as I continued preflight activities But at the end he told me that the Mx guy could smell it outside and that there was a fuel spill reported from a ground truck in the gate next to us that was the most likely cause of the smell. I continued preflight activities as the Captain finished working with Mx. and he said we were good to depart as long as the smell disappeared when we taxied out. We called the FA on taxi and she said it had dissipated and we departed. On arrival the smell returned and after we reached the gate and shutdown the Captain determined that he had not written up the issue properly in the origin airport before we departed. I believe the Captain was distracted with many tasks and worrying about departing on time which caused him to forget to write up the issue. It's difficult to find a single reason on how to avoid this event. Perhaps more training on specific events that require Mx write ups.

column121: We were on a 6 mile final when tower cleared a Cirrus to land in front of us. When this happened separation from the traffic began to decrease; tower then cleared the Cirrus for a low approach. This seemed to cause confusion in the Cirrus cockpit. We continued until the spacing was unsafe; the Cirrus appeared to be on the runway. At around 400 ft. we executed a go around. As we began to climb at go around thrust flaps 8 the Cirrus began to climb as well giving us a TA and tower asked us to side step to the right. I began a turn to the right as the pilot monitoring watched the traffic below us carefully. While our focus was on avoiding the traffic we neglected to call 'positive rate' and raise the gear. This led to a delay is raising the flaps form 8 to 0 to clean up the airplane. Since we were already at pattern altitude we made the decision to leave the gear down since we were moments away from needing to lower it again. Towers poor spacing was the initial cause of the event. However our focus on keeping visual separation from the traffic led us to neglect some of our duties. Although traffic avoidance was and should be our top priority in that situation. We could have called a go around earlier when we saw that there could be a potential conflict. This would have given us more time and led to less task saturation.
column123: While on about a six mile final tower cleared a Cirrus to perform a short approach to a touch and go in front of us. As we continued the rate of closure was greater than tower anticipated and tower changed the Cirrus clearance to a low approach only. We continued our approach until about 400 ft. AGL. At this time it appeared the Cirrus did a touch and go and was on the runway for a long time. I felt that the separation margin was too small and called for a go around. We completed the first portion of the go around but then the Cirrus had started his upwind and was directly in our path. We prioritized maintaining visual separation with the Cirrus and complying with ATC separation instructions and failed to bring gear up and do a climb sequence until we were on a downwind and ran the after takeoff and then another decent check. After this we completed all check lists and had a safe landing. Poor aircraft separation by ATC. It sounded like there were two controllers in the tower; one being trained and the other a supervisor. Waiting too long to call for the go around. We waited until a go around caused too much going on and made us miss checklists and call outs due to high work load. Misinterpreted instructions by the Cirrus. When ATC changed the landing clearance for the Cirrus it was unclear if they understood what ATC actually wanted. I think the biggest thing that could be done to avoid similar situations is to call for a go around earlier when we saw there might be a conflict with spacing. There were cues earlier in the approach indicating a potential for loss of separation; but it was also possible for us to land had the Cirrus followed instructions in a timely manner. We should have erred on the conservative side to not put us in an overloaded task situation.

column121: [Captain and I] operated from ZZZ to ZZZ1. On this flight we had MEL 29-11-XX; which was for an inoperative hydraulic pump 1B. This MEL required our minimum flight weight to be above 38;500lbs. Our flight load for this particular flight was extremely light with 3 Pax; 1 [standard] bag; 0 Heavy bags; 1 plane side bag and 300 lbs of ballast. Along with excess fuel to help our weight we landed roughly at 38;900 pounds; giving us only 400 pounds of useable fuel on the plane; not enough for the 45 minute reserve buffer; planned at 2099lbs; legally required under IFR.This was my first time experiencing this MEL and I saw the extra fuel for the MEL on the release and after considering the light passenger load both myself and the Captain concluded that we were going to be close to our minimum flight weight upon landing so he asked the fueler to add 300lbs of fuel and 300lbs of ballast to help pad our landing weight; but at the time we both failed to consider the reserve fuel and it was not until I mentioned at a later date that we would have been below our flight weight if we had to go around. At this point he realized we did not have our proper reserve fuel. We had plenty of fuel in the tank but we would have not been in compliance with the new limitation in place set by the MEL.Possibly more awareness on the flight plan of low passenger flights in conjunction for this MEL or a separate fuel column on the release when the fuel is to be used as weight so the crew can consider the fuel as unusable.

column121: FOD (Foreign Object Debris) on the ground in the BWI back alley gates has been a problem for months with no signs of improvement. BWI Ground Operations does not have an effective FOD Awareness Program. We sat at the gate for nearly 90 minutes preparing for our flight. During the delay while waiting 50 minutes for five bags from Flight #XXXX (which never arrived); the ramp personnel had plenty of time to pick up the FOD in and around the Safety Zone. Excessive FOD was present before; during; and after the push off BWI Gate XX. No effort was made to remove the FOD. BWI Ramp Personnel walked by; stepped on; and ignored FOD all over the flight line. As we were being pushed back I asked the Ramp Crew to pick up FOD (papers; gloves; concrete gravel stones; plastic strapping material; etc.) to avoid ingesting FOD in the engines while we were starting engines. Because of the confined space in the back alley; the lead aircraft is more likely to blow FOD into the engines of the second aircraft. We called BWI Ground Control to remove FOD from the area at the top of the back alley where FOD had accumulated in the vicinity of the electric light control building. Also; the concrete along the vehicle road adjacent to the black storm drain grating is breaking up between BWI Gates XY and XZ. Chunks of concrete; stones; and gravel litter the ramp in this vicinity. The ramp looks as if it has been breaking up for weeks; but nobody has made the effort to remove the concrete FOD until BWI airport can make repairs.The BWI Station Manager needs to take responsibility for the FOD Awareness Program.  At this time; there is no evidence that BWI has an effective FOD Awareness Program.  Leadership for an effective FOD Awareness Program starts from the top.  Leaders need to train all employees to participate in the FOD Awareness Program on a daily basis and enforce compliance with the program.  The BWI FOD Awareness Program exists; at best; as a 'lip service' program. Bringing this issue to the attention of leadership falls on deaf ears. My impression is that BWI leadership; to the highest leadership levels; does not care to address or fix this ongoing problem. We need to collectively protect our engines from unnecessary damage resulting from FOD. BWI Airport Operations needs to repair the concrete breaking up near the vehicle road adjacent to the black storm drain grating between BWI Gates XY and XZ. In the meantime; Company BWI Ground Operations needs to take responsibility for removing the concrete debris. I immediately notified BWI OPS by radio of the FOD hazard. I am not sure of what action has been taken to remedy the safety concern.

column121: I began work on Aircraft X with my crew as the card person. I occasionally do the card and this was the first time in years that I had done a flight with this many items on it. When I printed out the departure staging guide I saw there were 2 carts of freight totaling about 3000 pounds; 3 quickpacks and about 88 bags planned for the flight. After I assigned the items (1 of the freight in pit; the other freight in pit 4; the quickpacks in 5; and the bags in 4) we began to load the flight. The first item of freight was very heavy and difficult to load into pit 3. Took a lot more time than expected and by the time we were finished we only had about 27 minutes left to finish the flight. I went to get the bags and on the way to the bag room I saw the Supervisor and told her that we were running behind after loading the 1st item of freight in front and that I wanted to hold off the second freight because there wouldn't be enough time.She said it was ok and to go ahead and hold it off the flight. I picked up the bags and loaded them into their planned pits. Finally I decided to load the quickpack boxes last into pit 5. I didn't notice that one of the boxes had dry ice in it and was Dangerous Goods (DG). When it was time to close out the flight on the scanner it would not allow me to because I didn't have 15 bags loaded together with the Dangerous Goods. column121: Cleared for visual approach and cleared to land on RWYXXL. [Commercial flight] canceled their take off clearance so [ZZZ] Tower told us to continue the visual approach with a canceled landing clearance. We were 7.5 miles out direct to the Final Approach Fix in LNAV (Lateral Navigation) and the armed glideslope had captured at about 3;000 MSL providing a constant descent. We were Flaps 5 at 180 kts. To create spacing I called for gear down and flaps 20 and rolled the speed back above 20 maneuvering speed. The plane began to slow and pitch down with flap extension. I called for flaps 25 when the gear showed 3 green and the EICAS (Engine Indication And Crew Alerting System) showed 'Autopilot' indicating it was still working but in a degraded mode. I then saw GS FMA (Glideslope Flight Mode Annunciator) now had a line thru it. At this point I disconnected the autopilot and leveled off visually. The altitude was about 1400 MSL; 1000 AGL. I told the Pilot Monitoring I was going to maintain 1000 AGL until established. Right after I leveled off the [ZZZ] Tower announced low altitude alert. During the debrief the Pilot Monitoring said he saw the glideslope go full scale below us and then shoot up to full scale above us near the autopilot disconnect. I continued to maneuver visually to the runway centerline at 1;000 ft. Once established we cycled the Flight Directors and the glideslope centered back to where we were on the approach. Continued visually and landed. Wrote up the discrepancy in the logbook.  Fatigue didn't cause it; but it may have slowed my processing of everything that was happening kind of at the same time.  Don't allow the glideslope to capture early. Choose another vertical mode until on or very close to the LOC (Localizer).
column123: We were cleared for the visual to [Runway] XXL and subsequently cleared to land approximately 10SW of the airport. We were level at 3000 when approach was armed and glideslope captured. In order to slow and create space the Pilot Flying called for gear and flaps 20. After we received an AUTOPILOT EICAS and the GS FMA (Glide Slope Flight Mode Annunciator) had an amber line through it. The Captain continued visually onto centerline; the Flight directors were turned off and turned back on and approach rearmed. LOC and GS FMAs activated and appeared to act normal. Autopilot/Glideslope malfunction. ATC canceling our landing clearance and clearing an aircraft for takeoff on our planned runway caused a distraction about the same time as the malfunction.

column121: During the flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ; while attempting to acquire the landing data for the arrival into ZZZ; the ACARS indicated NO COMM. The PM received the ATIS information through the radios and determined the landing data numbers via the company manuals in the EFB. The ILS XX for ZZZ was subsequently placed in the FMS prior to the brief; and Runway XX was briefed as the landing runway as per ATIS. While established on the ZZZZZ 3 arrival and checking in with final approach; ATC stated to expect Runway XYL. The PM verbally stated the fixes for the XYL ZZZZZ 3 arrival. Both the PM and PF then switched to the ILS XYL approach plate on the EFB and briefed that approach. While flying the ZZZZZ 3; both the PF and the PM discussed the two different split-off points. The first split-off is for landing East or West. The second Split-off is for landing XX or XYL. I was the Pilot Flying and was established on the ZZZZZ 3 Arrival when I noticed the indicated waypoints were still for Runway XX. As I stated that we were navigating for Runway XX; Approach Control asked us to make a right turn towards the proper waypoint for the XYL arrival. This event was caused by not verifying the correct runway was placed into the FMS after a runway change was given by ATC. Contributing factors for this event would be the initial distraction resulting from the failure of ACARS. Another contributing factor would be the lack of currency/proficiency for both the PF and the PM. This lack of currency/proficiency was briefed as the threat in the brief for both the takeoff as well as the arrival. A final contributing factor would be the lack of familiarity with ZZZ for the PF as this was the first time flying into that airport.First and foremost; flight path management is paramount to a successful outcome to any flight. When given any changes in altitudes; airspeeds; headings; runways etc. by ATC; each pilot is responsible to confirm and verify those changes. If task saturation begins to set in; notify the other pilot and let them assist you with reducing your saturation level. Always clearly understand where you are during any aspect of a flight. Within the extremely dynamic environment we find ourselves in during any flight operation; a lack of currency or proficiency can and does have a negative effect. Under the circumstances of COVID-19; it is still incumbent on each pilot to maintain the highest level of professionalism possible.
column123: I was pilot monitoring; prior to descent the ACARS went NO COMM; so I was gathering weather and doing landing data manually- we had set up for and briefed for XX as that was the previous active runway on our ACARS there is a reasonably complex STAR with altitudes and speeds. column121: We departed ZZZ without the flight release PIC signature.  The following summary is not offered as an excuse for this or to lessen the mistake that was made only to advise what happened and most importantly prevent it from happening again.  The weather for this flight was unusually good; only some forecast light chop at FL380 to FL410 for the first 200 miles of flight.  The FO (First Officer) and I spoke about this and decided to stop our climb at FL370 till past threat.  As we approached the gate I signed the release I thought; evidently the release did not go thru as expected.  The gate area was only partially full as our load was only 50 passengers. The aircraft was hot as the temperature was 106 degrees F and externally air was hooked to the aircraft. We dealt with that and unhooked the external air and started the APU to cool the aircraft.  During this time the FAs (Flight Attendants) boarded the aircraft and were briefed by me.  I was notified shortly after taken seat and starting the downloads to my EFB (Electronic Flight Bag) that the lights would not come on in the main cabin so we called Maintenance and they arrived quickly to fix the issue;  Quick fix and we continued; made the mask PA and we pushed early.  As we were pushing the FO noticed that the runway had changed to a west flow so runway change number 1; we completed the starting engines flows and set the parking brake and did not move.  We then got clearance to taxi and advise to set up for a south runway departure; change 2; we held position and as we completed this change we were advised we could depart on the north runway if we would be ready after the short taxi to Runway XX.  I called the FAs and asked if they would be ready for a short taxi; the response was yes. I accepted the short taxi; change 3.  We had set up for Runway XR before push; then after push Runway change XX; runway XYR and back to runway XX. Three runway changes after push along with checking and changing the route of flight as each runway has a different departure procedures and resetting the MCP 3 times.  Both the FO and myself have been on this aircraft for many years and both of us felt like we were in the green and had trapped all of the issues that had happened.  We never got an ACARS message saying the flight release had not been signed and during the distractions the final trap was missed as we briefed the takeoff data based on what we expected to happen.  The lesson which I learned on this flight is even when you feel like you're in the green; stop and run through your flows. This was the first time I ever took the runway without physically touching the closeout and it will be my last!  We were notified enroute that the release was not signed by Dispatch; signed release via ACARS and continued uneventfully to destination.  When you feel like your in the green; stop and run all the traps one final time before taking runway.

Cross checking the altitude the airplane was at; it was descending through 6800-6900 MSL and the altitude restriction is at 7000. JILNA was a melded waypoint on our flight plan off of the BRIXX 2 RNAV Arrival; that had been melded once we were cleared for the approach. When the last waypoint of a STAR procedure is common to the first waypoint of the instrument approach procedure; the FMS may automatically meld the waypoints. The altitude constraints contained in both procedures for that particular waypoint is expected to be melded as well. In other scenarios; the last STAR waypoint contains a 'fly vectors to intercept' leg. This waypoint can also be the first one for the approach procedure and the pilot may manually delete the 'fly vectors' or copy the approach waypoint of the same waypoint on the STAR; which will also meld both waypoints.Embraer has received reports of the airplane not complying with the published altitude constraints during transition from STAR to instrument approach procedure. Investigations have revealed that an altitude violation may occur when two common waypoints are melded; either automatically by the FMS or manually by the pilot; where the last waypoint of the STAR and the first waypoint of the approach procedure has the same name; but different altitude constraints. As a consequence; the FMS constructed vertical flight path may not respect the altitude constraint; despite the altitude constraint indications of the FMS FLT PLAN page; VSD (Vertical Situation Display) and PFD (Primary Flight Display) are correctly displayed. The VNAV guidance may result in a constructed flight path above or below the published constraint. To prevent the violation of an altitude constraint; after a common waypoint is melded automatically by the FMS or manually by the pilot; perform as follows; Delete the altitude constraint at the melded waypoint; manually re-insert the altitude constraint in the FMS.

column121: Earlier today; I received a phone call from my Chief Pilot asking about a plane that I flew over the weekend that had a fuel leak. I explained to him that while we were on a turn; we requested a lavatory service. When the lav tech came out to service the plane; he indicated to me that he was unable to service the lav; nothing would come out. I ended up calling line Maintenance to come out and trouble shoot. Once they arrived and tried to fix the issue I was made aware that they would be unable to fix the issue in a timely manner and said that we would be swapped into a another aircraft. Shortly thereafter; I received a text (which I did not hear) and then a phone call asking me to close out of Software from the company. I then proceeded to log out and started to pack up my stuff to head to the new aircraft when the fueler; who was just outside with the original aircraft; said 'I have something you need to see'. When I followed him outside; he showed me that when he added pressurized fuel to the plane; fuel slowly started coming out of the bottom of the right wing root; about 3 feet down from the fuel panel. I then called line Maintenance back (as they had already left the aircraft) to let them know about the fuel leak and that I was no longer logged into Software and was unable to write up the this new issue. I confirmed with them my gate and that I was the plane with previous lav issue. I said that I would leave a hand written note describing the new fuel issue on the captain's yoke and line Maintenance said that would be fine.This event was caused by the discovery of a new mechanical issue after I was logged out of Software. Contributing factors include: my inability to sign back into Software with an old aircraft after I have been assigned a new one; trying to maintain a timely schedule for the passengers who were moved to another aircraft/gate and trusting that line Maintenance would note the new mechanical issue from my phone call and the hand written note that I left on the yoke and write it up themselves when I am unable. Allowing a pilot to log back into an aircraft after they have already signed out and discover a mechanical issue. Or maybe having Maintenance write up the issue while the pilot is still on the phone when they are notified that the pilot is logged out and unable to write up an issue.

column121: ZZZ Arrival ATIS C was current; advertising visual approaches to Runways XYL; XXL; and XXR. Prior to descent the Captain and I had thoroughly briefed visual approaches to both Runway XYL and Runway XXL. We requested Runway XXL on initial contact with ZZZ TRACON and were granted the request before ZZZZZ on the ZZZZZ2 STAR. We were vectored after ZZZZZ1 onto a left base to Runway XXL; then a turn to join final; which accompanied the visual approach clearance and change to Tower on [frequency]. I called Tower advising we were on a visual approach to Runway XXL and would be parking at gate. Tower responded with 'Runway XXL; cleared to land.' About a minute later; I noted that Tower instructed traffic to cross Runway XXL downfield at either Taxiway V or Taxiway R without referencing us; which I noted as strange. While on final; I noticed that a different aircraft had pulled up to the hold short line for Runway XXL at Taxiway Y10; and that I had not yet heard that crew interact with Tower. When we were on approximately a 1-mile final; the crew of the aircraft holding short called Tower advising they were ready for departure. Without referencing us; Tower stated 'RNAV to ZZZZZ3; Runway XXL; cleared for takeoff.' As soon as we heard this; the Captain stated to me that we would be going around; and we recited the first 3 calls we would make when that happened. I keyed up on the radio and stated 'Traffic on short final; Runway XXL.' By then the departing aircraft had entered the runway. Tower responded with go around instructions including a right turn to a 270 heading and a climb to 4;000. I read them back; and the Captain and I properly executed a go-around. I cleared the right side of the aircraft for any traffic landing XXR; noted there was none; and stated 'Clear on the right.' As we began the turn; TCAS sounded a traffic advisory. I noted the yellow target on TCAS was indicating 800 feet; and stated aloud that the traffic had just lifted off and that we could disregard the advisory; as we were turning away. Tower apologized for the mistake and sent us to approach for re-sequencing and an uneventful visual approach and landing on Runway XXR.The crew of the departing aircraft appears to have failed to visually check the final for traffic before calling Tower for a takeoff clearance; and again prior to taxiing onto the runway for departure. The Air Traffic Controller appears to have forgotten about having cleared us to land; or appears to have been situationally unaware of our position prior to issuing the takeoff clearance. The Runway Status Lights (RWSL) on Runway XXL appear not to have worked; either because my aircraft's position on short final failed to trigger the red stop bars; because the departing aircraft ignored the RWSL red stop bars; the RWSL malfunctioned; or because the system was improperly overridden by the Controller. Another system that appears to have failed is the Controller's ASDE-X safety logic; because it appears my radio transmission was the primary reason he initiated the go-around instructions. Typically; when departing traffic crosses the hold short line with an arriving aircraft on short final; ASDE-X safety logic sounds an alarm. An additional contributing factor is the resurgence of traffic levels after a significant prolonged drop stemming from the outbreak of COVID-19; which may have led to complacency on the part of the departing crew and the Controller.Departing crews need to diligently check the final for traffic before taxiing onto the runway for takeoff; and ideally before even calling ready for departure. Failing to do so before calling ready violates basic airmanship and sets the Controller up for failure. That said; the Controller should have had use of a memory aid or reliable automation to indicate and help him remember that Runway XXL was being used as an active arrival runway; that we had been issued a clearance to land; and that we were on short final to that runway at the time heissued the departing aircraft's takeoff clearance. Interviewing the crew of the departing aircraft would also shed light on whether the RWSL had illuminated and; if so; whether they proceeded onto the runway with the RWSL stop bars illuminated. If this is the case; retraining would mitigate this event from happening again. Interviewing the Controller would provide insight as to whether he overrode the RWSL; whether the ASDE-X safety logic worked properly; and other details about the work conditions that shift including staffing and fatigue; which; if undesirable; could be corrected to help mitigate the recurrence of this event.

column121: We started our takeoff roll at ZZZ. It was the FO's (First Officer's) leg. Shortly after the 'set takeoff thrust call' my window on the Captain's side started to slide open. I'd estimate our speed at 40 kts. It was barely open so I said 'continue' and reached up to close it. However; the window would not close and actually felt like it was coming out of the track. I assumed the window would easily close and that we still had plenty of time to safely reject at low speed if it wouldn't. At that point I became distracted and was worried that the window was falling in. At that point the FO asked if I wanted to reject and I said 'yes'. He initiated the reject as he saw that I was handling the window. As I brought my scan away from the window the reject was started and I noticed the airspeed was about 100 kts. The aircraft quickly decelerated as it was very light. I expected the airspeed to be less than 80 kts based on the short amount of time we had been rolling. The FO continued to stop the aircraft. At that point I took controls. He called the Tower and I made a PA to the passengers to remain seated. We then taxied off the runway at Taxiway X and coordinated with Maintenance to have the brakes checked. They gave us a thumbs up and we taxied to the gate. At that point the window was stuck in a half open position. We shutdown at the gate and switched to another aircraft. Rejecting immediately when the window started to slide open would have prevented the distraction and the rejection would have started at a slower speed. I assumed two things: that the window would easily close and that we were still below 80 kts when the decision was made. It may have been; but at the light weight the aircraft accelerated quickly and I think by the time the actions began we were over 80 kts.
column123: At approximately 40 kts during takeoff roll; Captain side window slid open. Captain called continue and attempted to close the window. A few seconds later I looked over and saw the Captain was struggling to get it closed. I stated that I recommend we reject and he agreed. His hands were still on the window to prevent it from slamming back so I initiated the reject procedure. I did not notice the top airspeed; but I would estimate visually about 100 kts; autobraking did engage. Aircraft came to a stop abeam Taxiway X. Notified the Tower. We were instructed to exit on Taxiway. We stopped on Taxiway and called Company. Maintenance met us on ramp and checked the brakes. We taxied in. Window was unable to be shut. When Maintenance came to the flight deck and were able to move the window forward the handle seemed loose and the squeeze grip seemed loose so we all conferred and removed the aircraft from service.I specifically remember observing the Captain check his window just prior to calling for the before takeoff checklist so I think it was secure. We should have rejected as soon as the window slid open to prevent from getting to the higher speed. The aircraft was light so acceleration was very rapid.

column121: BZN ATIS can be received late due to terrain; no Digital ATIS; and early descent to land RWY 30.  When we initially tried to get ATIS; it was actually Johnson City; WY.  When we did actually get it; it was a little late and required re-briefing to change the plans.In addition; the company pages need more information.1 - Runway 12 is preferred; even up to a 10 knot tailwind (per AirNAV.com); although that information is not specific or clear on the chart; which simply says Runway 12 is preferred.  The additional information of up to a 10 knot tailwind would be helpful to ensure we are planning; for the most likely scenario.  In our case; the wind was 6 knots from the NW; so we were not sure which runway to plan without ATIS.  Knowing they operate with up to a 10 knot tailwind on Runway 12 would have helped. 2 - Company pages note a safety alert that states; 'terrain east of the airport does not allow for a normal descent to a straight-in-landing to Runway 30.'  Note it does not state what 'normal' is; prohibit a landing west; or prohibit 'trying' with early configuration and being prepared to go around or joining a left downwind visual to 30.  To me the Company page sounds a little like a prohibition; or at least; that it is not recommended.  But it needs to be clearer.  If it is prohibited; it should say that.  If it isn't; provide additional information.  Maybe it should state something like:'Terrain to the East of the airport does not allow for a normal descent to a straight-in landing on Runway 30.  If attempted; configure and slow early to maintain the VNAV path; and if unable; prepare for a go-around and fly the RNAV 30 via the FIDEP transition or if in day visual conditions with terrain in sight; enter a left visual downwind and visual approach to Runway 30.'

column121: After takeoff and during normal cleanup procedures; the caution light came on with an associated ECAM.  The Captain pulled speed to ensure we did not over speed; a quick glance at ECAM said max speed 230; I believe.  As PM; I confirmed it was not a Quick Action or ECAM exception.  I assumed control of aircraft and radios; and stated ECAM Action.  The Captain reviewed the ECAM and began to troubleshoot [the] problem.  The ECAM had very little information; and then he referenced the QRH.  I was coordinating with ATC to stop climb at 10;000 feet (safe alt in sector) and advised them of our speed and desire to hold. Captain confirmed max speed of 230 knots from QRH; so we slowed to 220 to provide a margin.  The slat/flap indicator showed slats were almost up; significantly less than 1.  We lowered gear to burn down gas to below max landing weight.  While still in holding; we selected flaps 1 and obtained normal indications on the slats.   Once all briefings; checklists and QRH procedures were complete; the Captain resumed flying duties and I requested to exit holding and obtain vectors for approach to Runway XX.  Flaps and slats moved normally and the landing was uneventful and normal. Captain taxied to gate and passengers deplaned. Flaps and slats retracted normal on the ground.  We discussed the need to declare an emergency; but did not initially since we were not sure of the actual problem; once flaps/slats moved normally; it seems all systems were normal.Aircraft may have sat on the ground during the COVID flying reduction; and therefore it seemed; to me; there might have been an indication problem or squat switch problem.  We did not declare an emergency because the aircraft seems to have a computer or indication problem and slats lowered normally once we started to configure.  In retrospect; any flight control problem is reason to declare emergency; but not sure if we then should undeclared once all was normal.  I have not flown much in the past 7 months; so I may have reverted to previously learned procedures.Any flight control issue is an emergency; even when corrected.  Better maintenance on aircraft.

column121: On Sunday; (date) I was called off reserve to fly Aircraft X under Ops Spec XXXX; with a ferry permit; from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. As far as I knew the flight went smoothly and according to plan; but I got a call on Tuesday; (date); informing me that the R1 slide had deployed when maintenance personnel opened the door later that day. I am not positive what happened; but here is what I recall: being that no flight attendants were on board; it was up to the flight crew to disarm the doors. During our approach briefing; the Captain had briefed me about disarming the doors prior to maintenance personnel opening the L1 door. I understood the Captain to be saying 'it is critical that we disarm the L1 door quickly upon arrival; before personnel open it from outside.' Upon shutdown I reiterated to the Captain that I would disarm the L1 door right away; which I did. I can not remember exactly the captain's response when I read the 'cabin doors' item on the parking checklist; but I was under the impression that we were only worried about the L1 door; and that we were turning it over to Maintenance; so they would handle the rest. If I remember correctly; I only disarmed the L1 door. My recommendation would be to not perform the parking checklist until all doors were disarmed. As a brand new First Officer with 3 trips under my belt since consolidation; I should not have assumed anything; instead of assuming there must have been an exception to the '6 disarmed' response on the parking checklist; or assuming that the Captain had done this before and knew a procedure that I did not know.
column123: At the conclusion of a maintenance flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ; the disarming of the doors was not verified. During approach brief; I briefed that the L1 door needed to be disarmed before anyone tried to open the door from the outside. We parked the aircraft; shut down the engines and did the parking checklist. Upon reaching the door verification; I stated 'to go' because we had to disarm the doors ourselves. We got up and I went to the back and disarmed L2 and R2; leaving the front doors to the First Officer. As I returned to the flight deck; I double checked L1 to make sure it was disarmed. I then returned to the flight deck and shut down the aircraft. I did not re-verify that the parking checklist was completed. I was informed yesterday that a slide had deployed after our flight. I did not verify the doors disarmed; to finish the parking checklist. I also should have double checked both front doors; after disarming the back.

column121: Normal day; normal passenger operations; on Aircraft X; performing ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight. With APU being under MEL; started engine number one at the gate according to normal checklist. Cleared to push out of the gate; to the blue line. The initial push back was mostly smooth. Aircraft pushed on a slant angle on the green line and stopped. Tow truck driver contacted the flight deck; stating that he will pull us to the blue line. Since then; the mild tensions and sounds were sensible as if it felt that the angle of pulling forward to the blue line was kind of steep. I; personally; could not see the tow truck from the right seat. Shortly after; we heard a bigger noise and aircraft started to move forward that followed immediately by the driver asking us to set the brake in a rushed voice; Captain acted promptly; and we stopped the aircraft on time and smoothly. I personally did not feel any impact. We stopped with an angle on the blue line. The driver mentioned that the tow bar broke and he is going to disconnect and contact the ramp safety. We communicated with the Ramp; Operations and MX (Maintenance) Control. Captain communicated with the flight attendants and made an announcement to the passengers informing them about the nature of problem. Within 10 minutes or so; with the supervision of our MX personnel on the ground; a new tow truck; new tow bar and a new driver towed us back to the same gate. This time it was very smooth. We found out that a scratch line and a shallow dent exist on the lower right-hand side of the aircraft. It happened by the shallow impact of the fuselage with the roof of the tow truck. Captain wrote up the damage in MX logbook. Dispatch and Flight Operations have been informed. Everybody acted professional during and after the event. Don't know if the tow bar breaking happened because of the angle & the tension exposed to it; or it was the material failure. Tail swap happened shortly after; and we performed the same flight on ship (tail). If a tow truck driver is not happy with the location of the aircraft or if for some reason they are in a tight spot; or any other unusual issue; they can always consider us as a team and communicate any unease with us; so we all figure out how to get out of it. My assumption is that if we were unhooked from the tow bar on the green line; the entire event could have been avoided. It could only cost me a simple radio call to the ramp; I guess.
column123: These are my recollections as I remember them: We were operating Aircraft X operating out of gate X. Aircraft X was operating with MEL APU Inoperative applied. We complied with procedures for engine start with external pneumatic air source & completed the appropriate normal checklists. Ramp tower assigned us a push back onto the blue line. The push back seemed normal with the exception that the AC (aircraft) was at an odd angle. I attributed this to the push crew having to avoid the construction adjacent to N11. The tug driver announced that he would get us over to the blue line & proceeded to turn the jet that direction. At this point I could sense some stress on the tug/towbar combination but nothing that seemed abnormal. As the driver proceeded towards the blue line the noise the towbar was making got louder until we heard what I'd describe as a pop or snap. At this point the jet rolled forward due to forward momentum & the driver or wing walker said set the brakes. I estimate the jet moved forward about 10 feet as I was applying the brakes. We verified that there were no injuries to any of the push back crew & were informed that everyone on the ramp was safe. I stopped the jet as judicially as I could; taking into account that the FA's (flight attendants) were probably standing; conducting their safety demonstration. The driver announced he needed to have the Ramp Safety Supervisor conduct an inspection & we called Line Maintenance to survey the situation. We called the cabin to verify there were no injuries to guests or crew & subsequently a PA was made by me to inform the guests of our situation. Line Maintenance asked us if we could taxi the jet back to gate under power which I declined; not knowing the extent of any possible damage. A new towbar & tug was connected to the jet & we were towed back to gate. After the checklists were completed I proceeded to do a visual inspection; where I found an approximately 5 foot scrape on the underside of the fuselage; outboard of the right side nose gear door. I made another PA from the L1 door area informing the guests that there would be a tail swap & what our new gate was; then made an AC logbook entry describing the damage I observed. The flight proceeded as normal to ZZZ1 after a 2 hour delay to get everything ready on the jet we swapped into. Not sure if time was a big factor or not. The ramp personnel did not seem rushed but we did push back several minutes after departure time due to the jet being fueled late. Parking an A-321 at [this] gate with the current construction process ongoing may present a challenge to the push back crew due to the longer fuselage & trying to avoid the construction area adjacent to gate. My biggest suggestion would be for the push back crew to communicate any difficulty they may be having with any ground operation. In this circumstance we could have easily stopped the jet; set the parking brakes; & requested a taxi from our current position. We strive to comply with directions given; however; sometimes we need to ask to amend those instructions to meet the current situation.

column121: After a successful CAT III landing; we had crossed the two inboard runways and were taxiing north on taxiway towards gate. The FO; who was on the first trip back after one month off; did the after landing flow and confirmed our gate with operations. I thought we were cleared into the gate via spot; but this was not the case.As we were rounding the corner for spot and passing Aircraft Y that was on the line just south of spot; I confirmed with the FO that we were indeed cleared in as I had been distracted switching from low vis taxi diagrams to normal taxi diagrams as the vis was very good; shutting down the Number 2 engine; in addition to the fact that the FO was a soft spoken person. I only mention this as I wasn't surprised I hadn't heard them confirm our clearance to taxi into the gate as I was busy concentrating on the other threats just discussed.As rampers were visible from spot and were marshaling us into the gate; we pulled into the gate normally. Approximately 20 feet short of our final parking spot ground reminded us to contact ramp. We immediately contacted ramp; who was understandably very unhappy with us and we apologized for our error.Needless to say; I take complete responsibility for this incident and am embarrassed I allowed it to happen. I have learned a couple of things from this incident- first; that I need to be extra vigilant when some crew members don't have a lot of recent experience; secondly; when we had discussed that the ground ops were our biggest threat for this CAT III approach; I need to truly take it to heart and be extra cautious to help mitigate the threats present during this segment of our flight.

I proceeded right away to the exit row and briefed both passengers and they both were ok to sit in an exit row. The lady passenger did say that she noticed I had not briefed them before the flight. column121: ATC held the flight high.  Were given clearance to descend to lower altitude. Aircraft was 7;000 feet high on path.  Began expedited descent to catch up to path; ATC then gave level off of FL290.  Around FL320; Pilot Flying noticed traffic appear on TCAS below at FL280 and started to adjust vertical descent rate. Crew could have ignored the high on path profile and also descended slower; but that would have caused problems down the road.
column123: Switched to a frequency that was very busy. The Controller was overwhelmed; we were getting high on the arrival but couldn't get a word in. Finally cleared to descend; the FO who was Pilot Flying started down with the boards out; but weather ahead didn't allow us to speed up to get down. We were 9;000 feet above profile and coming down when we got a TCAS Alert caused by the descent rate. The FO got busy to alleviate it but by the time he pushed a few buttons; it started saying 'Level Off!' So he disconnected everything and leveled the aircraft off. I told the Controller we were leveling off due to a TCAS conflict; but never got an acknowledgment; because [the Controller] was still constantly talking. After the traffic passed we went to our assigned FL290 and [the Controller] asked '(Call sign) verify your level at FL290.' [Controller] didn't have a clue what just happened. I confirmed we were at FL290 and gave us '...cross ZZZZZ at 9;000 feet…' I said we'd do our best but we'd never make ZZZZZ at 9;000 feet. [The Controller] didn't even acknowledge; so we started hurrying down. When we got switched to Approach frequency I told [the Controller] we'd be high at ZZZZZ and the Controller said 'I know; just do your best and descend to 6;000 feet.'With so many aircraft parked; with so many fewer aircraft flying; why is ATC so min-staffed? It seems the new normal is too few Controllers to handle the traffic that's there.

column121: Planned landing in BWI on Runway 33L. We were assigned to park at Gate X. On the current ATIS; it had a NOTAM that said 'Taxi F closed between Taxiway P and Taxiway T.' So we had an expectation bias to exit Runway 33L at Taxiway F and that our taxi-in instructions would be to taxi to Gate X via Taxiway P; E; and T. Partly contributing to this expectation was the fact that the last time I flew a month ago; there was also construction on Taxiway T between Taxiways H and F. We also had an additive condition which I briefed at the beginning of the trip that this was my first trip back to work after not flying for 30 days.However; after landing rollout and upon exiting Runway 33L at Taxiway F; we were given instructions by Tower to taxi to Gate X via 'Taxiway P; T to T; and contact Ground.' I thought the Controller had stuttered when he said 'T to T.' So I made the right turn from F to P; thinking he meant 'P; E; T.' We contacted Ground after making the right turn on to Taxiway P. Ground then told us we had turned the wrong way and should have been going the opposite direction on P; then T2; to T. We asked what Taxiway T2 is; since Taxiway T2 is not depicted anywhere on the 10-9 page. He said it is a new taxiway. I do not recall any NOTAMs saying there is a new Taxiway T2; nor where it is located. There was nothing on the ATIS about it.We did not cause any traffic conflicts and held at our current position so that outbound aircraft could taxi out. We were then cleared to our gate without any further incident.In the future; I will remember to stop the aircraft immediately and query ATC whenever there is any doubt or ambiguity in a taxi clearance. Also recommend that the BWI airport advise on their ATIS and their NOTAMs that there is a new Taxiway T2. Furthermore; I would recommend they use a different name for the new Taxiway; as the two different phrases 1) 'T to...' and 2) 'T2' can be easily misconstrued for each other in a verbal clearance.'

column121: Departure clearance was via ZILLI 4 RNAV Departure with LAUER transition from Runway 25R. Early in takeoff roll; after thrust was set; ECAM 'Hot Brake' annunciated. One of the brakes indicated 300 degrees. My decision was to continue the takeoff. At 'Positive Rate' callout I decided to leave the gear down to cool the brake. AP1 (Autopilot 1) was engaged somewhere before reaching DOCKR waypoint. LAX Tower had us contact SoCal on 124.3. Crossing DOCKR waypoint; the aircraft failed to turn left toward WEILR waypoint. I failed to notice that deviation. About 1- 1.5 miles past DOCKR the FO (First Officer) alerted me about the deviation. I selected HDG (heading) mode and turned left to intercept the course to WEILR waypoint. At Flaps 0 callout I also called for 'Gear Up'. SoCal gave us Direct TANDY at about that time. Flight was uneventful from then on. The course deviation was because I did not ensure NAV (navigation) mode after reaching 400 feet AGL. I allowed the hot brake and gear down situation to distract me from flying the aircraft.
column123: We are departing from Runway 25R; ZILLI4 RNAV Departure. To LAUER transition. When we passed DOCKER; we supposed to make left turn to WEILER; however we kept going straight on heading 251. So; I pointed to Captain to make left turn. As we are turning left; ATC gave us direct to TANDY. The curse deviation was because we did not confirm NAV (navigation) selected. We were in HDG (heading) mode.
