column121: Upon arrival to Gate X in ZZZ we were asked to call OPS. The Captain called them and we were reminded that we should call ramp before entering the ramp next time. I couldn't believe that I had made such a mistake after over XXXXX hours on the fleet and almost XX years of flying at the company with many many ZZZ arrivals. I looked at the Captain and I said; 'I am sorry I have no excuse;' which is how I felt. I then called the ramp and apologized. I called them on the frequency that I had set on stby at Comm 2 prior to the top of descend when I was setting up for our arrival to ZZZ. As we debriefed I started questioning the why of my mistake and I realize that I am taking for granted my lack of situational awareness as a result of my 7 month absence from flying.When I went to ZZZ1 I was very serious about it; during my OE trip I was still very conscious of my weaknesses because of my lack of recency but now as I am finishing my second trip after OE I feel that 'I am back' which obviously I am not. There were a few other threats that contributed to my mistake. We had thoroughly briefed a [Runway] XXL arrival and taxi in but had spent way less time discussing [Runway] XYR. Our set up for XYR and execution was great but created a distraction and increased the workload. We cleared XYR on Taxiway 1; were given instruction to cross XYL on 1 and call Ground. Both myself and the Captain were anticipating taxi via 1; but when I called Ground we were told 'Taxi via 2; 3 hold short of 4 and at the half way point on November call Ground at XXX.YY.' A lot of information to digest especially if you aren't very familiar with the airport; you have been out for a long time (this is the Captain's first trip after RQ (Recurrent Qualification) training and OE). We were both expecting to go straight on Taxiway 1.I told the Captain to stop. Which he very nicely did as he was also figuring out that we were not suppose to continue on 1. The Captain taxied as instructed; I called Ground Control and was told to taxi via 3; 4 to the gate. After making the turn on 4 we were instructed to give way to opposite direction traffic on 4 that was turning on 5. We then were told to turn right on 5 and continue via 6 to the gate. As I am debriefing this I realized that ZZZ unlike ZZZ1 or ZZZ2 doesn't instruct you to contact ramp. They simply say taxi to the gate/ramp. Finally as we were approaching the gate area I was trying to time my APU start so it is running when we come to a full stop; and I also noticed that there was a lot of vehicle traffic traveling parallel to us and I was a little concerned on whether or not they will stop at X7 for our turn. There was no traffic in the alley and we taxied to Gate X uneventfully.

column121: We were assigned the ZZZZZX RNAV departure off Runway X at ZZZ.  The clearance was to climb via the SID; top altitude of FL230 was set in the MCP. All the fixes and altitude restrictions were correct in the FMC; I was the PM; the airplane was light; so we had a good climb rate. The PF was hand flying as we approached the first fix which has a crossing restriction of at or below 10;000. LNAV/VNAV and VNAV PTH was selected. Close to the first fix the PF called for the autopilot as the airplane started its turn to cross the fix that placed the sun directly into our face which affected our visibility. As I turned my head to get my sunshade; ATC asked if we were going to stop at 10;000 feet; we got as high as 10;300 the PF turned the autopilot off and went down to 10;000.  In this situation I think turning the autopilot on earlier would have helped. Also anticipating the sun and take steps earlier to mitigate the effects of the sun would have helped us to maintain better situational awareness.
column123: Our departure SID was the ZZZZZX.  Our departure plan was for Runway YYR per the ATIS.  During taxiout our runway assignment was changed to Runway X with the same SID.  My First Officer ran the runway change checklist and briefed me on the changes to the SID departing Runway X.  During the climbout I called for the autopilot sometime prior to 10;000 feet.  There is a fix named ZZZZZ that has a crossing altitude of 10;000 or below.  Our automation level was LNAV/VNAV with the autopilot engaged.  Approaching 10;000 feet I noticed that the FMA went to VNAV PTH.  About that time; I also got a face full of morning sunrise.  It briefly made it hard to see and I had not deployed my sunshade or put on my sunglasses yet.  When my vision adjusted to the glare of the sun I noticed that the aircraft did not level at 10;000 feet.  It overshot the altitude by 300 feet.  I disengaged the autopilot and returned to 10;000 feet.  The Controller did query us on our altitude during the overshoot.  One other piece of useful information is that the aircraft was very light.  I'm wondering if the system was respecting a G-Load vs. an altitude because I have no other explanation as to why it did not level at 10;000 feet.  Factors that I feel contributed to this event were the runway change on the ground; high airport elevation; sunrise; fatigue and maybe our light weight.  Next time I will not accept the immediate line up and wait from ATC.  Instead I would re-brief the SID so that my situational awareness would be better.

column121: There was a line of storms crossing ZZZ.  We were told to expect holding at ZZZZZ.  We ended up holding.  We did one turn and then we got sent back on the arrival.  We ultimately got vectors from ZZZZZ1 and were following one Company aircraft.  The plan was to fly northeast about 30 miles at 5;000 ft to go around the weather and then come back south to land. Then the airspeed dropped to approximately 140 knots and the autopilot and autothrottles were disconnected.  I announced to the PM (Pilot Monitoring) that we were in windshear and I added power and started a climbing turn to the left.  The aircraft started accelerating and climbing; and we retracted the flaps.  The highest speed I saw during the recovery was 220 knots.  During this period; airspeed; pitch attitude and altitude was very difficult to control and we encountered what we believed to be severe turbulence.  The PM told ATC that we had severe turbulence and windshear and that we were turning to the left and climbing.  We tried to level at 5;000 ft and flew southwest.  ATC told us to climb to 6;000 ft for traffic.  I added power and the aircraft responded poorly.  Eventually; we got a climb going; but we were unable to stop the climb at 6;000 ft.  The aircraft continued to about 6;450 ft and ATC asked us what altitude we were going to.  PM told them that we were trying to get to 6;000 ft but were having a difficult time maintaining altitude with the turbulence.  On our way back down to 6;000 ft we got a TCAS TA for traffic at our 1-2 o'clock at 700-800 ft above us.  I continued down to about 5;800 ft to make sure we avoided that traffic.  We continued southwest and diverted to ZZZ1. If we had asked to stay in holding until we saw that the line had passed even further northeast of the field; it would have prevented this.  We had about 13.0 of fuel when we entered holding; so we had the time. [We were] unable to maintain assigned altitude; heading; and airspeed due to windshear and severe turbulence.

column121: I was operating flight to ZZZ. The weather was good and after detecting inadequate fuel planning and requesting additional fuel we departed on time and flew the filed flight plan. We were clear direct to ZZZZZ. Our ATIS was showing that we were expecting to land on Runway XX left.Knowing it was early in the morning we did anticipate a possible runway opening of either XX right or XY. When we were about three minutes from ZZZZZ; We were given the instructions to depart ZZZZZ on a heading to intercept the XY localizer. Although we had planned for the possibility of XY; this was a fairly abrupt and last-minute instruction from ATC. As briefed; this falls under the 'slam dunk' which was is always a threat; as I briefed for departure.We departed ZZZZZ on the assigned heading and began to set up for the intercept of the XY localizer. We were given a descent to 9000; then very quickly a decent to 6000; then a speed reduction to 170 and then briefly after that another speed reduction to 160 (until 5 out). All of this seem to happen in [a] very quick sequence. I was set up to intercept; set up to descend and began to slow down According to our instructions.We established our self on the ILS [Runway] XY without incident but when I realized that we needed to slow down; I called for flaps 22 'out of sequence.' (Typically flaps 22 is called with 'Gear Down'). I had already called for flaps nine; and just naturally called for flaps 22 knowing I needed to slow down.My First Officer (FO) followed the command and put in flaps 22. I naturally look down and scanned my instruments as I always do after a change command and I immediately realized that we were above the 200 knot threshold. I immediately took action - I pressed in the TCS (Control Steering) button; pitched up and began to slow down. As quickly and as safely as I could I brought the aircraft under the 200 knot limitation and completed the rest of the flight without incident.Upon landing I called my dispatcher; explained what happened; maintenance came out; they completed a full inspection and downloaded the information from the airplanes computer. We swapped airplanes so that the inspection could be completed and by the time we landed in ZZZ1; I had heard back from the maintenance supervisor. He told me that the inspection was completed no defects were found and the airplane was returned to service.I detected the problem. I always do a brief scan during critical phases of flight to confirm that the command and input was followed. So I did my scan after calling for Flaps 22 and immediately realized the error. I did not alert FO; as it was not necessary and I simply made the adjustments to the pitch and speed by using the TCS button. I feel there were 2 factors contributing cause to this event. The first was the additional time we had to spend on considering our planned fuel situation. This was definitely an added concern that both FO and I collaborated on before we even left the gate. Then; as Runway XY was opened and we received the 'Slam Dunk' vectors onto the ILS XY; was a second major contributor to this situation. My suggestion as to how to avoid this situation is to simply avoid the 'slam dunk' vectors. Had I asked for better vectors; I'm certain that this situation could and would have been avoided.

The FO and I both noticed and mentioned that the landing fuel numbers were very low for our standard operation. The NAV Log section of the release showed 1;829 lbs. which is planned fuel minus taxi and fuel burn. But the fuel calculation section showed 1;660 lbs. This concerned both the FO and I; as such a long flight with very little fuel to be landing with. We both discussed that the airplane was [under] fueled by at least 200 lbs. Therefore we both felt landing with 2;000 lbs. or worst case scenario 1;800 lbs. was low but a safer and acceptable number. The performance manual shows around 1;700 lbs. at 5;000 ft. is around 45 minutes of fuel. Knowing our fuel was tight; we did what we could to help conserve fuel by delaying the second engine start as long as possible; and we attempted a Flight Level Change climb by several and normal intermediate level off altitudes with only 7 miles in the opposite direction. We continued to monitor our fuel burn. Upon our initial descent; we noticed we had burned more than planned; but we had received a shortcut and still calculated landing with around 1;800 lbs. On a few turns before final; the right fuel gauge began to flash amber at us then continued to flash in and out as fuel moved around throughout the final approach. Upon landing; we had around 1;800 lbs. of fuel. I feel this margin of safety is extremely low for a safety conscious airline and program. The fuel management program should be providing us with more fuel not less fuel. We were [under] fueled and received no undue delays and were proactive in managing and conserving fuel. Our end result was landing with 1;800 lbs. of fuel. In a medium case scenario; if the airport shuts down for an aircraft emergency or anything else; a go around diversion to the closest company destination (ZZZ2 is 78 miles away); say 25 to 30 minutes at 8;000 ft. (1;100 lbs.); would have me landing with 400 lbs. of fuel and I would have had to make that decision immediately. ZZZ3 is the next closest at 117 miles. That is also if those stations both have personnel staffed to service the aircraft. While legal; and probably acceptable; this practice seems to create an unreasonable reduced margin of safety standards with the trade-off being cost savings. In addition; as a Check Airmen and experienced pilot; I have more wherewithal to be neurotically monitoring developing situations; and weather. I can see an average pilot easily being forced into a no-win situation or very unsafe situation with dire outcome.[We] detected and attempted to manage [the issue] upon review of the release and even with proactive measures; the aircraft still landed with an uncomfortable amount of fuel. [We] took proactive fuel burn reductions with no changes in landing fuel. The airline's new fuel management program and a lack of safety margins created by the program [were contributing factors].I suggest changing the standard practice of providing 45 minutes of cruise fuel from flight level altitudes and provide the crew with an accurate and manageable 45 minutes of fuel near 10;000 ft. which is where most people will need that extra fuel in the case of holding; delays; reroutes and diversions which more likely occur below the flight levels. Add fuel and increase the amount of minimum fuel required to be on the airplane for dispatch.

I sat in the row waiting for answers as to the protocols on what we were to do next. I touched all overhead bins around row X; the bathroom; bulkhead working station; and all surrounding areas that all could have been affected by this customer who tested positive. column121: Climbing out of ZZZ; at approximately 18;500 feet; we heard a muffled bang and felt yaw. The engine instruments indicated the number two engine EGT was near zero; and it was no longer producing thrust. I asked the FO to tell ATC we required a level off at FL190; and requested priority handling. I then directed the FO to read the QRH Engine Failure or Shutdown checklist.We asked ATC for return vectors to ZZZ. The landing runway was Runway XX; and strong; gusty winds favored this choice. We relayed number of souls onboard and fuel remaining to ATC.After the Engine Failure checklist was complete and the engine was secured; I spoke with the FAs; immediately followed by a brief PA to the passengers. I told them the number two engine has failed; we're returning to ZZZ; and we should be on the ground in 10 to 15 minutes.The remaining 'clean-up' checklists went well; and to my knowledge all steps were completed. We were a bit rushed due to our proximity to ZZZ. In hindsight we should have asked for slightly extended vectors to give us more time; as the approach brief was glossed over. Although it was clear VMC and we were familiar with the airport; it would have been best to do a standard brief. Also; I should have considered restarting the engine; as there was no abnormal vibration; but just occasional slight buffet. We made an uneventful; under max weight; Flaps 15 landing.The rescue trucks met us with one on Taxiway 1; north of the far end of Runway XX; and another group; I believe on the Apron near the fire station. We easily exited the runway on Taxiway 2X; and we told them we did not need any assistance; but to follow us to the gate. ATC and Crash Rescue were flawless. They were helpful; did not interfere; and followed up where necessary.Other agencies also contacted us in a professional manner; and we spoke to them in turn: Dispatch; Maintenance; Operations team; Chief Pilot; and [other] Management.
column123: Preflight and takeoff were without incident until climb through 18;000 feet. As the aircraft was climbing through 18;000 feet. I felt an abnormal airframe vibration along with thumping sound that seemed to come from the right side of the airplane (lasting a few seconds). Within a few seconds the #2 Eng Fail indication appeared accompanied with a roll back and aircraft yaw. Almost immediately the 'A' Flight Attendant called up and inquired if everything was okay. I informed her we lost the #2 engine; and we would call her back. The Captain told me to call ATC [and advise them] and get vectors back to ZZZ. We accomplished the Engine Fire or Engine Severe Damage or Separation Checklist as we began our descent back into ZZZ. The Captain briefed the Flight Attendants and informed the Passengers about our situation. During our descent; we encountered occasional airframe vibrations. We also completed the One Engine Inoperative Landing Checklist on the way into ZZZ. The Captain flew a visual approach backed up with the ILS to Runway XX. After landing we taxied to the gate (IAW Brake Cooling).

column121: Aircraft X apparently hit a set of stairs on pushback with their right wing tip unbeknownst to the crew or Marshaller. A ground crew member saw it and called it in to his supervisor; who called it in to the Ops (Airport Operations). The plane at this point was on takeoff roll and wasn't in contact with Ops via radio anymore. After getting airborne; Ops took it into their own hands and called Tower and told them to have the flight return to field. I received an message from the crew asking why the return to field; which is when I started to make calls. This happened while the crew was at 3;000 feet and turning around. Crew landed uneventfully and the plane was taken out of service with visible damage to the right wingtip. No request was issued for a return to field as I felt in the short time frame; and with how busy the crew would have been setting up an unexpected approach; that it would have been unsafe to add more to their workload. Operations staff need to be fully aware of their limitations in regards to operational control of flights. Perhaps there needs to be a rapid communication procedure for the ground personnel; as they had to make several calls to get the information to someone who could have made a difference quicker.
column123: After we took off and checked on with ZZZ Departure Control we were advised by the controller that Company wanted us to return to the airport. Upon questioning; the controller did not know the reason. I sent an ACARS message to our Dispatcher advising of an air turn back and asked why. His response was that he didn't know but would find out. We set up for the return to ZZZ and landed uneventfully and taxied to parking. Upon aircraft shutdown and secure a ZZZ maintenance representative met us inside the cockpit to advise us that the right wingtip possibly came into contact with a set of crew stairs during block out. We took a look at the wing and there was some minor damage to the right outboard leading edge slat just inside the right navigation light. At all times during the block out we were under the guidance and direction of the marshaller. Appropriate logbook entry made and reports submitted by both myself and First Officer. Reflecting upon blocking out; after engine start we cleared the mechanic and ascertained immediate area left and right were clear; I signaled the marshaller across the ramp and on the nose that we were ready to taxi out. We were marshaled straight out into the alley and given the signal for a left turn into the alley followed by a wave-off and salute. During the initial block out taxi roll; the First Officer mentioned the crew stairs seemed close; but from my position the stairs did not appear to be encroaching on the taxi lane and I continued to follow the marshaller's instructions. All marshaling signals were consistent with the aircraft being clear of any obstacles; and at no time did the marshaller give us a stop signal during the taxi out; nor did we feel any bump from the right wingtip possibly making contact with the crew stairs. I do not know if there was a wing-walker on the right wing due proximity of ground equipment between our aircraft and the aircraft to our right. I do recall a white ramp vehicle was encroached in the clear area to our right as we were blocking out; but the vehicle backed up out of the way. Recommendations: wing-walkers; all ground equipment clear; equipment safe boxes painted on the ground around the aircraft like in ZZZ1.

column123: In ZZZ; I called ZZZ Clearance and received our IFR clearance to ZZZ1 at approximately XA:30 p.m. local time. After a slight ramp delay; we pushed back around XB:10 p.m. The Tower at ZZZ closes at XB:00. We made all our CTAF calls and took off in clear VFR conditions. I checked in with departure at 1;400 feet. At that time Departure let us know we did not get our IFR release on the ground.I recommend once a Tower closes; even with a clearance received prior to closing; always contact Departure on the ground prior to departing and pick up your IFR release to destination. The cause was some confusion with already receiving the clearance and picking up the release after the Tower closed. Lesson learned is as described above; once Tower closes you need to pick up your clearance from Departure prior to taking off.

column121: During climb after departing ZZZ; we experienced light clear icing; which began around 12;000 ft and ended around 20;000 ft. During this time; we noted STALL PROT ICE SPEED status message displayed; as well as the WING and both ENG BLEED VALVE OPEN advisory messages displayed. Roughly around 24;000 feet and still climbing; we experienced a master warning EICAS message (A-I WING 1 LEAK). The FO was flying; so I asked him to maintain control of the airplane; and to handle the radios while I ran the QRH checklist. The checklist drove us to press the wing ice protection button out; which we did. Almost immediately the EICAS message disappeared from view. I brought up the ice protection schematic on my MFD; and verified the wing valves were closed. We continued and completed the checklist.We exited icing conditions around 20;000 feet; and it appeared that clear skies were ahead and above us. We decided to continue the flight and landed safely at ZZZ1.We decided that icing conditions were not forecast or reported on our WSI app along our route of flight. We also could not see any apparent icing conditions ahead. With this in mind; ultimately I decided that we could continue the flight safely to ZZZ1. I also did not feel that this warranted an in-flight call to Dispatch and Maintenance; however; I did call maintenance control after we reached the gate at ZZZ1. I informed the controller what we experienced; and we both agreed that a discrepancy no longer existed and therefore did not make an AML entry. At the end of our day; I made the next Captain aware of our event verbally when we got to ZZZ2.I wish that I had taken a picture after the wing valves were closed on the ice protection schematic on my MFD. I think we handled the situation well as a crew; and we both agreed that we could continue the flight safely.

column121: Upon arriving at MSO airport on [Date] at approximately XA:00 the winds were not favorable to execute the ILS to RWY (Runway) 12. The weather conditions to perform the RNAV GPS D were alternating between ceiling and visibility going below minimum conditions. We were communicating with Dispatch along the way and were discussing diverting to our first alternate; which [was] Billings (BIL). The ceiling and visibility at MSO was above minimums at time of arrival. We started the RNAV approach with a circle to land on RWY 30. After crossing the final approach fix at 6;800 ft.; and descending to our MDA of 4;700 ft.; we started to have some ground contact. The FO (First Officer) said that he saw the PAPI lights to the right of us. The approach did not allow for us to circle to land northeast of RWY 12/30. The only way to commence the circle was to fly over the airport and circle around to the west. We briefly discussed circling to the west and quickly decided that it would be unsafe to circle around the airport at night in low visibility with LLWS (Low Level Wind Shear) conditions in mountainous terrain. During the decision making phase I had inadvertently disconnected the auto throttle. We continued to the missed approach point. As we went around I had realized that the MAP fix was not in the box. As we looked at the approach plate and quickly made a climbing left turn on a heading of about 340. We asked ATC for a heading while we headed in the proper direction. Once WENKE was back in the box we realized we were right on course.At approximately 8;000 ft. we were back in radar contact and was giving a vector off the final approach course. ATC asked us if we wanted to commence another approach or divert to a different airport. After discussing the conditions that we saw and weather forecast to be deteriorating; we unanimously decided that it would be unsafe to conduct a circle to land night approach based on the current weather and forecasted conditions.We then told ATC that we were going to divert to BIL. We sent ACARS message to Dispatch telling them we were diverting as well. After landing at BIL; Dispatch told us that we were to refuel and proceed back to MSO. Dispatch then said the weather was not good enough to go back and was delaying our departure. After waiting about an hour Dispatch said the winds were improving and we should be able to do the ILS RWY 12 back into MSO. We departed BIL for MSO with BIL as our alternate if we could not get in. We executed the ILS to RWY 12. While in Billings we contacted ATC and they told us at that time that they did not have radar until about 8;000 ft. The controller said that he was not working at that time but discussed with the previous controller that we were right where we were supposed to be and we said we just were at a high work load and wanted to verify with them that we were on course.High workload with low ceilings; LLWS; at night in mountainous terrain. Having to circle with visibility below what was projected and inadvertently disconnected auto throttles to land.I feel like this approach is not a safe approach to do at night. I spoke with several carriers that land at this airport and this approach is not authorized.

column121: Crew was descending into ZZZ Airport at about [night] time. Weather revealed winds 350 with good visibility and MVFR conditions. With the higher winds out of the north; the crew elected to fly the RNP Approach which requires the PAPI to be operational to fly the approach. A review of the NOTAMs revealed this would not be an issue; though the REIL was out of service to this runway. Icing conditions on the approach prompted to crew to conduct a flap full landing with ice numbers. Additionally; Tower mentioned that they would be closing just prior to our arrival. The Captain; myself; briefed the autothrottles would be disconnected on the arrival; with the autopilot off once established inbound. I disconnected the autothrottles and left the autopilot on as briefed. We continued to configure through the landing checklist and saw the runway on the approach. Once we rounded out on final; I disconnected the autopilot and began slowing to our approach speed when the lights at the airport clicked off. I briefly shallowed the descent anticipating the possibility of a go-around and had my First Officer turn the lights to high which failed to bring the PAPI back online. Being VMC and within required company parameters for a safe approach; I inquired to my First Officer if he was comfortable with continuing under the conditions which he was. I corrected descent angle and the flight landed without any further incident.This was the flight crew's first time flying this approach; my first RNP approach in a while; and my fourth night landing in about 2.5 months. This RNP Approach requires the PAPI to be operational to use. With there being no PAPI NOTAM; it was determined that it would be appropriate to fly it. After we had landed we found that the Tower; attempting to enable the pilot controlled lighting; had inadvertently switched all lights off. This was corrected with my First Officer turning the lights back on but the action failed to turn the PAPI on. The ATIS had called for gusty winds out of the north but; once we were established on final; I noticed we had a quartering tailwind at 15 kt. which caused me some confusion. The light issue and shifting winds prompted me to shallow out the approach due to the possibility of a go-around. However; with the airport lights on minus the PAPI and in VMC conditions; I figured the safest course of action was to continue given the fact that we were within parameters required to continue the approach and land. My thinking was a go-around late at night; in mountainous terrain and icing conditions with a possible changing weather pattern; may not be the best idea given we were still within tailwind parameters and touchdown requirements for landing. To me; this incident illustrates how important it is to appropriately manage [non-forecasted] distractions; especially during high workload phases. Additionally; it's imperative that we strive to remain current even during prolonged periods of stagnation.When weather is in vicinity; ensure [that] the most accurate weather is obtained from Tower if necessary. Relay concerns of airport issues to ATC or go-around. Be wary of Tower closures near arrivals to airports. A reminder that higher elevation airports present unique challenges which must be reviewed and briefed prior to flying into them. A reminder to chair fly approaches to destination airports; especially if the approaches you intend to follow are unfamiliar. The importance of maintaining appropriate approach currency. Speed management and adequate monitoring during all flight phases. A reminder to fly the airplane first and; if mounting distractions cause confusion; go-around.
column123: I briefed the descent and approach with Captain; Captain as pilot flying. Reviewed FMS approach briefing card. Verified all NOTAMs and approach requirements per the chart and current ATIS. Moments later we both acknowledged that we didn't see the PAPI to the left. CA (Captain) asked if I found the circumstances to land safe versus a missed approach late at night and snow in the forecast. [We] agreed it would be safe to land given the real time circumstances. Great example in how reality and goal for safety require pilot judgment.

column121: It was the Captain's leg on a return flight from ZZZ when we were given the ZZZZZ3 SID. We were given a standard take off clearance from Runway XXL (no heading; altitude; or fix to fly) and I; as the pilot monitoring; engaged the autopilot modes as directed. After double-checking I correctly engaged NAV mode; we were still in HDG with the only white needle navigation being from ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 and then on the rest of the departure. Since we were still in HDG mode with what I remember was runway heading bugged; we were heading directly for the terrain off of the departure end of XXL. We received hasty instructions from ATC to turn left immediately to get away from the terrain; which we complied with. We were in VMC and could clearly see the terrain; which we had already climbed above when the instructions from ATC came through to start the immediate turn. We never received a GPWS terrain alert. Once established heading back to ZZZZZ on the departure; the Captain had disengaged and reengaged the NAV button to finally arm FMS mode. ATC then advised us to resume the departure and continue our assigned climb altitude to 17;000 feet. No further communications between us and ATC about what had happened. The rest of the flight went on normally and without incident. Really make sure on RNAV departures that when you select the NAV button that the FMS mode activates and if needed spin the heading bug to the headings provided on the charts to avoid conflicts like this.

column121: The crew departed ZZZ on time after calling maintenance to reset a Rudder Trim Limiter ECAM malfunction. Pushback; start; taxi; takeoff and climb out were uneventful. Passing FL260 for a cruise altitude of FL270 the First Officer (Pilot Monitoring) identified a flashing oil quantity advisory reading and a low oil pressure indication on the #1 engine system display. Due to the aircraft's momentum and vertical rate of climb the Captain (Pilot Flying) elected to level off at FL270 as planned. Initially the zero oil quantity and low 60 PSI pressure indication were not accompanied by an ECAM message and system status indicated normal. Within a couple of minutes a series of intermittent ECAM cautions and warnings occurred leading to an engine shutdown condition. The amber ENG 1 OIL LO PR Caution illuminated first on the ECAM display. The crew responded by initiating the company non-normal checklist strategy. The Captain announced 'my aircraft' then the First Officer verified that the ECAM was not a Quick Action or ECAM exception item. The Captain elected to remain flying and also took control of the radio. It was a crew awareness only caution so the FO (First Officer) then checked the QRH for follow up items. This Caution does not direct the crew to adjust thrust settings. During this process the caution [message] cleared itself without any inputs from the crew but the zero oil quantity and 60 PSI indications remained. At this point the ECAM display was clear and system status indicated normal. Shortly thereafter the red ENG 1 LO PR warning illuminated on the ECAM display. This occurred intermittently 3 times and then cleared itself each time resulting in a normal system status display on the ECAM. Oil quantity remained at zero and pressure was now steady at 40 PSI on the system display. These intermittent ECAM warnings lasted for approximately 2-3 seconds and then cleared to a normal status for roughly the same amount of time. The next time the ECAM warning illuminated it remained steady and the crew followed the ENG 1 LO PR warning procedures and shutdown the engine. The crew notified Center and requested a radar vector descent to final for the engine out approach at ZZZ1. The non-normal indications initially occurred just prior to the ETP (equal time point) between ZZZ and ZZZ1. However by the time the ECAM directed engine shutdown the flight had progressed passed the ETP and was at a normal descent point for ZZZ1. Dispatch was called using the iPad crew phone and notified of the nature of the emergency and decision to land at ZZZ1. The flight attendants and passengers were briefed about the Precautionary Landing at ZZZ1 and the possibility of airport fire vehicles near the aircraft. After shutting down the engine and notifying ATC; the crew requested and was given a vector and descent direct to a left 10 NM base at ZZZ1. Descent and approach were very stable and normal. The Captain flew the descent and approach with both the autopilot and auto thrust on. Crew requested ARFF (airport rescue fire department) for the landing and cleared the runway for a brief inspection of the engine. On request of the crew the fire department followed the aircraft to the gate. Shutdown at the gate and passenger deplaning were normal. Note: ATC handling by ZZZ Center; ZZZ1 Approach and Tower were outstanding. Handoff from Tower to ARFF at ZZZ1 was seamless and well coordinated. Flight Attendant performance was also outstanding and the passengers remained well informed throughout the emergency. Although oil fault indications were somewhat intermittent and erratic the fact that multiple independent sensors indicated a problem caused the crew to shutdown the #1 engine when directed by the ENG LO PR Warning ECAM. After the flight; maintenance personnel initially reported normal engine oil quantity on a sight gauge even though the engine instrument remained at zero. Initially crew suspects a partial blockage or pump failure in the system without oil loss. The engine oil quantity and pressure indications were initially both alarming and confusing. As the adrenaline level increased for the crew due to the perception there would be an engine shutdown there was also a level of doubt that the indications were accurate. Low oil pressure on the engine instrument should be accompanied by a Low Pressure ECAM Caution or Warning. Why did the pressure remain steady in the amber range with zero on the quantity? This is an uncomfortable situation because our training does not address multiple oil failures without ECAM warnings. It puts the flight crew into one of those gray areas where a Captain is expected to make a decision based on the information he has on hand in a situation not covered in training. The natural instinct of a pilot is to shutdown an engine before complete oil loss to prevent a catastrophic failure. In this occurrence engine indications identified a problem well in advance of ECAM warnings. Yet crew training and aircraft procedures generally do not address engine shutdown without ECAM warning checklist direction. Should crews be given shutdown discretion in the absence of ECAM warnings and checklist? In this situation the Captain elected to continue as the Pilot Flying while the crew worked through the non-normal checklist strategy. Even though most aspects of company's non-normal strategy were performed correctly the overall pace and structure were hampered by the Captain continuing to fly. In this case the checklist strategy would have been better managed if the Captain had delegated flying to the FO. For example; when the ECAM directed the 'Engine Master Switch-Off' both pilots confirmed it was the #1 engine but the Captain positioned it to off. Procedure dictates that the non-flying pilot position the switch to off.

column121: On descent into ZZZ; we momentarily exceeded Vmo by approximately 1 knot for less than 3 seconds. I later completed an AML entry and notified Maintenance Control. There was no operational impact.   I was the CA and PF. While on descent into ZZZ; ATC halted our descent at FL240. This put us behind our VPATH solution. When we were next cleared to descend; I elected to go into Vertical Speed Mode; selecting 2000 FPM in order to recapture the VPATH. The task saturation over the next few seconds took my scan away from our airspeed; and we surpassed and we surpassed XXX knots; our 'barber pole' airspeed. I immediately disconnected the AP; overrode the autothrottles and raised the nose of the aircraft. The max airspeed reached [was] XXY knots for a second or two; before returning to green numbers. There appeared to be no adverse effect on the aircraft or passengers. I later completed an AML entry and notified Maintenance Control. I had not flown in 3 weeks; due to my inactivity on reserve status. I now know that I must be more diligent on my scan; especially when I have not flown in a while. column121: Takeoff and initial climb from DCA; Runway 01. Captain Pilot Monitoring; First Officer Pilot Flying. Pre-flight duties completed and route review completed at gate. Engine start and taxi was normal to Runway 01; before takeoff checklist completed to the line before crossing Runway 04; below the line after crossing Runway 04. As we taxied to runway; Aircraft Y was cleared to cross Runway 04 before us on another taxiway then into the box. As we were approaching Runway 01; Tower Controller asked Aircraft Y if they were ready for departure; Aircraft Y responded they needed 2 minutes. Tower asked if we were ready for departure and we responded we were ready; completed final checklist items. We lined up on Runway 01 and were cleared for takeoff. I do not recall checking FMA for NAV annunciation as we taxied on to the runway and checked final for traffic. Light passenger load/light takeoff weight. After takeoff; aircraft climb was rapid with a quick change to Departure frequency. We were at clean-up altitude quickly after takeoff. After thrust set to climb power and frequency change to departure (prior to check-in on frequency with departure) I noticed FMA annunciation was RWY TRK and we had not yet initiated a left turn for the departure. I told the First Officer to turn left; which he accomplished; initially coming left to approximately a 290-300 degree heading. I cross checked Nav Display for 1 NM circle around point PLVIA and outside references. I do not believe we entered Prohibited Area 56A or Prohibited Area 56B. After initial left turn; we then turned back to the right to rejoin the departure. A turn to point ADAXE would have required an aggressive right turn; so we turned to rejoin the departure between ADAXE and BEBLE After turning to rejoin departure I checked-in with departure control when they asked if we were on frequency. Remainder of the flight was uneventful.This was my (Captain) first flight back on the line after several months away due to combination of leave of absence and quarantine for close contact with [someone] with COVID-19. I had just completed recurrent training the week before this flight. In the pre-flight briefing the First Officer had noted that with light passenger loads the aircraft takeoff and climb would happen quickly. Given my lack of recent flying; I should not have accepted departure prior to the aircraft in front of us on the ground; even though I felt I was in the green. I was slow to notice we had not initiated left turn on the departure where I would normally expect to begin a turn; possibly due to lack of recent line flying experience; the combination of quick climb after takeoff to acceleration altitude and frequency change slowing my monitoring and recognition of aircraft not being in NAV mode. Though I did direct the pilot flying to make a left turn; if I had done so earlier we would have been able to maintain the departure track without tracking close to Prohibited Area 56.The time from takeoff to overshooting the departure turn on takeoff from Runway 01 at DCA happens fast! I would like to see a similar event during simulator training to illustrate just how quickly you can get close to Prohibited Area 56 after takeoff from DCA when combining a timely distraction with lack of aircraft going in to NAV mode. PLVIA with 1 NM ring on NAV display did assist me as a barrier for this event.

column121: My first trip 'solo' as CO [Commanding Officer] was going well. I had a good crew and we performed well as a crew. On arrival after receiving vectors for approach to Runway XXL and established; the PF was looking around - sighting...flaps were at 15...I was focused on the required speed and frequency change at ZZZZZ; and the Relief Pilot was daydreaming as well.  At 1;000 feet the PF called 'stable'...and I saw his speed and ILS tracking were spot-on...and then we both realized at the same time that the gear was still UP and the flaps were at 15!!  He called gear down and flaps 25; which I did out of habit as response to the fallout.  I realized then; at the same time he did; that the approach was NOT going to work; at which point we both called 'go-around'.  The go-around was at 800 feet AFL and was UGLY!!  Go-arounds from this altitude are often UGLY!!  The subsequent vectors and second approach went as it should and we landed safely...the desired outcome.  The debrief at the gate was thorough and each of us contributed; as well as took appropriate blame for our individual contribution to such an embarrassing and actually humiliating event.We each had recently been through a simulator check.  The Relief Pilot and I (CO) each having less than 40 hours in type; and the FO having just returned from a 7 month period of not flying.  Combined total flight time of this 3-man crew exceeded X0;000 hours.  However on this day we were each victims of a few different causal factors:  fatigue...we had just flown XA+45 hours from ZZZZ; neither of us slept well the previous night; and we were each the victims of relative inactivity due to COVID-related restrictions; each of these led us to be distracted; lackadaisical; and only partially effective as a crew.Causal factors contributing to this outrageously ridiculous display of airman-ship are deemed to be at least the following: longer layovers; [lack of] more well established activity schedules during our layovers-even during times of social restrictions; [lack of] better food onboard flights for crews; [lack of] better procedural discipline is possibly another even considering each of us had been through simulator training very recently.

column121: On Aircraft X to ZZZ; we were given a turn to base for a visual approach to XR inside the final approach fix 600 feet above the FAF.  We realized we weren't going to be able to complete the approach under the stable approach criteria so I called the go-around at 1;000 feet AGL. Once we got the aircraft climbing I called ATC saying that we are going around. ATC said climb and maintain 3000 feet; we were already climbing and had a high rate of climb because we only had about XX people on board.  While we were cleaning up the aircraft and setting up the FCP; I realized our Climb rate was high and we were approaching 3;000 feet quickly. I said 'watch your altitude' and asked ATC if we could get 3;500 feet. ATC denied it and said to maintain 3;000 feet and contact departure. Unfortunately; the correction of bringing the nose down and power back happened too late and we climbed through our altitude by about 200 feet. The correction came and we corrected our altitude back to 3;000 feet. On the second attempt approach tried to do the same thing to us again however we denied it and asked to be vectored for the ILS.  ATC turned us to intercept the final approach course too close and I told them we won't be able to do it due to us having a tailwind; and that we are going to need to intercept it from the other side. I told ATC the intercept we would need. On that attempt we completed the approach successfully and landed with no further complications.Due to having a poor vector for the approach; and no warning of a close approach; we ended up high on a visual approach to Runway XR. For that reason we decided to go-around. The altitude assigned to us was only about 1;200 feet above the altitude we decided to go-around at. By the time we got the aircraft configured for the go around and contacted ATC we were even closer to that altitude. Due to having a high workload in that environment; a light weight; and being already close to the altitude assigned to us the climb rate was too high when I made the call out to the Captain. I also tried to rectify the situation before it happened by asking ATC for a higher altitude but was denied.Deny the visual approach and ask ATC to just fly the ILS to give us more time. Say unable instead of asking for a higher altitude.
column123: Today on Aircraft X to ZZZ we were given a turn inside of the FAF for Runway XR into ZZZ. ZZZ Approach had us at 3;000 feet. The FAF is 2;400 feet. We were unable to widen the approach due to a snowstorm to the west and had been cleared for the visual. We were too high; so we completed a missed approach. On the missed we went above our assigned altitude of 3;000 feet by 200 feet. We requested higher but were rejected; so we descended the 150-200 feet. On the second attempt; approach tried to give us the same turn at the same altitude. We asked for the ILS. We were again given a bad vector; however; farther out. We were given a 060 heading to intercept. Due to a 40 knot tailwind we flew through and requested a 120 heading to join. It was accepted. We landed successfully.We got a bad vector inside the final approach fix while 600 feet above the FAF altitude. We were given no indication or expectation of a short approach. We were too high and too fast for our approach. We conducted a go-around and subsequently climbed 150-200 feet high.

column121: We struggled to even get in a pushback call on Hobby Tower frequency. It was busy with high volume takeoff and landing and ground movements. We had briefed a taxi out from Gate to Runway 4. Tower and Ground were combined. The airport was using Runway 4 for takeoff and landing. Our first instructions from a very busy Tower Controller were unexpected. Tower said taxi via [Taxiway] Z; hold short [Taxiway] D. We had no way to ask for clarification. The frequency was very congested. Our role seemed to be to clear the alley to allow inbound company aircraft. The pace that the tower controller was speaking was impressive and very busy. Other Company seemed to be confused on the radio along with our crew. The pace was something you hear on LGA Ground frequency.We were issued further taxi instructions to follow Company to Runway 4. We verified our crossing clearances across [Runway] 13L and R. We discussed that the controller was in the Yellow. We used extra vigilance during this crowded taxi out to Runway 4. The pace never relented for the controller. He was doing a great job. But the situation was excessive for a routine departure out of our always bustling Hobby airport. It came as no surprise to us that we were cleared for takeoff on Runway 4; even though we were #2 in the lineup. We instantly questioned this; and our clearance was canceled. This seemed like a minor error to us; but it was confirmation that the professional controller was indeed in the Yellow. We departed minutes later without incident.Staff this busy airport with the correct amount of controllers. Loading up flight crews in this critical phase of flight over weak staffing is hazardous. I'm not sure if the guy was alone up there. He was really doing a great job. We know as crews; when the controllers are overloaded; we try to not make the situation worse with fumbled radio calls. The airport was operating in the Yellow; any small non-normal from an aircraft on the frequency could have made things go bad very quickly. We could have waited to move from our pushback into the alley until the radio calmed down

When he arrived; I let him have it. I told him that the weather was below legal landing minimums; and that flight landing after us was probably done illegally. The RVR when we went missed had dropped to 800 after we passed the FAF (Minimum RVR for landing on Runway X is 1800). I can assure you when we got to minimums we saw nothing. column121: During cruise flight at 40;000 ft. in the vicinity of ZZZ we began to smell an electrical type smoke. Moments later the A Flight Attendant called the flight deck to report smoke in the cabin. Simultaneously the master caution came on for ELEC and the TRU (transformer rectifier unit) light illuminated on the overhead panel. I as Captain was Pilot Flying and initially transferred control to the First Officer for me to chase down the TRU checklist. I accomplished the checklist; noting that approach mode with the flight directors would be unavailable... At this point the smoke was getting thicker; and we decided to accomplish the smoke/fire/fumes memory items. After communications were established we notified ATC and asked for a left turn direct to ZZZ1. We considered ZZZ2 but figured in terms of time we were about the same distance away due to our altitude; and that with a straight line to ZZZ1 we would be able to keep both our heads in the game running through checklists and monitoring the aircraft vs a circling descent into mountainous terrain. It was at this point that the First Officer made me aware that all his flight and NAV displays had failed. He thus transferred control back to me as the Pilot Flying and he took over the smoke/fire/fumes checklist in the QRH.ATC told us to expect one of the north runways into ZZZ1; but we told them we wanted [Runway] XXL as we were just on the north side of the airport so that was closest. We requested direct ZZZZZ on the ILS to backup our visual approach; and used our emergency authority to proceed at about 320 knots in order to expedite landing. At this point the First Officer discontinued the smoke/fire/fumes checklist at step 20; having noted at step 16 that we should not delay landing in order to complete the checklist. We then briefed and ran a descent and approach checklist. I asked the First Officer to call ZZZ1 OPS to let them know we were coming and for them to relay the info to Dispatch but at that point the #2 radio and comm panel had failed and the ACARS was no comm. It was with the master caution recall on the descent checklist that we realized how many issues were piling up beyond the TRU and smoke. Looking up after being prompted by the recall we saw a solid portion of the overhead panel was lit.With the glare from the smoke and setting sun we were only able to pickup the airport just outside of ZZZZZ. I disconnected the autopilot and proceeded to fly a visual approach backed up by the LNAV track for the ILS XXL. I quickly realized that electric trim was inoperative and proceeded to trim manually. With the landing checklist we also discovered that the auto speed brake would not arm; so I asked the First Officer to back me up for the manual deployment. We landed in the touchdown zone and exited at gate without incident where CFR was waiting. We stopped in order for CFR (crash fire rescue) to do a quick external inspection. As it was pretty quickly obvious the smoke was inside the aircraft and they weren't seeing anything outside; we asked them to get out of the way so we could get to a gate and let our passengers stop breathing fumes.After shutting down the engines the APU appeared to be supplying only partial power and the ground call horn sounded constantly. Due to this issue the cabin was already dark; and knowing we were dealing with an electrical issue we opted to remove all power from the aircraft and performed the secure checklist. Then we took a breath and asked each other (at the same time) 'well; how'd that go'. Of course sitting on the ground I feel like I can armchair quarterback the situation and nitpick some of the decisions; but overall I feel like we handled the situation well. We had good crew coordination given the circumstances (on O2) and the First Officer did a great job of running the checklists as well as keeping an eye on my flying once we had to transfer controls back to me. It did feel weird turning away from ZZZ2 since it was practically right below us; but I still feel like it was the correct decision given the circumstances and the amount of time it would take to descend; and how much of a distraction an orbiting descent into mountainous terrain would be while trying to deal with smoke.One thing I would do differently has to do with after the situation was over on the ground. I ended up talking with the Chief Pilot; then the firefighters; then the mechanic outside the aircraft on the ramp. By the time I got back inside I couldn't find the flight attendants to debrief and see how they were doing. Upon opening the flight deck door the A had told me that they were all fine; but I would have liked to make sure and check in with them individually. I called scheduling to try and get them to transfer me in order to at least talk with them on the phone; who then transferred me to the scheduling desk where I waited on hold until it disconnected. I still hope to talk with them at some point to learn how things went in the back and find out what we could have done better for them.
column123: During cruise flight at 40;000 ft. in the vicinity of ZZZ we began to smell an electrical type smoke. Moments later the A Flight Attendant called the flight deck to report smoke in the cabin. Simultaneously; the Master Caution came on for ELEC and the TR (transformer rectifier unit) light illuminated on the overhead panel. The Captain was Pilot Flying; and initially transferred control to me; in order to run the TR checklist. He accomplished the checklist; and it was around this same point the smoke was getting thicker; and we decided to accomplish the smoke/fire/fumes memory items. After communications were established the Captain told me to notify ATC and asked for a left turn direct to ZZZ1. We considered ZZZ2 but figured in terms of time we were about the same distance away due to our altitude; and that with a straight line to ZZZ1 we would be able to keep both our heads in the game running through checklists and monitoring the aircraft vs a circling descent into mountainous terrain. It was at this point that I noticed all my flight/nav displays and radios had failed as well as ACARS No Comm" being displayed on the FMS.  I immediately notified the Captain and said that it might be better if he flew.  He agreed and took control back as the Pilot Flying and I took over the smoke/fire/ fumes checklist in the QRH. ATC told us to expect one of the north runways into ZZZ1; but we told them we wanted [Runway] XXL as we were just on the north side of the airport.  We requested direct ZZZZZ on the ILS to backup our visual approach; and the Captain used his emergency authority to proceed at about 320 knots in the descent order to expedite landing. A short time later I advised the Captain that I'd like to discontinue the smoke/fire/fumes checklist at step 20 since I had reached a decision point in the QRH; and it appeared I would most likely be heads down for almost all of the rest of the flight into ZZZ1 with this exhaustive checklist; and not be able to properly; and safely perform my duties as a PM.  I came to this decision based on the fact that step 16 states we should not delay landing in order to complete the checklist. He agreed.  We then briefed and ran a descent and approach checklist. The Captain asked me to call ZZZ1 OPS to let them know we were coming and for them to relay the info to Dispatch; but I reminded him that the #2 radio and comm panel had failed and the ACARS was no comm. It was with the Master Caution recall on the descent checklist that we realized how many issues were piling up beyond the TR and smoke. Looking up after being prompted by the recall we saw a solid portion of the overhead panel was lit. With the glare from the smoke and setting sun we were only able to pickup the airport just outside of ZZZZZ. The Captain disconnected the autopilot and proceeded to fly a visual approach backed up by the LNAV track for the ILS 17L. I noticed during the approach that the Captain had to trim manually; which led me to believe that we had obviously lost electrical control.  With the landing checklist we also discovered that the auto speed brake would not arm; so the Captain asked me to back him up for the manual deployment. We landed in the touchdown zone and exited at gate without incident; where CFR (crash fire rescue) was waiting. We stopped in order for CFR to do a quick external inspection. As it was pretty quickly obvious the smoke was inside the aircraft and they weren't seeing anything outside; we asked them to get out of the way so we could get to a gate and let our pax stop breathing fumes. After shutting down the engines the APU appeared to be supplying only partial power and the ground call horn sounded constantly. Due to this issue the cabin was already dark; and knowing we were dealing with an electrical issue we opted to remove all power from the aircraft and performed the secure checklist. A short time later; CFR  and a maintenance person were able to find the cause of the TR failure and pulled one of the TR boxes out of the E&E bay (electronics & engineering); which showed significant electrical fire damage. Lesson learned: maintain awareness of the type of emergency and aircraft state; compared to how long QRH steps could take you out of the critical Pilot Monitoring role. This checklist taught me to bring my head back up and get a grasp on the fact that we were in a rapid descent; over mountains; with half of our displays and comms out and I was only half aware of some of the radio calls and aircraft state. This was more concerning to me."

column121: Lost SA partially on arrival. Approach gave us a 240 heading and asked us to call the field. I had selected managed speed out of 10;000 and was configuring. Extended gear descending through 9;200; so we could continue to slow. Aircraft wasn't slowing. Captured LOC; but overshot a bit. Glide slope didn't capture. Once I saw the PAPI I saw I was low I leveled; continued to configure and slow. Leveled at 1;000 feet AFL momentarily to rejoin glideslope and ensure configured for stabilized approach. Had runway in sight the whole time after turning final; met gates at 1;000 feet AFL and 500 feet AFL; but felt behind and should have gone around. Maintenance delay; unfamiliar airport; late runway change; long day (nearly 9 hours of flying); no approach control (ZZZ Center handling approach due to COVID outage).I should have asked for vectors onto the approach rather than accepting visual. ZZZ is surrounded by high terrain; I was unfamiliar even though I felt I had prepared carefully; vectors would have provided a less dynamic environment. Also; if I were in a similar situation; I would go-around and ensure I don't press when I feel at all like I have lost SA. Also; the high altitude made slowing the aircraft down more difficult. I didn't include that in my briefing. I know better; but after the long day I failed to consider that as a factor.
column123: ATC gave us a 90 degree plus vector for Runway XXR and asked us to call the field. We had it in sight and were cleared for the visual. We were above the glideslope; with flaps 1; put the gear down to slow down; and used managed speed. The approach was armed; caught; but overshot the localizer because the aircraft wasn't slowing down. The glideslope didn't capture and we were then low on the glide slope as we passed through it from above. We leveled off; slowed down and finished configuring. We were within stable criteria at 1;000 and 500 feet; but it was a messy approach.Cause - Long duty day; extended due to maintenance. Bad vector from ATC and pressure to go visual. Approach was closed and Denver center was handling approach.Don't be pressured into accepting a visual at night with mountainous terrain. Go-around if an approach is feeling uncomfortable. Slow down earlier when at a higher elevation airport.

column121: The airplane was released with Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) deferred; thus required air-cart start procedures in the gate.  Preflight; airplane setup; briefings; checklists; crew duties; paperwork; ground interactions were all normal; and (Minimum Equipment Lists) MELs were complied with.  Normal air-cart start and subsequent pushback were all normal.  After clearing the ground crew off the headset; the Right; Number 1 Inner Tank Fuel Pump faulted.  We complied with the instruction to turn off the pump; and contacted Ramp Control and Maintenance on separate radios.The Captain worked with Maintenance while the First Officer worked with Ramp Control.   The Captain discussed the need to do a deferral and the First Officer received instructions for us to taxi to spot for off the gate maintenance; or something to that effect.  Neither of us had ever heard of such a thing; and I told the First Officer to say; 'No; we're not doing that.'I called on my cell phone and told them about the situation; and we began discussing the need for a maintenance deferral; and whether or not we had enough fuel under the circumstances.  I suggested we look at deleting the alternate from the flight plan if it would be legal to do so.  The Dispatcher said he'd begin working on it.  It was about this time that Maintenance suggested we go to a designated spot for hot refueling.  I again said we wouldn't do that and that the best plan should we need fuel would be to just taxi into the gate we just left; shut down; get fuel; and have Maintenance sign off the fuel pump.  Maintenance told me that that wasn't the best idea because if we did that we'd have a long delay and have to do the paperwork over again.  I called Dispatch back and he said there was no way we could just do the deferral and that we'd need to go back for fuel; and I said fine we will do that.  As a note; Dispatch told me that he had also never heard of hot refueling. At that point I told Maintenance what we were going to go back into the gate.  Maintenance proceeded to explain that the hot refuel was done all the time and that the FAA and that Company Safety had approved of the procedure.  He was adamant that the hot fuel was the best way to proceed.  Ramp also confirmed the procedure; so after discussing it as a crew; we agreed it sounded like a legitimate request; and we agreed to go to the spot and proceed with the fueling there.  When we arrived; we were stopped by a pickup truck pulling close to the airplane that made me stop.  There was no further guidance from Ramp; other than to ask us to pull the tail clear of a taxi lane.  A second vehicle with built-in airstairs arrived at the airplane.  He began giving us hand signals that made little sense; and eventually hooked up to the intercom system; and asked us to shut down the engines.  I suggested that was not a very good idea and that we could have done that in the gate and that we were there for hot fueling.  He then said to just shut down engine number two and to open the door so he could give us a fuel slip.  I asked the First Officer to do an after landing flow to make sure we were caught up; and then to open the door after disarming the slides.We received fuel; a fuel slip; coordinated hand signals; ran appropriate checklists; did a cross-bleed start to get engine number two back on line; accomplished the after-start checklist; and taxied via Ramp's instructions.  The First Officer made adjustments to the aircraft performance data and we ran a new performance briefing; noting a two knot increase in the new V speeds; and feeling comfortable that we had returned to safely normal operations. We proceeded to taxi and takeoff with normal operations.At cruise we received a message from Dispatch that we didn't do a new weight and balance.  He asked for our fuel onboard; we sent them. Either an ill conceived procedure or a lack of adequate resources for flight crews to safely conduct this procedure.The Pilot in Command shouldhave stuck to his first decision.  And from a more proactive approach; a checklist should be developed and added to the QRH.  The maintenance deferral flowchart should mention the need to revisit weight and balance. requirements and anything else we might have missed.  Additionally; I would highly encourage a module during simulator training that runs crews through this exercise and the use of new flow charts and a checklist.
column123: The flight blocked out and then had a maintenance problem.  Right Inner Tank Inoperative. This not a flagged item; so the decision was made to put the aircraft in a maintenance area on the ramp. The Minimum Equipment List (MEL) requires 8800 lb penalty fuel and adjust fuel for FL200. Fueling is allowed in the maintenance area.  Since it was not a block turnback; a new release was not required. We did the prescribed procedure with Maintenance and I then sent a mini flight plan showing the new numbers with fuel penalties. After fueling was finished; I sent an ACARS asking for the new fuel breakdown so the hub could send a new Weight and Balance. However; the plane had already blocked and departed without an up to date to the weight and balance. I informed the Duty Officer and then tried to send the new weight and balance. The new weight and balance never showed up in the crew's ACARS messages although it showed up in the playback screen in ACARS. So I copied and pasted and sent the information; but did not notice that the information in the weight and balance that the hub sent was the information from the original block out. Even though we had received the correct fuel breakdown from the crew enroute.  The flight landed at its destination and I talked with the crew and passed them on to the Duty Officer. The initial problem was caused by crew departing without an updated weight and balance. I suggest following procedures when an aircraft blocks back to a maintenance area

column121: It was night. We were on the ground taxiing to the runway.  We had a jumpseater in the cockpit as well. We were cleared across one runway and to taxi to our assigned runway. After crossing I called for the Before Takeoff checklist. The First Officer proceeded to accomplish those duties which included contacting the cabin crew. While the First Officer was communicating with the cabin we were cleared for take off.  When the First Officer was done with the cabin notification I informed him that we were cleared for takeoff. The First Officer ran the checklist. As I was taxiing to the runway there were a lot of lights due to the proximity [of] two runways beginning in about the same location. It was a little confusing and I verbalized my confusion by saying 'Is this the right runway' meaning the one I was about to taxi onto. The jumpseater piped in and said it was a different runway. I was referring to the one in front of me he was referring to the one to my left. So; I proceeded forward crossing the runway we were cleared to takeoff on looking for the entrance to my runway and stopped on the other side realizing I had been on the correct runway. Tower saw what happened and canceled our takeoff clearance. We were in fact on the correct runway; I just wasn't sure that we were. We never lined up for takeoff on any runway. We just proceeded across the one [we] were cleared to take off on. The cause was partly due to my limited use of that runway in the past and especially at night. There was a degree of unfamiliarity with that runway. Another factor was my accepting a takeoff clearance before the First Officer was back fully engaged with me and feeling a little rushed. On my part; I could have declined takeoff clearance until we were finished with the 'before takeoff checklist' and both of us of us could have been fully engaged in only taxiing.
column123: Pilots were not familiar with the runway configuration at night. Confused assigned runway with an intersecting runway.  We taxied through approach end after being cleared for takeoff. Tower said to cancel takeoff clearance and turn around taxi back and hold short of the runway. We complied. We reviewed our taxi charts and realized our error. The Captain and First Officer were not familiar with the runway configuration at night. From our perspective it seemed the runway lights to 35 may have been turned down and due to that it could've been mistaken for 32 as we expected the lights for an active runway to be brighter. It would have also been helpful to have moving maps on taxi charts. We would have realized immediately where we were. As it stood the lights being turned down confused the unfamiliar crew into thinking they had to taxi further to Runway 35. From our perspective it seemed the runway lights may have been turned down and due to that we could've been mistaken our runway as we expected the lights for an active runway to be brighter. It would have also been helpful to have moving maps on taxi charts. We would have realized immediately where we were. As it stood the lights being turned down confused the unfamiliar crew into thinking they had to taxi further to the runway.

column121: I was [the] Purser on Aircraft X. When we boarded I noticed the entire phone was missing from XLR Jumpseat. The cockpit also informed me it was missing and that it was okay to go. I said that used to be a 'no go' item. I have no way of notifying the cockpit if there was any emergency- be it evacuation; a threat level; a medical emergency; etc. I asked if there was another plane that we could take. I notified the system that we were checking within maintenance on an issue before we board. We still had 15 minutes left to board. I was told that I was to refer to the Flight Attendant Manual regarding other means of communicating. I'm not sure if you've worn a mask and spoken through a megaphone; but that's not really a reliable means of communication with a mask on. And it still does not allow me to communicate with the cockpit. We were on a type X aircraft where the other FAs are backwards facing and would not know if a situation were to arise up front. We were also advised that it was to be a bumpy flight and we might need to remain seated for the duration of the flight. An in-flight Supervisor met the aircraft. Captain said he would refuse the aircraft if I was uncomfortable. I said that decision should not solely rely on me. However; this was the second flight in a row where the forward intercom was broken. This one happened to be completely missing a phone. The one prior was hanging off a screw. A Mechanic also came up during boarding to see what the problem was. I said this should be a 'no go' item referring to the missing phone. He said he deferred it that morning and that the part was awaiting the aircraft in ZZZ. So the aircraft had flown two previous legs before mine in this condition. I believe that a PA INOP is 'not' a no-go. A missing intercom should be a no-go item.

column121: High speed abort.Captain at controls.Cleared for takeoff and Tower advised aircraft on 5 mile final as we approached the RWY (Runway). Approximately 1/4 way down runway into our takeoff roll; Challenger announced going around left side. At approximately 1/2 way down runway into our takeoff roll; Tower directed us to abort our takeoff. We were in the high-speed regime at approximately 115 kts. I could see the jet going around on our left abeam; in my peripheral vision as we were aborting.Maximum reverse application w/ maximum brakes. Uneventful abort; cleared runway onto Taxiway F and brought jet to a stop. Manually held brakes while running all applicable checklists. 2 MLG (Main Landing Gear) trucks reached 610 C; others approximately 590 C. Brake temp cooling chart referenced 35 mins used; brakes took approximately 50 min to cool to 270 C. In the meantime; ZZZ Fire-Rescue examined MLG. No evidence of overheat. Conferred with [Maintenance Control] for any further guidance. Later; Maintenance came to the jet; examined MLG per [Maintenance Control] guidance and gave us a thumbs up.In the meantime; we had a conference call with Flight Ops Management and ZZZ Station Ops. Both gave us the ok to continue'.Maintenance Control sent us a new maintenance release; Dispatch sent Release 3. Brake temp left main was the highest temp; at approximately 240 C when we began taxi. No noticeable increases.We departed ZZZ; kept gear down for approximately 5 minutes til all MLG brakes were below 200 C and decreasing. Retracted gear and continued to ZZZ1 via the flight plan.As a side-note; we received an ACARS message at approximately 7;000 ft.; on climbout; directing us to return to gate for another check. We leveled at 9;000 ft.; called Dispatch for clarification. He talked to Maintenance Control and surmised the return to gate message was an old message and may have been caught up in the ACARS system somehow and decided to transmit to us after takeoff roll. Anyhow; message was deemed as received in error and we got a thumbs up to continue OPS (Operations) normal to ZZZ1. I'm not sure if this is something systemic to Company 2 ACARS interface or not; but this issue might need to be examined."
column123: Cleared takeoff at ZZZ with aircraft on 5 nm final. As we began our roll I heard the aircraft on final say they were initiating a go-around. Around 115 KIAS the Tower directed us to reject which we accomplished. We told the passengers to remain seated and we taxied clear to find a place to cool our brakes; get Maintenance to inspect our brakes/tires; and coordinate for a new maintenance release and Dispatch release while re-initializing our FMC. We accomplished all pre-flight; before push and before takeoff checklists again and accomplished an uneventful takeoff over an hour later and landing uneventfully in ZZZ1.
