column121: Aircraft X. ARD had previous write-up about compressor stalls on #3 Engine. Maintenance said the morning crew rejected the takeoff for compressor stalls; we read the write-up and maintenance action in detail and discussed the issue. We identified this as a potential threat to our flight. On push back; while starting #1 Engine; we got ENG 1 FADEC ALTN alert; we referred to the QRH; it also identified 'action code' as SW. After engine start; the Captain said we could recycle the switch and asked if I was okay with that; I replied if he was okay; I was okay. We selected FADEC ALTN; then selected it again to the normal function; the alert went away. Later as we taxied out; I thought about the PDM process and not consulting maintenance; but the Captain's action corrected the alert to the proper configuration without any alerts and without an AML write-up; so I resolved my dilemma internally. Prior to taking the runway; the Captain announced he was gonna run-up all the engines a bit higher than usual while holding the brakes to ensure #3 Engine was operating correctly; I replied it was a good idea. It was my take-off (hand flown as briefed) and everything went normal up to about 700 ft. AGL.About 700 ft. AGL; with the gear up and flaps extended; we heard loud bangs associated with a compressor stall (I only heard this before in the sim) and a jolting in the plane; there were no differing indications on any of the engine instruments (all three N1; EGT; and N2 indications were identical). Around 1;000 ft. AGL; the Captain said he was gonna shut the engine down; I said okay with the bias of the previous write-up in the ARD; also thinking we'd go thru the process of 'Throttle-Idle; Fuel Shutoff Switch-Off' (I admit this wasn't the calm and rehearsed engine failure problem in the sim; and I was a bit anxious about the actual compressor stall). About that time; Tower called us and said we had intermittent flames shooting out of the left side (#1 Engine); the Captain said 'left side; I shut down [Engine] #3' (paraphrase). I looked down and noticed 0 fuel flow and the engine N2 decreasing while the banging continued. I exclaimed 'Let's start it back up' thinking #3 wasn't the problem and we definitely needed it if we had to shut down #1! The Captain quickly returned the fuel cutoff switch to on and I saw the N2 increase. I turned the autopilot on (as briefed if we had a problem) and announced I was disconnecting the auto throttles while the Captain told Tower we were returning to the field for compressor stalls and advised ATC. Tower told us to turn left downwind for [Runway] XX and I told the Captain 'I got the plane and the radios' and I replied to Tower. With the autopilot on and above 1;000 ft. AGL; the plane accelerated above Vf and I asked Tower if 2;000 ft. MSL was okay to level off; Tower replied yes. As I started the heading guided turn to the left; I adjusted the altitude to 2;000 ft. and manually retarded all the throttles for level off then selected airspeed 200 knots. With the throttles out of take-off power; the banging went away; I believe Tower said the flames stopped. While flying downwind abeam the field; I began to setup for the approach [Runway] XX; adjusted the minimums (already had it preselected); and announced I was moving the flaps to 15 degrees since they were still extended. Tower asked if we had the field insight; I replied yes and Tower cleared us the visual approach [Runway] XX and cleared to land; I repeated the clearance but said we were gonna fly out a bit to get our normal visual glidepath. After the Captain programmed the FMS and inserted the ILS frequency into the NavRad page; I called for the approach check and turned base to final; on dogleg; I began the descent on glidepath before intercepting the localizer and called for the gear down and before landing check. With the final configuration and checklist complete; I asked the Captain if he wanted the landing since we were an emergency; he took control of the plane with the autopilot on while I briefed him of the FMAs. Landing was uneventful.  We taxied clear onto taxiway XX and waited for the fire truck's inspection. With the all clear (no fire); we terminated the emergency and taxied to parking.Engine compressor stall.Some missteps between the crew while successfully resolving an engine compressor stall. Better crew coordination would simplify resolution.

column121: Being vectored onto the final approach course 26R; we had a brief encounter with a wake turbulence. And then again during the landing flare to the point where it was becoming a problem to maintain a stabilized approach path above the runway in ground effect. Did not have time to notify air traffic control that this happened. I don't know if we were behind a heavy previous arrival. But we were getting really close to having to go around from the landing flare. The roll motion was becoming such a problem with keeping the aircraft stabilized; and aligned with the runway. I was actually shocked that we touchdown as smooth as we did. I asked the pilot flying if he thought that was a bit unusual his statement was 'I was just one more jolt away from going around'. Wake turbulence encounters in Atlanta are becoming an every week problem; more like almost every inbound leg into Atlanta problem. Also it seems there is little consideration given to the fact that we may be departing behind something that might be a threat as well. I'm beginning to think that there's nothing much going to be done about it until something serious happens. Often the wake encounter threats are not much of a problem if there's sufficient crosswind push the wake away from trailing aircraft; from my experience it does not take much to all. However I've learned that this is still a problem at some point on the arrival or departure procedure. For example a crosswind on the departure runways will clear you of the wake threat for takeoff; but might present a very real problem in trail of a heavy navigating to a point; to the same on that departure or arrival. Especially if it's a direct head; or tailwind now.

column121: Upon stepping aboard Aircraft X; I immediately detected an odor that had a burnt wire smell.  The other FA's also made comments such as; 'What is that smell? It smells like something is burning' as they stepped onboard.  I was the D FA and began checking my safety equipment.  I looked in the galley to see if any circuit breakers had popped and also looked in the oven to determine if the odor was from a forgotten burnt meal.  All circuits were in proper place and there was no food in oven.  I then walked down the aisle to determine if the burnt-wire smell was coming from the aft galley.  I stopped at Row 21; aircraft right and stepped up on Seat 21 D as the odor was very strong above the OH bin.  I could not visibly see any sign of smoke but the odor was quite strong.  I then walked back up to fwd galley as I saw that the Captain was beginning a briefing.  Captain stated that this aircraft had just come out of 'mothballs' and had just cleared a major inspection in State X.  He stated that it had just arrived to ZZZ and the Captain of that flight informed him that a smoke alarm for the aft cabin activated upon landing.  Captain stated that this happens from time to time and poses no threat of fire.  All of us 4 FAs told him that we smelled a burnt wire odor in the cabin.  A male individual; name unknown; representing Maintenance stated that we 'probably were smelling new carpet glue'.  Captain waited for the Maintenance personnel member to step off of the aircraft and then told us FA's that if we were not comfortable with the odor that he backed us and would insist that we fly a different aircraft to ZZZ1 or return to hotel if aircraft was not available.  All 4 of us FA's unanimously and instantly stated that we did not feel comfortable on this aircraft and we wanted to change aircraft in the interest of Safety First.  I then told the Captain that I noticed the odor was particularly strong by OH compartment of 21D.  We then walked to that row and Captain also noticed that it had a strong odor of either 'heated dust' or 'hot wire' on the lighting ballast.  He then asked me if I personally felt safe taking this aircraft. I told him that I am very safety minded and the odor was not normal or usual to me.  We all stayed in the first class seating area and continued personal conversations among us.  The Captain was not present as he was talking to Operations.  After approximately 15 minutes of remaining in the first class seating area; the other FAs noticed that my voice was getting hoarse and that I was beginning to lose my voice.   To the best of my recollection; I believe that C FA; and B FA; both stated that their throats felt scratchy.After approximately another 15 minutes of staying and waiting for a decision onboard; in the first class seating area; we were told by [the] Captain that we were changing into different aircraft for our flight back to ZZZ1.  We then deplaned the aircraft and walked to the other waiting aircraft.  My voice remained coarse for an additional 30 minutes and I developed a migraine during the boarding process.  I had the migraine the entire flight to ZZZ1; and it continued until early afternoon of date.  Additionally; I awoke on the morning of date with a sore and scratchy throat.  Both my migraine and scratchy throat subsided around 1400 hours on date.  I have had a continuous low-grade headache since date through present date.  I did not seek any medical attention as I 'normally' suffer from low grade sinus headaches regularly and use an OTC nasal spray along with Tylenol.I commend our Captain; for valuing and backing our decision to prioritize safety first.I would hope that Aircraft X was ferried back to ZZZ without full crew and guests in the pursuit of safety.

column121: While preflighting a stub flight we received an amended flight plan from Dispatch. The Dispatcher said that there was a bend in the flight plan and that he wanted to remove that. Because this was a stub flight our application struggled to upload the correct flight plan. It kept wanting to upload our original flight plan. The PACOTS east routing (Pacific Organized Track System) for that day was our original flight plan which had us departing the 130W longitude for DACEM onward to pick up the IRNMN arrival into LAX. However the Dispatcher rerouted us to fly from 140W bypassing 130W to begin an arrival using the RYDER arrival. This confused not only us but departure Area Control who had our original flight plan in their system. We departed the gate with the correct uploaded ATC flight plan but possessed on our iPads the amended flight plan from Dispatch... in addition our FO (First Officer) refused to coordinate with Dispatch to revise our our flight plan to its original format which resulted in erroneous flight progress forms from ACARS. To be clear the flight plan only deviated towards the latter end of the flight with the confusion resulting from the Dispatcher uploading an erroneous flight plan to remove a bend in the flight however that was not loaded to the PACOTS east routing for the day. Our FO contacted SFO radio to confirm our routing was correct with our FMS but neglected to inform Dispatch who thought we were still flying the amended route he had given us. It would be helpful if the company would provide guidance regarding how procedurally they would prefer crews coordinate changes to flight plans with ATC. Do they prefer we coordinate with ATC directly or would they prefer that we contact Dispatch and ask that they upload the correct route and that we check it with ATC. It would seem there is a loophole in regards to keeping Dispatch up to speed on changes to flight plans. I believe there is language in the FOM regarding any changes to the flight plan to notify Dispatch of those changes. In this case the changes were minimal however the arrival time differed by about 6-8 minutes from the original flight plan and the amended one from Dispatch. Dispatch was unaware that this stub flight was not flying the amended flight plan they sent us. When I; as the relief pilot; arrived from my break on the flight deck I noticed the erroneous flight progress forms and notified Dispatch who then sent us the revised flight plan. Dispatch was unaware that we were back on our original PACOTS routing. This was accomplished 2+45 into the flight. However if I had not done this it would not have gotten done as the FO refused to contact Dispatch to clear up the confusion. please advise. The First Officer refused input from both the Captain and myself; the relief pilot; to contact Dispatch and get them in the loop regarding discrepancies from filed flights from amended ones. Stub flights caused more confusion than necessary. Clear guidance is needed from company on how they prefer the crew to remedy route discrepancies from Dispatch versus filed. Do they prefer the crew to contact ATC and fix the problem ourselves or do they prefer Dispatch to get involved and fix the discrepancy.
column123: Just prior to pushback; we received a message from Dispatch with regards to a change in our flight planned route. We delayed pushback until receiving new flight plan. Only change was to end of route after waypoint at 140W. We then called Clearance Delivery and did a full route verification. They still only had the original; unchanged route. Since the only discrepancy between the flight plans was at the end of the flight; we opted to depart. After departure; we received the flight progress report that showed the modified route (after 140W). During flight; after checking in with San Francisco ARINC; we asked for a verification of our cleared routed. ARINC verified it was the original flight planned route. We then sent a message to Dispatch with our cleared route and received an update. Dispatch believed we requested a look at modifying our route to remove a 'dog leg' segment from our route which we hadn't.  We were a STUB flight and that might have been a factor as the original flight was near to the arrival time. The change to our flight plan wasn't requested and wasn't essential to safety. Unless critical to flight safety; last minute changes to flight plans (especially international) can cause miscommunications and errors in navigation and should be avoided.

column121: During climbout on a heading of east on the ZZZZZ2 SID while passing 8;000 feet between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 we got a TCAS TA regarding traffic descending off ZZZZZ3 on the ZZZZZ4  flowing south at 1 o'clock; 3-5 miles ahead that was no factor.  This is something we see every day on climb out or descent in and out of ZZZ due to climb and descent rates.   ATC then called traffic at our '10-11 O'clock 3 miles descending to one one (11) thousand I called 'traffic in site no factor; they're passing above and behind us.'  ATC then asked our Altitude.  I replied 'level 10;000 feet.He asked our altitude again; I replied 'Level 10;000 feet; he said he saw us at 10;500 feet and gave us an updated Altimeter setting; and cleared us to climb to 17;000 feet.  Passing 12;000 feet he asked us what altitude we were passing.  I replied '12;000 feet.'  He then replied 'That's what we show as well.  For some reason I had you at 10;500 feet back there. I have a phone number to copy when you are ready.'  We took the number down; and he said 'Call us when you get to your destination to discuss a possible pilot deviation.'The Captain called when we got to ZZZ1.  The Controller Supervisor who answered said he had just sat down; had no idea what we were talking about; said he would do some research and call us back.  5 minutes later he called us back and said; 'After review; the previous Controller showed you slightly high and stopped traffic on the arrival at 12;000 feet (which I thought was at 11;000 based on his advisory call).  Then showed our altitude correct in the climb after he inquired again passing 12;000 feet.  Said there was no conflicts or loss of separation; not a big deal; and that he would just file it as an RA report and close It out; however; we had no known RA's; nor any TA/RA indications for the potential conflicting traffic passing above and behind us?  The ATC Supervisor didn't take any further action or questions; and wished us a safe rest of our day and left It at that.  We thought It would behoove of us to fill out this report regardless.Wrong altimeter setting.  We had a lot of distractions from multiple visitors on the flight deck at the gate while setting up cockpit and during the before start checklist (flight attendants; gate agents; deadheading crew and commuting pilots who we knew who stopped by to visit).  Flight attendants held off boarding passengers who were held up at the door; until catering; who arrived at the aircraft late; had cleared the forward galley and aisle; and got them their snack/sanitary packages set up to hand out.  So this backlogged the jet bridge; had the flight attendants coming in and out of the cockpit along with the commuting pilots; and gave us a lot of distractions.  This back log seemed to frustrate the agent; for It was the flight attendants who were keeping the passengers out of the way until they were ready for them.  For that; the gate agent was rushing to close the flight (We still pushed 10 min early).  The FA A seemed rushed; and just closed the flight deck door before verifying if we were ready or saying 'seated and stowed;' which was nonstandard.  These multiple interruptions (which seem to happen every flight these days) just added up; we had the current ATIS printed off; but when back tracked to get caught up; we missed the altimeter settings; which must have been set from a flight a day or two prior due to the difference in what It actually was at the time.Verify; Verify; Verify; Trap the Errors; Don't let the distractions of the daily operations knock you off your game.  It was a beautiful cold VFR morning; flying with a Captain I had enjoyed flying with in the past; so I felt we were both comfortable and familiar with how each other operates within the SOP's and as a person.  The Aircraft had sat overnight.  I would like to see more operational (non-flying) related distraction/awareness incorporated into training.  The day prior on a separate flight we had a passenger removed by law enforcement for non-compliance/and possible criminal related activity.  Gate agents are constantly under stress to get flights out on time or early.  To top It all off; everyone has been under stress of the pandemic; furlough related; or state of the airline related issues.-"

column121: On approach to ZZZ; the ATIS was obtained with reported winds of 340 @ 15 G 28. The airport was configured to land east; utilizing Runways XL and XXC. The First Officer (FO) and I discussed how this was odd and not desirable as the tailwind component with gusts was at our 10 knot limitation. Additionally; the ATIS stated there were wind shear advisories in the area. On final approach inside the FAF; maintaining target airspeed within Vref +10 was extremely difficult due to the high wind gusts; shifting winds; and shear. As pilot flying; my airspeed was hovering at +10 with occasional jumps up to +20. The wind vector on the MFD was showing winds at 030 between 20-35 knots until 100 feet or so; where the winds sheared to 340 at an unknown speed. I touched down within the touchdown zone but off centerline by approximately 10 feet. Taxi to the hanger was uneventful and no damage was noted. During the debrief; the FO and I agreed a go-around with a request to land on a Westerly direction should have been made. The cause of this event were gusty winds; poor traffic flow decision by ATC; and undesirable speed control by the Pilot Flying due to windshear.  ATC decision to land to the east with reported winds of 340 @ 15 G 28. This decision by ATC caused an unsafe tailwind condition when coupled with very strong and gusty crosswinds. Additionally; myself or the FO should have requested a landing to the west. However; the First Officer and I determined that any request would be denied as ZZZ has a reputation for not accommodating these types of request in order to maintain efficient traffic flows. There is pressure to land with the prevailing flow of traffic at a major airport like ZZZ when the crew sees other aircraft landing in the existing conditions; even if the crew would prefer an alternate runway. I strongly believe ATC created an unsafe situation that may have inadvertently pressured pilots into landing with a tailwind in gusty conditions. When I made the decision to conduct the approach; a go around would have been the correct action when the wind sheared at 100 feet.

column121: This was originally scheduled as [Flt Number; Route] However that flight was cancelled due to the inbound aircraft diverting due to a reported autopilot/ILS (Instrument Landing System) failure during an attempt at a Cat 3 Autoland approach. Flight [Number] was rescheduled as a ferry flight [Number] to ZZZ; using the diverted aircraft.The aircraft had some autopilot maintenance done at ZZZ1; and was signed off cleared for flight. Upon arrival at the gate in ZZZ2; the Captain reported that the problems with the autopilot and the ILS were not fixed. Both he and the First Officer stated that the exact same malfunctions occurred on both of the past two flights. They described the Captain's ILS as erratic--intermittent ident; azimuth and glide slope drifting stop to stop and blanking out. The aircraft did not intercept course or glide slope on a Cat 3 approach. On the inbound leg; they described a 30 degree left final approach course LOC (Localizer) intercept where instead of rolling left; the airplane rolled right and turned away from final approach course; prompting the Captain to take over manually. They continued to fly a visual approach due to improved weather conditions since their earlier attempt. The Captain said he had made several ACARS ELB (Aircraft Communications And Reporting System Electronic Logbook) entries at the gate in ZZZ2; but had not received any acknowledgement printouts. Because of this; he had notified ZZZ2 maintenance via radio. The gate agent asked my FO (First Officer) and me how soon we would be ready to push back for ZZZ. We replied that there were open write ups that first had to be worked out or deferred; then released. Shortly after that; a Station Operations Supervisor arrived at the gate and expressed an expectation that we would quick turn the aircraft and depart for ZZZ. There had been no maintenance on the aircraft; nor any service. A Maintenance Supervisor arrived and stated the jet was ok to fly as is; with no open write ups. It was clear that there had been a breakdown in communication between the previous crew and the ZZZ2 Station in regards to the status of this aircraft. They became pushy about getting us off the gate. I was clear that this could not happen until these known; reported discrepancies were written up and resolved. I asked about aircraft servicing (fuel) and catering (food and water). The Pilot Mobile app showed that we had crew meals on this flight. (Both of us require Special Meals due to dietary restrictions.) The Operations Supervisor then went on a tirade about no catering at ZZZ2 and how everyone knows that. Her vehement response surprised both of us; as there was no context or cause for it. The maintenance supervisor continued to insist the aircraft had been fixed in ZZZ1 and was good to fly. I called Dispatch to see if we could get some help from [Maintenance Control]. The controller noted there were no open ELB write ups and therefore no reason to delay departure. No one seemed to register that the previous crew had reported multiple malfunctions of navigation equipment on an evening where IMC (Instrument Meteorological Conditions) was a huge factor. So I said to [Maintenance Control]; with the ZZZ2 Maintenance Supervisor and Operations Supervisor within earshot; that I would have to refuse the aircraft unless they properly documented these discrepancies; and either fixed them or legally deferred them. Meanwhile; the First Officer had called the [Flight Manager]. He recommended that we stand our ground on the maintenance issues; continue to be professional; and if we refused the aircraft to follow protocol. We had showed up at the airport slightly hungry; expecting that our crew meals would be boarded as listed. This was becoming a safety of flight problem; as the airport had few options for food at all; and the ones available were in the process of closing down. It was clear that if we were to have any food and water for the 5+10 red eye flight to ZZZ; we wouldhave to stop what we were doing and go find it. I called Dispatch back and tried again to explain the legal operational aspects of why it was important to document these inbound discrepancies. He got a different [Maintenance Controller] on the line and we had a better discussion. The new controller called the previous Captain for a personal debriefing of the inbound flight. That; in turn; got the requisite ELB documentation generated and the maintenance process started. column121: Departing during the waning stages of an intense storm. Winds were gusting close to 30 kts.. Windshear advisories were on the ATIS; however a flight landing 10 minutes before our departure reported only moderate turbulence with no mention of Windshear. Decided to let FO be the pilot flying. Climbing through 1;100 ft. MSL in a right turn to our cleared altitude of 4;000 ft.; the turbulence got very intense; with large; rapid; +or- 15 kts. fluctuations in airspeed. PF (Pilot Flying) called for flaps one; which I set; and thereafter he announced the autopilot was engaged. I had just changed to departure on the radio and then we were cleared to climb to 10;000 ft.; and to continue the right turn to our first navigation fix. PF called for flaps up; I selected the flaps up and then noticed the attitude of the airplane was falling below the horizon and we were starting to descend. I also noticed the PF trying to select 10;000 ft. on the altitude preselect. He was having difficulty setting the altitude selector as it was so turbulent ; so I stated: 'fly the airplane; we are descending'. The PF disconnected the autopilot and raised the nose after we reached about 3 degrees nose low attitude. During this time; our altitude dropped to about 1;300 ft. MSL (1;200 ft. AGL) and the GPWS 'Don't Sink' advisory sounded. We started to establish a climbing attitude so I directed my attention to setting the altitude preselect; setting the heading bug to our first fix; and the PF asked to also execute this fix in the FMS. After setting the FMS; I noticed our aircraft attitude was dropping below the horizon again and we were descending through 1;300 ft. MSL. Before I could command a correction; the GPWS 'Don't Sink' advisory sounded again; and the PF raised the nose. As we continued the climb; by this time the airspeed was climbing over 250 kts. and the aircraft attitude was raised to control the speed. The speed increased to approximately 287 kts; before starting to decrease. As the speed started to drop; the PF continued to raise the attitude of the airplane; and as we exceeded 25 degrees nose up I commanded the PF to 'lower the nose; our airspeed is decreasing; establish a pitch of 12 degrees'. By the time the airspeed stopped decreasing; our speed was about 5 kts. below the flaps up maneuvering speed. We accelerated and established a normal climb. From this point on; the rest of the climb was uneventful.

column121: Company Flights Aircraft X (event flight) and Aircraft Y had all the elements in play for a severe collision during taxi operations at ZZZ airport; had it not been for the keen and alert awareness of the First Officer (FO) on our flight.Other Company Flight Aircraft Y had just landed on Runway XXC; exited onto Taxiway B; and received clearance to back-taxi on Runway XXR full-length and proceed to the gate. Shortly thereafter Aircraft X received taxi clearance to taxi to Runway XXC via Taxiway P; cross Runway XXR; left onto Taxiway G; and join Taxiway EX.Both flights were taxiing toward the intersection of Runway XXR and Taxiway P when it is assumed that Tower saw the potential collision as both aircraft had 'ALL LIGHTS ON' indicating that Aircraft Y was taxiing with clearance on an active runway; and Aircraft X was preparing to cross an active runway with proper clearance. Tower then attempted to modify the taxi clearance for Aircraft X but made an error by initiating the call with Aircraft Y's call sign. The transmission was unfortunately interrupted by a third aircraft trying to transmit as the Tower was attempting to correct the call sign; resulting in the amended clearance transmission being unintelligible to both Flights X and Y.Aircraft X was underway at a nominal taxi speed; and Aircraft Y was observed taxiing at a higher-than-normal speed as they back-taxied toward the turnoff point at the end of Runway XXR. Taxiway P enters at a slight angle preventing the Captain of Aircraft X from clearly seeing any approaching traffic from his right. As the Captain of Aircraft X; we had full intention of entering the intersection as initially cleared. Just prior I initiated a Safety call by saying 'Clear left.' At that point the FO looked right and said; 'Wow; they're moving fast; and don't think they're intending to stop.' Hearing that; I immediately began a full stop of our aircraft prior to crossing the hold short line; followed by turning our lights off; and yielding to Aircraft Y; in case we were the ones in error with the crossing clearance. Startled that we had just avoided a serious collision; we discussed the possibility of us missing a clearance or how that collision seemed inevitable had we not made the final 'Clearing check' prior to crossing the runway. Because of the frequency congestion with Tower working all three frequencies (Clearance; Ground; and Tower) and the fact that we didn't actually cross the hold short line; we held any immediate inquiry as to the miscommunication of the clearance to ourselves.Upon further discussion among ourselves after departure; we were certain that we did not miss any clearances from ATC and that this was a certain potential mishap that needed further investigation to acknowledge the chain of events from going unrecognized in the future.  We discovered that both aircraft had the appropriate clearance to be where they were and that there was an attempt by ATC to issue an amended clearance to us. Tower initially called Aircraft Y then quickly attempted to correct to Aircraft X; but the transmission was interrupted by a third aircraft rendering the call sign and amended clearance unintelligible for either aircraft to be warned appropriately about each other.Due to the angle to which Aircraft X was approaching Runway XXR; there wasn't a good line of sight for the Captain to see any approaching traffic back-taxing on Runway XXR until it would have been too late. It was only due to the vigilance and discipline from the FO in effectively communicating the immediate danger that we were we able to avoid a severe collision given the circumstances.It is believed that Tower was operating at reduced staffing levels even though there were a lot of aircraft movements at ZZZ that evening. This was likely due to COVID protocols in place with ATC. The increased workload enabled him to issue clearances to both Flight X and Y to be on Runway XXR at the same time if timing was ideal. In thiscase; an amendment to the clearance was attempted to be issued; however; time was not in our favor for the Tower to initiate the call with the wrong call sign and be interrupted by a third aircraft making the transition intelligible by either flight.

column121: Day VMC. Conducted initial approach [Runway] XXR. PF (Pilot Flying) called missed approach into ZZZ [Runway] XXR due to windshear with airspeed loss below 500 ft. AFE (Above Field Elevation) with advancement in override thrust. Subsequently received windshear caution. After selecting TOGA and pitch up flew flight director. No windshear escape guidance provided as the windshear was not sustained. Thrust was advanced to GA (Go-Around) RSV as a precaution. Stable in the missed approach maneuver with no caution windshear; PF called Flaps 4 due to flaps full configured. Gear retracted at a safe altitude with positive climb rate. Flew ATC assigned runway heading with missed approach climb profile. Subsequent approach flown to the ILS profile with Flaps 5. Flew the glide slope to RWY [Runway] XXR. No windshear event occurred. Received wind report with gust factor 28 kts. Selected manual speeds to increase approach sped until 4-5 kts. until after passing 500 ft. AFE 'stable' call the target speed was reduced. Maintained visual descent rate with visual cues and instrumentation of the ILS. During round out to flare automation set the aural 'sink rate' message. FO (First Officer) announced correcting due to the aural call and confirmed with a cross check the sink rate was induced by maintaining descent rate with the descent maneuver to coupled round out pitch rate simultaneously for the landing maneuver; not due to windshear as the speed was stable. FO and CA (Captain) on debrief both acknowledged the aural alert at post flight and both agreed with given conditions the approach to landing was stable given the conditions. Touchdown was within LTP (Landing Threshold Point) distance.Second approach with Flaps 5 configuration allowed for a higher approach speed and acknowledging the wind factor with increase in target speed for gusty conditions allowed for less susceptibility for the same condition. Automation with sensor inputs from other automated systems is subject to its own set design limitations and may not reflect positive confirmation of the event with pilot judgment of the same situation monitoring the same event. Such as automation latencies detecting the windshear event prior to the windshear caution; or sink rate alert while the pilot is initiating real time assertive maneuvers in turbulent conditions. Inertial vertical speed descent rates measure acceleration as it filters out noise of turbulence conditions causing a lag as opposed to real time judgment of the flight crew.

The crew agreed that a tech stop was in the best interest of safety and it was decided that ZZZ1 was a suitable gateway for this; the flight was diverted to ZZZ1 to add fuel. I ran the Emergency Evacuation checklist to secure the aircraft; grabbed the fire extinguisher (not needed) and stood at the door directing the passengers to continue up the jetway; 'do not take bags or stand in the jetway; and to proceed to the terminal.' I directed the First Officer to go to terminal. There were a few passengers slowing the process trying to grab their carry-on bag; but were directed to stop and continue to the terminal. Once all passengers were off; I directed the FA's to go to the terminal while I swept the aircraft to be sure all crew and passengers were off. I then proceeded to the terminal. At the terminal I found the crew and deadheading crew members at the door; several passengers and agents and the smoking bag lying on the floor next to the ticket counter. I then directed all persons to leave the area; and requested Law enforcement with/dogs and fire and rescue to the bag. Asked the gate agent to call medical assistance and found the affected passenger sitting in the terminal; which I directed Medical to her location. At that point I was alarmed that the threat had followed us to the terminal and was concerned as to its contents. I then briefed fire and rescue; Maintenance as well as corporate security and law enforcement. I directed the deadheading crewmember who had carried the bag to seek medical attention. We coordinated for the FA's to stay nearby to facilitate the eventual allowing of 5 passengers at a time to go back to the secured aircraft to get their belongings. The First Officer was having chest pain and went to the hospital. I declined medical treatment. And met the ZZZ Chief Pilot who assisted me in the process remaining. There were burns on the owner of the smoking bag; and she also went to the hospital. There were no other injuries or incidents associated with the emergency deplaning procedure...but there was some uncertainty among the many constituents affected by the procedure; gate; ground; maintenance. etc. I was relieved from duty with 'p' for the remaining duration of the trip. I received follow up calls from ZZZ Chief Pilot on multiple occasions and was grateful for his support. I also contacted directly Union Safety and spoke with [Representative] who provided assistance and guidance during and after the event. Overall the procedure works; but should be expanded to a joint training scenario. I was most alarmed to learn. That the (brave) deadheading crew member had carried the smoking bag with him during the deplaning and it eventually ended up in the terminal with no oversight. The direction was to deplane away from the threat; not take it with us.The cause was allowing of the charging device and vape apparatus onboard the aircraft as a carry-on. The positive outcome was due to emergency deplaning at the gate procedure and pre-briefing. Well trained and professional back-end crew was outstanding. First Officer reverted to training and promptly called fire and rescue. However once passengers were off; there was confusion and potential danger which needs to be mitigated for future events. Communication and full understanding and procedures associated are necessary.I suggest the need to continue the use of and to training of the 'Emergency Deplaning at the Gate Procedure'. Would recommend suggested briefings for the crew. Also believe joint training would be very beneficial to role play these scenarios...there is a lot going on and many potential pitfalls. This affects all constituents of the normal process; but also many others. Being released from duty by the Chief Pilot was appreciated; however as a reserve pilot; working to get my time for the month; Pay - No Credit does not help in any way. In fact it prevented me from flying another 4 day trip I could have held; and subsequently puts me at zero(0) hours going into the middle of the month.
column123: It was the first leg of the start of the sequence. I had just met the CA (Captain); for the first time; that afternoon. Along with the first time working with the FA's (Flight Attendants). Boarding started as normal; the CA and myself went about our preflight duties. We had finished all our checklists and were just waiting for the Gate Agent to inform us of boarding being complete. As we sat waiting to close up FA-1 shouts up to us 'We have a fire in the cabin'. In the time that it took the CA and I to get over the initial shock factor; the FA's immediately began an 'Emergency Deplaning' of the aircraft. From my advantage point I had no clue how bad the fire was in the cabin. I did not hear any call for an 'Evacuation'; or see any doors and slides deploying; so I assumed that the FA's were just doing the 'Emergency Deplaning'.The CA went to the QRH immediately. I got on the radio to ops and told them of our situation. That we had a fire onboard the aircraft; we were 'Emergency Deplaning' into the terminal; and we needed ARF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting).The CA and I had completed everything we could think of to help the FA's with the situation in the back. Still not knowing how bad things were in the cabin the CA instructed me to exit the airplane. I did so and then followed my 'evacuation' duties when outside the aircraft. As I exited the flight deck I found a clog of passengers not moving out the door. I made my way through them to find a group of passengers have congregated on the jetway. I instructed them to move and get in the terminal building. This helped the flow of passengers off the aircraft. I found one passenger in visible distress on the jetway. I did a quick assessment of the passenger and then asked if they were OK. The passenger complained of burns on their arm. It did not look bad so I asked if they could walk. The passenger said yes. So I got the assistance of another passenger to help them into the terminal. I also instructed them to take the bag that the hurt passenger said was theirs and was standing next to. Later I would find out this was the bag that was smoking. It was not smoking when I was on the jetway and I was unaware this was the threat on the aircraft. I never would have thought that the threat would be off the aircraft in the direction the passengers were going. Or taken off and left unattended.After the passengers were off the aircraft the FA's were coming off and then asked where the bag was. I asked 'What bag? The one on the ground in the jetway?' They responded Yes; that was the one that was smoking. At that point I realized that I sent it inside the terminal. I remembered what passenger had it and told the supervisor; that was on the jetway; that I could identify them to find that bag.The CA completed his final check of the aircraft and we proceeded into the terminal. The bag has been cordoned off at the gate and people were being kept away. The CA remained at the gate until ARF arrived. I took the FA's and proceeded to an unused gate to keep us together and away from the situation.The incident started with a passenger's bag there was no control over the problem. There was some confusion over what procedures were started and what roles the flight deck crew had in an 'Emergency Deplaning'.It was also confusing how and why the fire; smoking bag; was put onto the jetway. The use of the 'Emergency Deplaning' was very appropriate to this situation and did exactly what it was intended to do. However there is not a clear signal; that we knew of; that signals to the flight deck that an 'Emergency Deplaning' is in progress. There was also not an immediate action item; QRC; or QRH procedure to reference for an event like this for us on the flight deck to help. It felt as if we were making it up as we went along. Merging our evacuation checklist and duties into the 'Emergency Deplaning'.There is also no defined plan for fighting an onboard fire at the gate; that at least theflight deck is aware of. Just so we know what to expect. Example; that if we are to expect the fire or threat to be taken off the aircraft mid-deplaning.The event was a success; it was extremely helpful that the flight deck knows about 'Emergency Deplaning'. However there seems to still be confusion on roles; how to help with and execute an 'Emergency Deplaning'.

column121: Upon descent on the RNAV arrival; the aircraft ahead advised 'moderate turbulence at 10;000 ft.… We as a crew evaluated the deviations options and concluded to stay on route and cross the next fix at 9;000 ft. The area north and south of course on the radar were shaded with darker colors. The current inflight night visibility was zero with moderate to heavy rain lightning and St Elmo's fire. Upon crossing the fix we begin to encounter moderate turbulence. The autopilot was engaged; 250 kts. speed selected. After passing the fix and right about when the smart turn over another fix began we received an immediate CLIMB RESOLUTION ADVISORY and a RED traffic appeared on the Multi-Function Display (MFD) in the 11 o'clock position.I; the Pilot Flying; began the TCAS TA/RA actions and call-outs disconnecting the autopilot; complying with the RA climb instructions. The Captain turned off the Flight Directors as per company procedures. Due to moderate turbulence the aircraft began to rapidly slow below the selected 250 kts.; so I; the Pilot Flying; selected TOGA (Take Off/Go Around) to equalize the descending energy and avoid a stall or near stall condition. With the lack of Flight Director (FD) lateral guidance the MFD became primary for lateral guidance for the turn over the fix; the red threat traffic appeared between us and turning left to rejoin the arrival. As we began to level off and reestablish vertical and lateral guidance ATC queried us. The Captain; who was Pilot Monitoring; was tasked with selecting the Flight Directors ON and selecting the desired modes to return us to course and altitude in a rather bumpy erratic flight condition. I; the Pilot Flying; with hands on a push to talk advised ATC of complying with a TCAS RA. As we began to turn back to course the previous red threat traffic reappeared yellow and a 'TRAFFIC; TRAFFIC' was heard; so we remained leveled off and slow turned towards the course. After establishing guidance; and positively managing the aircraft's speed and energy we began a turn towards the next fix. We as a crew were task saturated controlling the aircraft in moderate turbulence and complying with the TCAS RA and were merely queried by ATC; never advised of traffic by ATC or given any lateral guidance after stating we were complying with a TCAS RA. It was only several moments after we were reestablishing on course avoiding the traffic that ATC assigned a heading. Most disturbing during the irregularities of moderate turbulence; TCAS RA with traffic conflicting the turn; and turbulence induced energy state beyond authority of the auto thrust; ATC tries to immediately give us a phone number to call instead of any assistance in weather or traffic guidance.The portion of the RNAV arrival; during the event; has 6.5 miles to descend up to 2;000 ft.; slow 40 kts.; and smart turn 51 degrees; coupled with a very changing tailwind of 150 kts. at 20;000 [ft.] slowing to 36 kts. at 10;000 [ft.] and the aircraft's FMS plotting the deceleration to approach mode between fixes thus requiring manual speed selected management; it is a very busy part of the arrival.Casual factors were night with St. Elmo's fire; lightning causing a very dark outside and requiring bright instrumentation that is difficult for the eye to follow in moderate turbulence. Possible other factors of AUTO FLT FCU 1 FAIL immediately after the event. ATC was extremely busy. I think another big factor was ATC confusion of what we were experiencing; due to the fact we were both task saturated controlling the aircraft and avoiding a mid-air collision ATC communication became a lower priority. With reduced traffic separation ATC becomes an integral part of every flight; if the manuals would include 'advise ATC' as a step; and clear guidance on priority of traffic avoidance in relationship to lateral guidance and where it is seen or sourced this could help."

column121: While we were on base leg on the RNP Y Runway 2 approach to MGGT [airport]; someone on the ground pointed a green laser and it flashed in the cockpit a few times; twice hitting me on the right eye. We were in between GT504 and GT503 with the aircraft fully configured; I was PM and since it was my first time flying into MGGT; I was looking outside to get a mental picture for future reference and situational awareness; trying to identify the runway;  when I saw a green laser beam being pointed at the aircraft; I called it out to the Captain and he kept his head down but I was hit twice on the right eye before I could go head down. I reported it to the Tower (in Spanish). The Captain asked me if I was OK; and I just mentioned that my eye felt drier than normal. (I've had the misfortune of being hit by a laser while flying before; so I knew the sensation). We continued to approach and landing without any further incident.Unfortunately; these types of events are almost impossible to stop; unless we wear protective eye gear; there is nothing we can do but lower our heads if a beam is being pointed to the aircraft.
column123: While on approach; circling left arc to final; RNV Y 02; MGGT; about 145 knots and 2;000 feet AGL; FO (Non-Flying Pilot) observed a green laser coming from the low 10 o'clock position. I asked FO if he was OK and he said his eyes were drier than normal.Suggestions - Patrol the terminal area in vicinity of airport more often. Make area more sterile. Prosecute those who attempt to lase airplanes as they land at airports.

column121: I was PF; hand-flying.  On departure; we were cleared to 10;000 feet.  Northbound on the SID; climbing through approximately 7;500; I increased pitch to avoid a small build-up off the nose.  Climbing thru approximately 8;800 feet; I realized that I was going to have a difficult time leveling off by 10;000 feet.  I asked the CA to advise ATC of the potential altitude excursion and aggressively; but smoothly; reduced pitch to level off.  I exceeded our assigned altitude by 450 feet; and promptly descended back to 10;000 feet.  ATC did not seem concerned by our deviation and cleared us to 16;000 feet.This was one of my first sequences after a 6-month leave of absence.  The CA is new to the airplane and new to the seat.  These factors contributed to our poor altitude SA and slow cross-check.Our threat-forward briefing focused on our lack of recent flying.  We needed to be even more vigilant to trap decision and execution errors.

column121: We were given taxi instructions from the gate at GSO to Runway 23L via Kilo; K6; with expected delays due to traffic into ZZZ. We taxied down Kilo; but the sign for K6 was located 'after' the intersection of Kilo and K6 (not before); so we continued past the intersection; and then saw the late sign for K6. We stopped and asked ATC if we had in fact gone past K6; which they confirmed but said 'no problem'. We asked and received permission to taxi forward on Kilo and execute a 180 degree turn at the taxiway near the entrance to the cargo ramp; which GSO Ground approved; then taxied down Kilo again to K6; and waited for our flow time to ZZZ. The problem could have been easily avoided if the taxi intersection sign had been placed ahead of the K6 intersection (facing towards K5 vs. the cargo ramp); instead of after the intersection.I would suggest that the taxiway K6 sign be placed 'before' the intersection of Kilo and K6; so that a pilot taxiing down Kilo and looking for K6 would actually see it. Where it sits currently; past the actual K6 intersection; does no good to anyone; and is conducive to other pilots missing this intersection. A sign is cheap; compared to the potential problems.
column123: During taxi at GSO we were taxiing to Runway 23L from the terminal via J3; K; and K6. We had passed taxiway K6 and continued straight on taxiway K. During the time we passed it; I was running the before takeoff checklist where I tried being outside of the airplane but the entire checklist is verifying the inside components are set and completed. The sun was also glaring in from my right side due to its position where I was partially blinded through the whole taxi even with sunglasses on. When I completed the checklist I looked up and saw the approach light systems for Runway 23L and looked behind and saw we missed K6. I advised Ground that we missed K6 and asked if we'd be able to make the turnaround we told them we'd have to wait until we were at the end and the Captain said we were able to so they said continue back K to K6 hold short Runway 23L. The Captain told me the sign for K6 is also after the taxiway and if you don't see that there isn't a taxiway past the sign it's already too late because you have to continue straight on K. When we taxied back; I wasn't able to confirm what sign was before K6 intersection. [Causes of the incident include] running the before takeoff checklist; sun glare on my side of cockpit; and the possibility that the K6 sign is after the taxiway. This was the last leg of a 4 day trip.

column121: On the Arrival into ONT SoCal Approach assigned vectors to sequence behind a 747. We were vectored directly behind and above the preceding 747 for 26L when we were cleared for the visual approach to 26R. ATC advised to maintain visual separation. At that point; due to concerns of descending behind the heavy aircraft; I offset right of course and attempted to parallel the 747. My intention was to remain clear of the 747's wake vortices. As we continued the approach and began to converge with the other aircraft; ONT Tower issued clearance to S-turn to the right if necessary. At that point we were too close to the runway to make any effective maneuvers and still maintain a stabilized approach. We then received a 'Descend' RA and continued descending on the visual approach to 26R while the adjacent aircraft executed a climb and go-around from 26L. In retrospect I believe a better course of action would have been to discontinue the visual approach or ask for delay vectors to increase separation from the heavy aircraft. ATC should have issued more realistic vectors to sequence us further behind the 747.
column123: Descending on the Arrival into ONT; SoCal Approach Control gave a maintain current HDG [instruction]. We visually acquired a 747 at our 12 o'clock position approximately 5 NMs. SoCal then gave us a right turn to a 140 HDG; then subsequently a 170 HDG that placed us at the 6 o'clock position of the 747 approximately 5 NMs behind. Once established on the 170 HDG; SoCal cleared us and the 747 visual approaches; 747 to Runway 26L and us to 26R and told us 'Caution wake turbulence and maintain visual separation with the 747'. The Captain did not want to be in a position to be at a 45 degree angle behind the 747; which would've increased the chances of getting into the wake of the 747; so as we were descending for the approach we received a descend RA and Aircraft Y executed a go-around for a climb RA. When we noticed that it would be challenging to do the approach and simultaneously staying out if the heavy aircraft's wake turbulence; should've asked the Controller for a vector or turn before starting the final portion of the approach.

column121: Our alternate was ZZZ2 exactly because ZZZ3; ZZZ4; ZZZ5; and ZZZ6 were not suitable weather-wise. The original flight plan had fuel to fly ZZZ-ZZZ1; go-around and fly to our alternate of ZZZ2 landing with a fairly standard REMF; as I recall; certainly not enough fuel to shoot a second approach in ZZZ1 and comfortably divert to ZZZ2.This was our third and final leg of the day; following a ZZZ-ZZZ7 turn. It was our second day of a three-day trip and we felt reasonably alert. If we had to divert to ZZZ2; I suspect we would have been close to timing out in our block time; from a passenger standpoint; ZZZ2 made a lot of sense with the ability to re-crew in a base. By the time we blocked in ZZZ1 we had completed 7:30 actual flight time. I know I was tired at the end of the day. Time compression in ZZZ between second and third leg.1. The flight plan for our final leg was not yet available for downloading and consideration before top of descent ZZZ7-ZZZ (leg #2). Flight planning on the ground felt very time compressed.2. We were switching aircraft in ZZZ.3. We were supposed to have been boarded crew meals for our second leg (ZZZ7-ZZZ) but for some odd reason; the FO's hot meal was boarded and I was offered a hodge-podge of a snack box; beef jerky; a cookie; three dried apricots and a packet of honey. I snacked on that offering but needed to find a real meal back in ZZZ between flights.4. Please appreciate the 64 minutes on the ground is from parking brake set on Flight number; (inbound flight); complete the parking checklist; collect our belongings;  traipse over to a different gate (thankfully; the gates were close); download and review: Flight Number's OFP; NOTAMs; and aircraft maintenance and history; review weather on WSI iPad app; pre-flight a new aircraft; load and check the FMC; brief flight attendants especially on the weather conditions; receive an ATC clearance; departure brief between pilots; accomplish both the pre-flight checklist and before push checklist; and then release the parking brake for push-back.Given the lower ceilings and reduced visibility with snow-rain mix and strong direct gusty crosswinds in the TAF I felt it prudent to add contingency fuel. I called our dispatcher at the gate in ZZZ and we agreed to add approximately 30 minutes of fuel; specifically; 3;000 pounds. I had hoped that our dispatcher was cognizant the conditions forecast in ZZZ1 warranted more consideration than a milk-run; day; VFR landing; but truthfully; I had a whisper of uneasy misgivings. Perhaps I felt this was the fuel plan SABRE popped out and there could have been more... more human QA to it... perhaps. Then again; maybe it was nothing... yet the voice in the back of my mind wasn't letting up. Something felt unsettled. Was our dispatcher a little susceptible to Automation and Anchoring Bias... was our dispatcher's Situational Awareness appropriately elevated? Was her Review/Monitor/Predict loop firing on all cylinders? I decided: 'I'll set it aside for now--relax; captain--it's probably nothing.' (spoiler alert: it turned out to be nothing but the ambiguity of whether it was or not; before and during the flight was distracting.)I do not have the ATIS but I did reconstruct the conditions from a historical AWOS archive01 XA:51Z: 330/19G26 6SM -RASN BR BKN009 OVC016 02/01 A29.60 PK WND 3303301 XB:51Z: 330/18G27 3SM -SN BR BKN008 OVC013 02/01 A29.61 PK WND 3203201 XC:06Z: 330/16G29 3SM -SN BR BKN010 OVC015 02/00 A29.61 PK WND 3202901 XC:14Z: 320/16G24 2-1/2SM -SN BR BKN008 OVC 013 02/00 A29.61 PK WND 3202901 XC:23Z: 320/14G28 1-3/4SM -SN BR OVC010 01/00 A29.61 PK WND 3202901 XC:30Z: 330/18G22 1-3/4SM -SN BR BKN008 OVC012 01/00 A 29.61 PK WND 32029The ATIS stated ILS RWY XXL and RCC (Runway Condition Code) 5/5/5 at XJ:00Z; XXR/YYL and XY/YX CLSD; and variousCLSD taxiways. The RCC time stamp of XJ:Z caught my attention as being roughly 16+ hours old.[Aircraft type] landing crosswind component 'guidelines' in the Flight Manual Limitations Chapter:RCC 5 and 6: 40 knotsRCC 4: 35 knotsRCC 3: 25 knots'NOTE: The crosswind guidelines presented...... The use of these guidelines should be based on the current weather conditions and thepilot's ability and experience level.'Even with the recent uptick in flying the overwhelming majority of us are feeling 'rusty'. Generally; with my XX+ years flying experience it seems to come back fairly quickly but I definitely don't feel the same high level of finesse as I did a year ago. I'm aware of it; very aware. I'm working diligently to trap the errors and as minor as they seem there are more of them.Actively seeking and countering threats; setting the right tone on the flight deck; and ensuring we are working well with dispatch these are some of the best tools we have. Overconfidence bias especially in challenging conditions while none of us are flying as much as we usually do is probably at the top of the list. Going the extra step of resolving seemingly small ambiguities seems especially appropriate right now. Plan continuation bias; expectancy bias; and optimism bias creep into the mix a little more insidiously than usual. The ever-present threat of complacency has absolutely not waned. I wonder is Dispatch in the same boat? I suspect so. I want to be cognizant and understanding of that likelihood--we are a team and we need to lift each other up.A little over an hour prior to touchdown we began planning our ILS runway XX approach and landing with the most current conditions at the time. We reviewed the NOTAMs; assiduously marking up the myriad of closed taxiways on our -9 pages. We pulled landing performance data and reviewed it intently. With the strong direct and gusty crosswinds we might have preferred a flaps 40 landing on Runway YX but it was closed.I felt the RCC 5/5/5 at XJ:00Z (16+ hours old) was a remnant and if we just encouraged dispatch to make a call to ZZZ1 Tower; we could get something much more useful; more akin to an hourly observation. Actively countering the ambiguity of a very stale RCC given the worsening weather conditions. Making allowance that Dispatch is planning and monitoring somewhere between several and a small slew of flights they aren't going to catch everything. The ACARS reply from 'X Dispatch' for an updated RCC:'ZZZ1 CITY OPS SAYS 5/5/5.THEY WON'T UPDATE THE NOTAM/FICON UNTIL THERE IS SOMETHING SIGNIFICANT TO UPDATE.'Ambiguity not resolved. Concern we were being led down a path... heightened.With time for more nuanced decision points running out; I replied to X Dispatch:'Name; JUST WANT US ALL TO HAVE THE SAME UNDERSTANDING ABOUT HOW CRITICAL I VIEW A CURRENT AND ACCURATE FICON* WITH THE GUSTY DIRECT CROSSWIND TEMP/DP 02/01... I WILL NOT ATTEMPT A LANDING WITHOUT IT. IS THE 5/5/5 FROM XJ:00Z OR HAVE THEY MEASURED IT MORE RECENTLY... I WILL NOT ALLOW A GREEN BAY OFF THE ENDCOMPLACENCY FROM ZZZ1 CITY OPS TO SUFFICE. PLS INFO FODM OF THIS'(*FICON; I should have used 'RCC' instead)X Dispatch reply:'OKAY.I GOT THE [Flight Operations Manager] IN ON A CALL TO ZZZ1 TOWER. FODM IS UP TO SPEED ON THE CONCERN. THEY REPORTED: RWY XXL AT XS:54Z. 5/5/5. 100 PCT WET.AGAIN; THEY DO NOT ANTICIPATE TO UPDATE UNLESS THERE IS AN ACCUMULATION ON THE RUNWAY OR ANOTHER CHANGE IN CONDITION.'Did I feel like we were pushing a rope? Yes. Yes; I did. I felt like we were being dismissed and my confidence in X Dispatch was significantly diminished. I felt like X Dispatch was not proactively leaning forward in the saddle and was content to accept whatever ZZZ1 City Ops said. Rather than feeling supported; rather than feeling like the increased risk was being adequately considered and mitigated; I felt a certain inappropriate nonchalance had insidiously permeated. I feel like Ihad to kick up a ruckus to finally get an RCC 5/5/5 at XC:00Z--as the XS:54Z RCC was still 7-ish hours old... DURING a RASN event. Finally; I feel like the fact that nothing bad happened adds to the confirmation bias that it was much ado about nothing... right up until it's not nothing. And 'Not Nothing' happens in a blazingly fast moment.What could I have done differently and more effectively?I should have called X Dispatch from ZZZ7 on leg #2; asking her to work up our leg #3 early--I could have alleviated the time compression I felt on the ground in ZZZ.In retrospect; I wish I had noted the XJ:00Z RCC from the ATIS available in either FD Pro X or just pulled the ZZZ1 ATIS on ACARS before pushing and added resolving the stale RCC to the fuel increase phone call with X Dispatch.I should have used 'X' words in the ACARS messages with dispatch to convey the level of my unease.I should have started descent planning and landing in those conditions at Top of Climb (TOC) to allow more time to get 'the ball rolling'.I should have taken the time to call after the flight; to debrief with our dispatcher... really wish I had done that.Ongoing concerns/questionsX Dispatch:1. How early can I ask for a flight to be planned?2. What fuel contingency plan is appropriate in these meteorological conditions for delayed arrival (E.G.; holding while treating the runway) or the preceding aircraft doesn't clear the runway in a timely manner or a gusty wind event causes an unstabilized approach condition? To name but a few possibilities...3. What could I have done differently from X Dispatch's perspective? I would like the feedback to make me a better Captain.ATC:1. How long before an RCC gets updated? Is there an upper number of hours? 2 hours? 36 hours?2. In these particular conditions of strong gusty crosswinds and rain snow mix; what is an appropriate update interval to give us 'end-users' a reasonable level of confidence in the data?3. How are RCCs actually determined?I am going to end this unusual report with a few words from a recently would-have-been furloughed-but-took-advantage-of-voluntary-separation-program and much-liked coworker. It's important to recognize that Name was an administrative co-worker. He's not a pilot himself but he certainly recognized how important his part in the team mattered. We could all profit from his example. 'I made it my goal to make sure every pilot left the flight planning area with a clear head. No matter what issue they had coming in the door; when they went out to fly that issue was taken care of or they knew that I would do my best to take care of it and follow up with them on itsoutcome. I did not want to be the one to cause a distraction. I was proud to be the one who cleaned up the distractions.''...cleaned up distractions' ... Indeed.

column121: After landing on Runway 31 we exited at taxiway Tango. We told Ground Control we were going to gate. Ground Control instructed us to 'turn left on Bravo; right on Lima; taxi to the gate.' I taxied toward the gate and suddenly; out of the darkness in front of me I noticed multiple; 2-3 foot tall; UNLIGHTED taxiway edge posts. I immediately stopped the aircraft and was able to make a hard left turn to barely avoid hitting the posts. It immediately became apparent that taxiway Lima is actually on about a 45 degree angle from off of taxiway Bravo vs what I thought was a 90 degree right turn. For whatever reason; there is an UNLIGHTED; 'false island' between Taxiway Lima and the ramp. Due to the conditions of darkness; a very bright new terminal and gate area; and unlighted taxiway edge posts; it was very easy for me to turn right onto taxiway Lima and then focus on taxiing straight ahead to gate right through the 'island.'

She said my mask had to be replaced between each sip.  I identified myself as an employee and told her I disagreed with her interpretation of the policy. I told her I was actively drinking and she said; that what I was doing was not allowed and reiterated; I had to put my mask up between sips.  She also immediately threatened to 'Go to the pilots' when I challenged her interpretation. I complied with her dictate; though I believed it to be errant; and put my mask up; dropping it only between sips of my drink thereafter.  Of note; the Flight Attendant deadheading adjacent to me left his mask down for long periods of time while eating and drinking; so it appears he had the same opinion as I did.  Afterwards; when she passed back by; I asked her if she would give me her name as I felt I needed to report this incident; since she threatened to go to the pilots and I considered her interpretation of the policy to be errant.  She refused to give me her name and said she was ' Going to the pilots' now; because I asked her name.   If Airline X intended her rule to be the standard; then I'm certain Airline X would specifically state that mask must be replaced between sips and bites as opposed to actively drinking or eating.  I reread the policy and I still believe her interpretation is errant.  I also checked with the ZZZ Chief Pilot office and they also believe there is nothing to support her interpretation of the mask policy.In summary; I believe her actions; specifically developing her own policy and her abrasive engagement has the high potential of creating additional conflicts with passengers and unnecessary distractions to the cockpit.

column121: Arrived at the airport at XA:45. The station representative met us advising he had just received an email further pushing our departure back to XE:00. He also advised they were unsure as to whether there were even parts on hand to repair the aircraft correctly and wondered if it would even depart that day. We settled in the crew rest area to wait and see. At XC:51; I received a call from a Company A representative asking how we felt and if we were still good to fly. They said Maintenance advised they would have the plane fixed in about an hour. We advised we were good to go. I then called Dispatch to advise and keep them in the loop. The Dispatcher emailed us release revision 2. We reviewed it and headed out to the aircraft. As we arrived outside the aircraft; Maintenance was still aboard working on the aircraft. At XD:35; Maintenance finished with the aircraft. We then boarded the aircraft to find it on battery power and the GPU (Ground Power Unit) running but the over voltage warning light indicator on. We flagged down personnel to get a new GPU. At XD:45 the APU (Auxiliary Power Unit) was started. The replacement GPU arrived as the APU completed powering up. We then began our preflight. At XE:20; the preflight was finished. At XE:35; Maintenance finished the logbook and maintenance brief. We then blocked out. During this time I became aware of Company A Maintenance Control pressuring the on-site Company B maintenance personnel to 'line out' the other maintenance personnel's write-up stating 'Undocumented speed tape found concealing stripped and unsecured mounting screw to extruded MCD (Main Cabin Door) Manual Vent Door Drive (Pressure Vessel) cover panel'. This was found in Aircraft X's logbook. Maintenance Control wanted this done so as not to draw scrutiny to it by the FAA. Thankfully and appreciatively the Company B Mechanic refused to assist in this cover-up.This is the consistent behavior I have observed from the pressure Company C exerts on this operation to dispatch the aircraft on time at all costs. In the past several years I have submitted safety reports and FCRs (Flight Crew Reports) observing willful and wanton disregard of DDG (Dispatch Deviation Guide) procedures plainly written out. I've listened to Maintenance Control; on speakerphone; tell an on-site mechanic to 'Write whatever the hell makes the pilot happy to get that damn thing out of there.' I've had Maintenance Control denigrate me for not immediately pulling back into the gate with a problem but instead I followed procedure and called Dispatch for a three-way call with the problem. I've observed on numerous occasions and numerous stations Company B mechanics back-dooring the fuel sheets to make the numbers work instead of obtaining the fuel density to compute the numbers correctly to check the accuracy of the fueling process. I've had Company B mechanics on my jump seat share experiences of Maintenance Control telling them to check good" a system without actually testing the system. Thankfully as well; those mechanics told Maintenance Control their tickets were more important to them than their jobs. Both of those mechanics have since left Company B for more ethical workplace environments.My observation is the attitude in Maintenance Control is a mixture of arrogance and fear-driven to kowtow to this pressure. The pressure is passed down the chain from Company C to the executive level to the middle managers to the line supervisors to the line workers. This culture is a very dangerous one. It severely erodes the necessary safety and trust in the process required for it to work as it is designed. I have personally had so many of these instances where I have found incorrectly complied with DDG procedures both by blatant disregard and ignorance. I and several of my colleagues have experienced an extreme increase in time and concern when reviewing the log and maintenance procedures. I personally am not trained as a mechanic. The amount of items that we can see and have found greatly concerns us. Our concern is the amount of Maintenance egregious violations and errors we can see are so numerous and regular; how safe; complete; and compliant is the work; like the heavy checks and line maintenance behind the panels and cowlings that we cannot see. Our fear is this is going to lead to injuries; loss of life; and more aircraft damage and hull losses. The solution is straight forward and already established. Enforce strict adherence to maintaining the aircraft and equipment as directed by our FAA-approved maintenance program."

column121: Aircraft X.  Ground Service personal brought Hazardous Cargo paperwork to the cockpit about dry ice being loaded in the aft cargo compartment and live animals being loaded in the forward cargo compartment.Normally live animals are loaded in the aft or bulk cargo compartments which are heated by engine bleed air. If carrying animals in the aft cargo compartments we make sure the cargo heat switches are in the high position which will warm and maintain the compartment temperature between 65F and 75F.  Due to the dry ice being loaded in the aft we are not allowed to have animals and dry ice in the same compartment.I was told by the ground service worker that they load live animals in the forward cargo compartment and do this regularly because the forward cargo compartment is heated. I explained that it is heated with cabin air that has flowed through the E & E compartments equipment ventilation system to cool the electronics and exhausted into the forward cargo compartment. We have no way of knowing what the temperature is in the forward cargo compartment is and no way of knowing if it is suitable for live animals.  We do have aft and bulk cargo compartment temperature indications on our air synoptic located in the cockpit. I asked Ground Personnel to swap the locations of the dry ice and live animals so that the animals could be kept warm for the flight in the aft cargo compartment.  I was told that this would be difficult to do because the dry ice would need to be moved to another canister and this would take time.  I asked to speak with the Ramp Supervisor and I spoke with the Station Manager. She explained that their ROM (Ramp Operations Manual) authorizes the loading of live animals in the Forward Cargo Compartment of the 777.  I explained that our Aircraft Operations Manual authorizes the loading of live animals in our aft or bulk cargo compartments only.  She explained that they have done this before and that I was not the first Captain to question this practice.I called the Dispatcher for the flight and discussed the situation with her thinking that she had seen this situation before and she had not.  She did some investigation and spoke with a mechanic and he told her that the forward cargo was heated. I explained to her what our manual stated and where live animals were to be transported.  The Station Manager directed the ramp personal to move the dry ice to the forward cargo compartment and move the live animals to the aft cargo compartment as per our operating manual.  I thanked her for her help and cooperation and explained that both of our manuals not being in agreement is a problem and that I would write this up so that we can get this discrepancy rectified so that we are all on the same page. The Ramp Operating Manual and the Aircraft Operating Manual not being in agreement on where live animals are to be transported caused a waste of time and effort.  Also; the animal's lives might have been in danger if the temperature was too low for the extended period of time of this flight. Both manuals (Ramp Operating Manual and Aircraft Operating manual) being in agreement would alleviate this problem.  Ramp Services and Flight [Operations] should get together and clarify the procedures for this subject.

column121: While on the RNAVM XX in ZZZ1 we encountered a GPWS event. At the beginning of the approach we had a tailwind and the descent angle of the approach caused us to be a little fast starting the approach. As the pilot monitoring I should have caught this issue sooner and brought it to the attention of the PF (Pilot Flying). Because of the speed the PF disconnected the autopilot/auto throttles and slowed the plane to the proper approach speed. During the turn onto final the PF was visual with the runway and let the nose drop which caused a momentary don't sink. He corrected and the warning went away. Still with the airport visual he tried to correct on the VASI and received another momentary don't sink call at around 700 ft. We continued the approach and the landing was normal. I don't have anything to add for [this report].I have learned many lessons from this very short flight. I haven't had much ZZZ experience and my FO (First Officer) who was PF has had very little. We tried to mitigate the possible issues by having a slow cruise speed of 210 kts. and trying to get ready for the approach early. We briefed the 3.4 GP and felt we were in a good position for the approach. With the unfamiliarity of the situation and the weather in ZZZ this day I missed the strong tailwind that was making our situation worse. This put us behind and we had to play catch up. It was turbulent the whole flight and when he disconnected the AP/AT my [situational awareness] went down because I was worried about his flight path at that time. As I look back at the event and if I could do this again I would have us discontinue the approach early and come around to try again. Once we continued and got out of the [weather] and had the runway visually climbing back into it in that terrain did not seem the safest option. But if we had bailed early it would have made the situation easier the second time.

column121: While flying into Burbank at night PF (Pilot Flying) / PIC (Pilot-in-Command) elected to do visual to [Runway] 15. Clearance was granted around JANNY [and] PF took a course that meant we would intercept the final approach course from the left of centerline. PM (Pilot Monitoring) noted that we were left of centerline and that there was terrain in the area. We crossed over the ridge line at the standard 5;500 ft. but thereafter while still left of centerline the PF started a descent. PM had terrain display up on MFD and was watching; there was never a yellow or red terrain ahead of the aircraft at anytime. Yet PM noticed that the radio altimeter was showing a reading while still left of centerline. The radio altimeter reading went below 1;000 ft. and got to around 800 ft. The PM called out the altitudes as soon as they were decreasing below 1;000 ft. and the PF took evasive action by disconnecting the auto pilot and stopping the descent. Almost immediately after the radio altimeter reading went away and we continued a normal descent to landing on [Runway] 15. Taking a visual to [Runway] 15 at night is unnecessarily risky. With margins very tight on the left side of the approach course; situational awareness is reduced at night. The benefits certainly do not outweigh the risks. We never received a GPWS yet we came within below 1;000 ft. of terrain on around an 8 mile final. It is easy to become complacent with your surroundings when you can not see them; so don't bother putting yourself in this situation... The company needs to put into writing that visuals to [Runway] 15 should not be allowed at night. As PM I should have called an immediate go-around the second I saw the radio altimeter go below 1;000 ft.

column123: All three crew members experienced an odor in galleys and cabin that smelled like glue and dirty socks during taxi out; after de-icing and before take-off. We were not met by any paramedics. We were not given any oxygen. We should have put our selves on it; but we were fatigued; confused and not in correct state of mind to be making first responder decisions for ourselves. We drank water in crew room for a couple hours. We all three went to the ER fives hours later still feeling bad; to get blood tested and oxygen for dizziness. Symptoms lasted for about 11 hours. Toxic fume inhalation from air quality issue in cabin caused confusion for crews state of mind during taxi out and deplaning. We safely disarmed our doors at gate to deplane but may have made a lack of announcements and we I'll during the process. Training for CSA and Supervisors for consistency in protocol for Air Quality issues when meeting crew that reports problem. Always contact me slink and paramedics for crew just as we would passengers.
