While there was an error I do not believe an FAR was violated because ATC was diligent and noticed we were not going to make the assigned restriction and re-cleared us before the restriction. Furthermore when I apologized to ATC they said no worries have a good night and they shipped us to the next Controller. I believe this could have been avoided if my Captain and I spent an extra second looking at the MCDU before ZZZZZ3 it. I believe factors that played into this were two long legs with a 4 hour delay in ZZZ1. To reiterate I do not believe an FAR or clearance was violated; but it was close so my Captain and I decided to write a report.

column121: We were on a visual approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ at 3;000 feet. Approach cleared us for a visual approach about 7 miles out and we were giving a heading towards the FAF following an airbus. PF set 2;000 feet in the MCP and we began a slow descent heading inbound to the airport. ATC issued a 'low altitude alert' at about 2;300 feet. We leveled off and intercepted the G/S just past the FAF. In addition; we had to rapidly slow since the airbus in front slowed rapidly and ATC wanted us to slow to approximately 150 knots or less. They really did not leave us much lateral room. We slowed and configured while descending. We were never near an obstacle; nor were we a threat to another aircraft. We were still above the 1;000 feet stable approach criteria (1;300 to 1;500 feet) and met the criteria proof to reaching 1;000 feet. We were lower than what was normally flow for that area but still seamed safe. Again on a visual approach. PF stated that he read 2;000 feet at the FAF and misread the altitude. The FAF altitude is 2;800 feet. I did not reverify it since we were visual and I was working on setting up radios and configuration for landing. I assumed he saw it correctly.I can't find where we violated anything. We were a little low for the area but still in a safe position to land and had visual clearance from all obstacles. I know next time to verify the altitude in the MCP from the chart myself. That is that only thing that may have stopped the lower alt in the first place.

column121: During pushback; the tug driver did not use proper terminology. I understand that the contract ramp personnel work many different airlines; but they should have a working knowledge on the aircraft that they are pushing back; as well as some type of standard phraseology and verbiage.Upon completion of the pushback; the tug driver asked me to set the parking brake; which I did; and using proper terminology; I told him 'Brakes Set; Pressure Normal.' A few minutes later; he said to me; 'Have a good flight.' I asked him if the tow bar was disconnected and if the bypass pin had been removed; and he said 'Not yet; I'll tell you when they are.' A few minutes later; he said again; 'Have a good flight' and he disconnected the headset before I could ask him again if the tow bar had been disconnected and if the bypass pin had been removed. I rang the Ground Call button; and I was trying to use hand signals to have the wing walker inform the tug driver that I needed to talk to him on the headset. During this time; I did see the tug backing away from the aircraft; with the tow bar; and a ramp person walking away with the bypass pin in her hand. It appeared that the ramp personnel were finally starting to understand that I was trying to get someone back on the headset; when I gave them a thumbs up signal. The ramp person gave me the thumbs up signal; and they knew we were all set to go. I received the proper Salute; started engines and we taxied away.The tug driver never told me that the tow bar had been disconnected and that the bypass pin had been removed. The tug driver needs to have a working knowledge of the proper terminology to inform the Captain that the towbar has been disconnected and that the bypass pin has been removed; and to wait for the Captain to tell him that it is OK to disconnect the headset; not to just disconnect the headset on his own.Communication is paramount to prevent an accident; and in my opinion; this tug driver did not understand nor use proper verbiage/procedure during the pushback.

column123: Crew was on approach. Initial ATIS reported ceilings 400 feet and 1/2 mile visibility. We were handed off to Tower and given clearance to land number two. Preceding aircraft was instructed to expedite turnoff after landing due to close interval. At approximately 800 feet. and at the top of the IMC layer; Tower canceled landing clearance and directed a climb to 2;000 feet and track localizer inbound. Crew conducted a normal go-around. Aircraft was vectored to a second approach and a normal landing ensued.

column121: While approximately 2 hours from our destination; we discovered that ZZZZ1 weather would not allow us to land at destination. We made a decision with fuel and time to hold and then subsequently divert to ZZZZ2. The communication barrier was difficult with the controllers and while that took place we were also using the radio for Dispatch. I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) and was coordinating the divert with Dispatch and the handling in ZZZZ2. Task saturation after a long flight was certainly a challenge. I also was having freezing issues with Jepp FD pro. After being handed to ATC; we had the approach and plan in place for the approach Runway XX. On the decent the controllers left us very high even after multiple requests for lower. The PF (Pilot Flying) was using FLCH and max speed brakes most of the time. We were able to get to an appropriate altitude safely. I had a brief moment of thought about still being in FLCH on decent and through saturation; I failed to mention it. Inside the IAF I set the TDZE as normal and confirmed with crew; as we were cleared the approach. We had still been descending constantly from events before; we never really stopped descending since just after the divert was made. As we were in the arc; we were completely configured for landing and I noticed that we had descended below the published altitude on the ARC. I quickly realized we had been still in FLCH and immediately said to stop decent. We were approximately 400-500 ft. Low. And after arresting settled at about 600 below. The PF and crew were in VMC conditions. CAVOK. We were approximately 1/2 to 3/4 of the way through the arc once I noticed. We had the airport in sight and the PF elected to stay at the approximate pattern altitude as we were over water in VMC and had the airport in sight and about to turn final. The approach continued visually and the PF made a normal landing and taxi to hard stand.

column121: I awoke at XA:00 on Date and was called just a few hours later and told I was being placed back on rest; and given a XP:00 assignment. I don't understand how I'm supposed to be able to function; with less than 12 hours to adjust. I attempted to go to sleep at XJ:00 but laid awake till almost XM:00. I was awakened just after XM:00 when my phone received a text alert that my schedule had changed. I have no way to silence text alerts without also silencing all phone calls. I attempted to go back to sleep but was stressed that I would sleep through the call and could never fall back to sleep. Scheduling finally called me at XR:00; giving me absolute minimum notice to show; when I was forced to call in fatigued. I understand that this type of assignment is currently legal on paper; it shouldn't be; but I have to tell you that I flew transatlantic flights for 8 years and was never as fatigued as I have been on Reserve under this domestic FAR 117 rules. This is ridiculous. This is the second time in only 10 days that I was switched from day to night duty with less than 12 hours notice and after being awake for less than 5-6 hours. I want to make our system work so that the flights can be covered; but this current system is a system of 'gamesmanship'. No one is on the same team. Why don't we have a system where everyone wants the system to work to get the planes and passengers where they need to be? It just seems like it has become a war between the company and the union and not a great place to work anymore.

column121: First leg arrives ZZZZ mid evening; and crew arrives hotel at approximately close to midnight; after a 13-hour duty all-nighter; rests until van departure the next evening ZZZZ time ; for a report time 2 hours later and a 2-leg 14:20 duty day with 10+ hours of flying to ZZZZ1 and back followed by another 1.5-2 hours to get back to the ZZZZ hotel. With a 3-person crew; and the FAR117 limitations; the ZZZZ1 turn begins with no one properly rested (due to the 3-person crew; each crewmember gets at most 3 hours of rest on the red-eye to ZZZZ on the first night; and arrives at hotel just after Window of Circadian Low (WOCL); unable to get much restorative rest. The next night's report time is at the *beginning* of the WOCL; meaning two nights in a row of disrupted sleep (unrelated to the ZZZZ1 turn; but indicative of the poorly-built nature of this trip; the third duty period of the 5-day pairing also includes a redeye; for a total of 3 min-rest 3-pilot redeyes in 5 days). Concerning the ZZZZ-ZZZZ1-ZZZZ legs; because of the 117 restrictions; depending how the Relief Pilot (RP)  and PM split the first leg or part of the 2nd; and the expected flight time of the ZZZZ-ZZZZ1 leg; no one gets decent rest. In our pairing; I as the RP slept first on the outbound leg for 2 hours; and the PM slept next for 3; and the PF slept the entire return leg (2.5 hrs). This was FAR117 compliant; but due to pairing construction is essentially too little; at the wrong time; and contributed to a degradation in safety. It is not helped by a 2-hour ground sit (during which it's impossible to rest because the countries authorities enter the airplane for a security sweep and postflight / preflight duties must be accomplished; and the constant loud noises and aircraft motion from cargo loading/unloading). So the RP and PM sleep a very small amount during the WOCL; and the PF doesn't get a rest opportunity until after the WOCL; when it may no longer be possible to sleep.This is bananas. ZZZZ1; and the country's airspace in general; is among our more challenging operations (language; altimetry; nonstandard ATC phraseology and procedures; night/weather; unfamiliarity with fix names; etc.). Setting up a minimum crew with back-to-back red eyes and little rest opportunity in that environment is dangerous. And the crew is then left to consider a fatigue call on the ground in ZZZZ1 - one of the worst places in the world to stop the operation for crew and airline alike.

column121: In cruise I messaged Dispatch and asked the RVR for [Runway] XXR.  They told me 1400 for [Runway] XXR.  About 30 minutes from arrival we started our brief. We briefed the arrival and the approach plate for [Runway]. We then briefed the CAT2 checklist. We both put 705 feet in our DH and verified it. We did the decent check and verified it again. Did the approach check and was getting vectors to [Runway] XXR. Gear down flaps 45 before the marker.  I called 1;000 feet cleared to land when I knew something was wrong. I couldn't grasp why we only had 300 feet left to go missed. Told the First Officer something wasn't right. We hit minimums at 705 feet AGL and I called the missed. Did the missed approach; cleaned up aircraft and did the checklist. Didn't take me long to figure out what I did. The RA for [Runway] XXR is 116 feet. We put the new DH in and took our time to get set up for approach.  We got vectors on the LOC and shot the approach to a landing.We both missed the right number for the DH. I knew the approach would be to minimums so I was looking at chart in cruise so I wouldn't miss anything.  Ended up on a go around at 700 feet AGL because we had the MDA in. It was first flight of day we both felt good. Just the low visibility at destination caused a threat.Even after the lengthy briefing and checklist usage the DH was still put in there wrong. What I have learned over my career is not to get upset at the moment you realize you did something wrong.  Great training over the years and good CRM has trained me to fly the airplane. Run the appropriate checklists and then discuss what happened at a safe time later.

column121: A little while after reaching cruise altitude; the flight attendants contacted us to let us know that there was a passenger who was not complying with the mask policy.  They were handling it per their guidance and keeping us informed.  Later in the flight there had been some other problems that they had informed us about. The First Officer and I had completed a bathroom rotation just before starting down into ZZZ when we got a call from the flight attendants informing us they were [having problems with this passenger]. They just wanted to be sure we knew this. I asked them to let us know if there were any problems.  Several minutes later; we received a call that this passenger had not taken kindly to the warning and had become 'verbally combative.'  I thanked them for letting us know; and asked if everyone was okay.  They replied yes; they were.  I asked them to keep us informed if there were any changes of if anything escalated; they said they would.  At this point we had begun the descent on the arrival into ZZZ; the First Officer had been flying the whole leg.  He had been managing the radios as well while I was talking to the flight attendants.  I considered that while the situation currently was Level 1; I felt it was most prudent to get the aircraft on the ground to protect my crew and the other passengers.  Additionally; felt it would reduce my workload as well as my First Officer's if we requested priority handling.  I told the First Officer what I was considering and why; and asked if he had any considerations.  He agreed that was a good choice.  I then requested priority handling with ZZZ approach and informed them of SOB and fuel remaining.  I had sent an ACARS message to Dispatch informing them of our situation.  I called ZZZ ops and informed them of the same.  I then checked in with the flight attendants to ensure things were okay; which they were.  I informed them we were accepting priority handling and would be on the ground as soon as possible.  As we passed through 10;000 feet we kept the speed up around 315 knots to expedite our arrival.  We were given radar vectors to a visual Runway X and landed uneventfully.  We had to wait a few minutes for our gate as it was occupied.  We pulled into the gate.  The passenger disembarked and the situation was over.  There were no injuries.  After the plane was empty the crew got together in the front of the airplane for a debrief of the situation.  At the end of the debrief I asked the flight attendants if they were okay and would be comfortable with continuing.  They all felt that they were okay to continue.  When the First Officer and I debriefed; I asked him the same and he was good.  I took a moment to assess myself and determined I was good to continue as well.It is worth noting that the flight attendants did a very good job of keeping us informed as to the status of the situation.  This was helpful and good crew CRM.  They were clear in their communication; calm and professional.  My First Officer also was a model of CRM and performed exceptionally to include his aircraft handling to expedite our arrival.

column121: I was the AFA (A Flight Attendant). Every part of the flight (boarding; climb; cruise; etc.) seemed to be going fine and seemed standard. When the pilots told us to prepare the cabin for arrival; I decided to look over the PAX (Passenger) manifest before tossing it. I had used it during the flight but only looked at part of it. To be honest; I didn't read over it before we departed. When I read over it toward the end of the flight; I noticed that one PAX was listed as a Special Assistance Passenger. This PAX was listed as needing a wheelchair and as blind. At no point was I aware that we had a PAX with a visual impairment. The PAX was boarded first and the person who pushed his wheelchair stowed the PAX's luggage. When interacting with the PAX on boarding; I handed him a sanitizing wipe and he seemed to have no trouble getting the wipe from me or getting to his seat; although I didn't really watch him go to his seat. At no point did the gate agent inform us that we had a PAX with a visual impairment nor did the person who pushed the wheelchair. When the B Flight Attendant asked the gate agent if we had any specials (for the PAX count form) the gate agent said we had one wheelchair. There was no mention of a PAX with a visual impairment.We did the standard briefings (announcements and safety demo); but neither of us provided a one-on-one briefing with the PAX. We were unaware of his visual impairment. After I realized our mistake on descent; I wasn't sure what to do. I had a brief conversation with the PAX; and he seemed to look me in the eye for the conversation. After I played the final descent announcement; I showed the B Flight Attendant the manifest and how it showed a PAX listed as blind. She was surprised to see it. We discussed our situation in regard to the PAX and the possibility of writing a  report.After we landed; the PAX gathered his belongings and deplaned without help. He also told the person waiting with the wheelchair that he didn't need it. He was traveling alone and without the assistance of a service animal. He only used a simple walking cane; not a red and white cane frequently used by people with visual impairments. He gave me no reason to think that he was visually impaired; but I understand that some disabilities are not apparent. When all the PAX had deplaned; I informed the Captain of what had happened and asked for advice. He said to fill out an report because we didn't do a required briefing. The B Flight Attendant and I knew that one-on-one briefings are required; we didn't know the PAX was visually impaired.I am concerned and upset that we potentially caused a safety incident with a PAX with a visual impairment. This is unacceptable. I hope to use this as a learning experience and pay closer attention to the PAX manifest before shutting the boarding door and proactively asking all gate agents about special assist PAX that we may have onboard. I say this with caution; though. We don't always receive the correct manifest; we sometimes receive incomplete manifests with no PAX information; and sometimes we don't even receive a manifest at all. While in the end; it was my responsibility to confirm with the gate agent about special assist PAX; I feel like there was a breakdown of communication between the gate agent and me. I wonder if the gate agent knew there was a visually impaired PAX on the flight. Perhaps there could be strengthened training for gate agents and flight attendants for recognizing special assist PAX. For flight attendants; also what to do if a special assist PAX is discovered during flight and certain briefings did not occur; as in our case. As stated before; I didn't know what to do in regard to the PAX.I understand the severe safety hazards not providing a one-on-one briefing could have caused if something went wrong during flight. I hope to use this as a lesson learned and not solely rely on being informed of all special assist PAX by a gate agent. In other words; I need to be more proactive; and I need to use my resources more wisely. My hope is that this can be used as a lesson for all flight attendants so that incidents like this don't happen again. We are first and foremost a safety industry; and we failed to keep to our safety standards.

column121: While executing the ILS to [Runway] XXR at ZZZ; ATC informed us that we were following a heavy and instructed us to slow to 170kts. The Captain and I saw the other aircraft on TCAS and judged the distance to be six or seven miles. We discussed the possibility of wake turbulence but we didn't think the spacing was an issue. Then; after switching the tower; at around 3;000 feet; we were instructed to start slowing to our final approach speed. We then configured the aircraft for landing and started running the landing checklist. While listening and responding to the Captain's checklist callouts; I thought I heard someone say 'approach clearance canceled; maintain 3;000'; but I was unsure of the call sign. This was partly because the Captain and I were in the middle of running a checklist and partly because there was another aircraft on frequency that had a very similar call sign. We were Company X Callsign ABBC and the aircraft ahead of the heavy was Company X Callsign ADDC (there were at least three instances during the arrival where an instruction was given and we weren't 100% sure who it was for). I interrupted the Captain and told him that I thought tower had just canceled someone's approach clearance and asked him to query ATC to see if it was for us. The controller responded with a very urgent tone and said 'That is affirm; Callsign ABBC your approach clearance is canceled; maintain present heading and climb to 3;000. I'll have a turn for you in just a second.' As the captain was responding to ATC; I pressed the heading button to maintain our present heading as instructed; but I was confused as to what to do next. At this point we were around 2;400 feet (about 2;000 feet AFE); so a hard go-around using the TO/GA button was not required. I was not really mentally prepared for the go-around and was having trouble deciding what to do next; but ATC sounded like they wanted me to start climbing immediately to 3;000 feet; which was already set in the altitude window; so I reacted to his instruction by hitting FLCH. This caused the aircraft to apply full throttle and pitch up to maintain our current approach speed of about 145kts. We maintain this climb for several seconds until I was able to dial the speed up and get the aircraft accelerating. With everything happening so fast; and not really being mentally prepared for a go-around; I called gear up while the flaps were still at 5 which caused the landing gear warning to sound. It was a very sloppy go-around but I don't think the aircraft was ever in an unsafe state.This was my first go-around in the actual aircraft. However; I have mentally rehearsed and practiced enough hard go-arounds in sim training that the procedure is pretty much automatic and I can execute it without much thinking required. However; I can only recall doing a soft go-around once during FTD training and; as I recall; in that scenario we were not yet configured for landing and the altitude assigned was below us; so it was a simple matter of stopping the descent and flying the assigned heading. We also discussed soft go-arounds vs hard go-arounds in training and I had recalled that using TO/GA was optional but not really preferred during a soft-go around. I think there needs to be more training on soft go-arounds and the SOP should give more guidance as to preferred methods in various scenarios. Currently; the SOP does not give much guidance on the subject other than reminding the pilot to retract flaps at the F-bug or XX knots above green dot. After landing; the Captain and I discussed what I could have done better. He suggested; and I agreed; that the best course of action would have been to press ALT to stop the descent and then start accelerating before starting our climb. However; after replaying it in my head all night; I came to the conclusion that; given the fact that ATC wanted me to climb; it would have been perfectly acceptable to switch to heading mode and then press TO/GA and execute my normalgo-around actions and callouts; even though we were well above 1;000 feet AFE. This would ensure the aircraft was maintaining a safe speed while we began to reconfigure the aircraft and would have eliminated a lot of confusion that I created while I pondered what technique I should use to get us to 3;000 feet while also cleaning up the aircraft. Perhaps this should be the preferred method to execute a soft-go around when fully configured for landing and a climb is required. But perhaps there's another aspect of it that I'm not considering. The technique of pressing ALT and accelerating aircraft prior to starting the climb also seems like it would work in most situations. That's why I think the SOP should give more guidance on the subject. If there were a preferred method spelled out in the SOP; then it would eliminate a lot of the confusion and both pilots would be on the same page instead of debating on a technique for a procedure that is rarely used when there isn't really time to stop and think about it.This experience has also taught me to be prepared for a go-around at all times; not just when below 1;000 feet on an approach. Although; the spacing behind the heavy looked good to us; we should have been more prepared for the possibility that ATC would call for a go-around unexpectedly.

I queued an ACARS to Dispatch 'call me med' and waited for more information. In the meantime; I got another call indicating the man now said that he just had high blood pressure and would be okay. The load was light and we agreed to move the man to the back row and to move other passengers forward. The Flight Attendant's temperature strip was inconclusive. This information was passed to Medical. We issued the man an N-95 mask; and he wore it. The advice from Medical was to provide Tylenol and continue to ZZZ. Paramedics would meet us at the gate.IMPORTANT; it was then that FA called back to say there was an identity mistake. The actual seat assignment was XX6; not XX1. This meant that the passenger's name was incorrect during the Dispatch/Medical call. The incorrect passenger name is omitted to avoid confusion. I sent the correct name to Dispatch via ACARS.On approach to ZZZ; the man aspirated on the carpet and floor next to the last row and could not wear a mask. FA's notified me of this on taxi-in.Because of the concern for COVID-19; we made the decision that we would have passengers deplane quickly; then allow either the paramedics to the passenger; or allow the man to deplane. Inflight Supervisor and Customer Service Supervisor were at gate and aware of the de-boarding plan. The paramedic overruled the plan and rushed aboard. I ordered the First Class cabin to deplane after the paramedic passed on his way to the back. I'm glad I did.The aircraft was towed away for disinfection. column121: DEN ground instructed us to taxi to RWY 17L from E4 via mike; hold short of ED. Once on Mike northbound Ground instructed us to turn right at ED and hold short of the approach end of Runway 17R. The FO (First Officer) was in the process of completing his delayed engine start flow as I started the turn on ED. At this point I noticed traffic on short final to Runway 17R and thinking to myself that it didn't seem right to turn on ED. I stopped the aircraft as soon as it was straight and pointed east on ED. I asked the FO if he saw a sign or hold short line on his side. I saw no signage in front of us and now felt extremely uncomfortable with our proximity to the Runway 17R approach path. At this point the Ground Controller told us we were supposed to stop 50 ft. further back. I looked behind us and noticed the left wing tip was over the east edge of Taxiway Mike. I could not see a hold line below the wing. We were switched to Tower. The Tower Controller gave us a number to call for a possible pilot deviation. Shortly after writing down the number we were cleared for takeoff. As we rolled down the runway I realized we failed to complete the final items.I spoke to the Tower supervisor later that day and explained the events as they occurred. He admitted that this hot spot is an ongoing issue; the hold area is not well marked and the Controller's intent was to have us pointed east to help move aircraft through the Runway 17R approach path faster. Unfortunately the Tower had to send around the landing traffic I was distracted with during the turn because they were not sure if we would stop. I have flown in and out of DEN since the day it opened and have never been issued a clearance like this. I have always been instructed to hold short of ED when aircraft are landing Runway 17R. I believe this type of clearance should be avoided; specially in an area that is a hot spot. The aircraft behind us which received the same clearance had to confirm the clearance and the intent to hold short immediately after turning.
column123: We had a leg planned for DEN-ZZZ with Runways 17L; 17R; and 8 being used for departure.  Going westbound; I programmed and planned and briefed a 17R departure. The captain briefed a single-engine taxi.  After block out we were advised of a 17L departure.  For me that is several threats; a runway change requiring FMC programming; retrieving new performance; single-engine taxi ( increased workload; 2 engine-start flows etc); and unavoidable time when only the Captains eyes are outside the cockpit during FO single-engine duties during hi intensity ground operations @ DEN. On taxi out we were instructed to taxi to Runway 17L via Taxiway M and hold short of ED.  At some point northbound on Taxiway M with a hold short instruction in hand;  I initiated start of ENG 1.   During the engine start; the ground controller gave an additional instruction to turn right on to ED and hold short of the Runway 17R approach area.  Due to my required duties during an engine start which aren't easily paused/stopped; I could not write down the instruction; nor could I refer to my taxi diagram so that I could act as a backup-another set of eyes in the cockpit; I was only able to say-back the instruction and nothing else. The captain had a response to me that conveyed that he heard and understood the instruction.  I pressed on completing the engine-start.   I was heads down completing my duties during our expected right hand turn onto ED.  Shortly thereafter I heard the captain make a comment about an aircraft landing on Runway 17R and he brought the airplane to stop.  It was several moments before the ground controller came on the radio to say that we were to hold short of the approach area which was now behind us.  We were then instructed to continue taxi; switched over to tower; given a phone number and cleared for takeoff.

column121: During the arrival; we were given a vector and then a direct to DSNEE. As we were still in the high teens; I suggested opening the speed window at 280 KIAS (assigned speed) and then spinning it down below 250 passing around 12-13000' (due to the Captain's relative inexperience). I informed SoCal of our desire for the ILS and crosschecked my instruments and noticed we were descending through approximately 8700' still doing 280 KIAS. I gave a corrective command and immediately pressed ALT HOLD (Altitude Hold); spun back the speed to below 250 KIAS; and deployed the speed brakes. I did not say; 'My Aircraft' but time was of the essence. We slowed and continued the arrival and landing uneventfully: there was no communication from SoCal referencing the deviation.Using SPD INTV (Speed Intervene); without its protection; coupled with the distraction of SoCal's request set us up for the deviation. Additionally; the Captain is new to both the seat and the airplane.[I] suggest using all available automation to the maximum extent. We could have instead entered speeds into the CDU at the abeam waypoints and allowed the aircraft to gradually decelerate on its own (or the DESCENT page speed).
column123: I was flying. Received a vector off the arrival. Chose to use speed intervene; 280kts. Just before I went to reduce speed to 250kts for 10;000; ATC asked if we wanted the Required Navigation Performance (RNP) Z. We had set up and briefed the ILS as I had been refused the RNP Z on a prior flight. First Officer (FO) and I got distracted discussing the pros and cons of accepting the RNP Z; descended below 10;000 ft. doing 280kt. The FO caught it. We leveled off; used speed brakes; got below 250kts; and continued decent. I am a new Captain. About 150 hours on the 737; which I haven't flown. I haven't flown in the last 2 months. These factors mainly contributed to a narrowing of the big picture. Additionally; I was tired. It was night. Last leg of 3 day pairing. More than anything; don't use speed intervene without a lot of extra caution. Putting the speed in the FMC is the better way to go; it only takes a couple of seconds longer.

column121: Better monitor FO actions. Increase awareness of calculating descent points using distance from the runway to approximate a 3 degree descent path to the runway in order to avoid unnecessary and lengthy low level segments.  Flying at 3;000 feet about 15 miles WSW of IND direct to BIGRD on the RNAV Y 5R. Approach asked if we had the field in sight; we responded that we did; and then we were given a left turn pretty much direct to HUUPS; which is the final approach fix on the RNAV Y 5R; and cleared for the visual approach. Tower then handed us off to Tower. During this time while I was switching to Tower I became task saturated with my PM flying duties from the frequency change; getting a landing clearance; and the FO requesting flap configuration changes. After we were cleared to land I noticed we were just about to level off at 2;100 feet. Well below a 3 degree descent path given our current position to the runway. I had not noticed the FO had set 2;100 feet; which is the altitude at HUUPS; and started a descent as soon as we were cleared for the approach. We leveled off at 2;100 feet and continued for some time before reaching HUUPS and continuing the descent for the runway. We were level at approximately 1;300' feet AGL for a while before descending for landing. I don't think this was technically illegal or in violation of an FAR; as we were cleared for the visual and in the process of making a descent for landing; but I do feel it's not a good technique to simply set the FAF altitude; dive and drive to that altitude; level off for several miles; then continue descent once over the FAF. We were not on a published portion of an approach; and well below a 3 degree descent path to the runway. This wasn't an issue for this particular approach; but it could become an issue at night in mountainous terrain or if there are obstacles in the area.

column121: The flight crew received our flight release indicating the MEL for the RH EEC. When the crew arrived on the aircraft maintenance was already on and working numerous issues on the aircraft. The flight crew was informed that a bite test showed no errors with the EEC and and at the time it was operating normally. It was believed a ground air start error was what caused the EEC to trip off. The MEL was signed off and the release amended to show its removal. A ground air start was conducted at the gate with no issues; and the aircraft was pushed back. After a cross bleed start and concurrent with the tug disconnecting the RH EEC tripped offline. The crew ran the appropriate EEC QRH checklist directing both EECs to be selected off. Since we had previously reviewed the MEL we elected to continue. During the takeoff it was noted that the auto throttles were not responding and takeoff thrust was set manually. During climb and initial cruise it was noted by both crew members that the left engine EGT was fluctuating 30-50 degrees but stabilized with cruise power set. After approximately an hour of cruise at FL390 and 0.78 Mach the aircraft passed a front causing the airspeed to increase above the assigned speed. Power was gradually reduced to allow the speed to decrease to the assigned value. As the power was increased back to maintain Mach speed it was noted that the left engine was stuck at flight idle and was not responding to thrust lever movements. The thrust lever was positioned to the firewall with no response. As the airspeed was deteriorating rapidly the aircraft offset from the airway and began a descent while a revised clearance was received from New York via HF to return to JFK. ATC issued a revised clearance to JFK and approved the initial descent to FL360. At approximately FL370 the engine again began responding to thrust lever movement. Further descent was not considered necessary at this point and we continued to JFK since we couldn't guarantee that the engine would not stop responding again. After getting the aircraft stabilized; [we] notified via phone patch and the flight attendants and passengers were briefed on the situation and decision to return to JFK. No emergency was declared nor any emergency services requested. The flight continued normally to JFK and accomplished a normal approach and landing to runway 31R with no further incidents. Upon shutdown the crew briefed on site maintenance along with [Operations and Maintenance Control]. The issues were also written up in the log book.

column121: SNA Tower cleared us for takeoff on 20R but changed our clearance altitude from 5;000 feet to 3;000 feet for crossing traffic. We were very light and the max power setting gave us a very very high climb rate. We had a LEVEL OFF RA at 2;800 feet MSL which was the easy part. We complied and did not go above 3;000 feet as a light aircraft passed directly overhead. I believe the separation was 400 feet. Complicating this situation; and the real reason for this report; was the fact that we were given a 3;000 feet clearance and our performance was so high; we got ALT ACQ around 1;000 feet. Our automation did not provide proper guidance as the speed reverted to flaps up speed (15) and the autothrottles wanted to go to max power (takeoff power 100.6%). Also; the cutback N1 was 26% less than takeoff power! My FO had to disconnect the Autothrottles to prevent them from surging back to max power after he set them to cutback and flight directors were commanding a climb well above 10-15 degrees even though my speed was below the shark tooth. I had to fly out of the situation and my FO gave great communication as he kept our SA in focus. I am not 100% sure what happened with the automation but I believe the ALT ACQ at such a low altitude caused some serious issues. This would not have happened with a normal 5;000 feet clearance; or if we were heavy with less performance or we were doing a normal takeoff profile.However; I am concerned that with a few more variables or a crew that did not work as effectively as we did today this could have been a much worse outcome. I am wondering if we should be given 3;000 feet clearances with crossing traffic. With a normal takeoff profile it would have been fine but the max power setting and with the large power cutback for noise abatement this was a tricky situation. Compliments to my FO who took action on the autothrottles to prevent an automated max thrust climb after he pulled for cutback by disengaging them and clearly communicating that part of the problem.

column121: We arrived in ZZZ at XA:00 local time. The aircraft was to remain overnight and we were asked to leave the APU up and packs on due to cold overnight temperatures. This method was used by the ground personnel in lieu of a ground heat cart since one was not available. We left the APU running as requested and left the airport. Upon returning to the airplane the next day we found the left wing tank which the APU was being feed from only containing 200 pounds of fuel. This is a concern as there is no one on the aircraft overnight to monitor the fuel low pressure lights. If there was a delay or other situation this aircraft would have run the left tank dry causing the APU to shut down. Most importantly there would be an unmonitored low pressure fuel low pressure light. The other concern for this configuration was the outflow valve was closed manually with the APU and packs on. I understand this configuration with an external air cart on the aircraft; but not certain it is appropriate for the APU configuration. If the main cabin door were to be closed this would pressurize the aircraft completely making it impossible to access unless the fire handle is pulled in the wheel well to shut down the APU.

Fortunately; maintenance found no damage on the inspection. The flight continued normally after we received a new release.There were numerous contributing factors that led to this place. This was my first international trip in quite some time. There were many issues related to COVID-19 and catering. Chief of which was no ice being available. I tried to coordinate with the station to get some even asking if the terminal restaurants had some they would spare. No luck. There was also a discussion between myself and the First Officer regarding the rarely used method to obtain the ATC clearance in ZZZZ.The First Officer said he wanted to get home early and I believe he initiated the call to ground for the push before I was ready. I hadn't yet removed my mask. I did not have my audio panel properly configured and my mask was blocking my view of those switches. Ground Control gave us a push clearance then added a last minute query as to which runway we wanted which the First Officer and I discussed and verified.I either missed the pushback crew saying they were ready or they did not initiate the standard sequence so I had to verify that they were ready. Ground then told us to hold our push and that stopped me from releasing the brakes at that point when I normally might have done so. There was also confusion with the pushback location. I could not locate it on the charts. We were also using a gate in a part of the terminal neither myself or the First Officer had been at before.As I was re-configuring my audio panel my watch flashed a [personal message.] Although I did not read it; I noticed it. That took my out of my routine and although I felt my legs relax after I thought I hit the pedals to release the brakes; they were still set.Although I have been with the company many years; I have also not been flying much lately; 4 legs in the last 90 days or so. I also don't know why my watch flashed a message when my phone was off.In the end it was a failure to verify the status of the parking brakes. I will redouble my efforts to ensure a verification that the brakes indicate they are released in the appropriate sequence going forward.

column121: The Captain briefed that he would fly the ZZZ ILS 27R. On the arrival abeam the FAF we called the airport in sight and were subsequently cleared #1 for the visual approach. In the turn towards the final approach I lost sight of the runway. I was expecting the Captain to maneuver the aircraft to align the airplane with the approach course prior to; or at; the FAF. He turned well inside the FAF to intercept a 3 mile final. I was not expecting this and felt behind the aircraft. While on the base leg we received a radio call from Tower 'low altitude alert; below minimum vectoring altitude.' This left me even more uneasy during the approach. I expressed my concern to the Captain. The Captain was able to re-cage my situational awareness and continued the visual approach. We rolled out on final; stabilized on glide path and made an uneventful landing. We thoroughly debriefed the flight; with much attention on the approach.
column123: The FO (First Officer) had never been into ZZZ; and I hadn't been there for years. Briefing the approach; I handled the terrain" item by saying something silly like "I don't know of any." In fact there was no high terrain; but there were close-in obstacles. I mentioned that we might well get a slam dunk visual but I did not communicate to the FO my idea of normally being comfortable joining the final on visual approaches inside the FAF; about 3 miles out at 1;000 feet AGL. If I had done that fuller briefing; he would not have been surprised when I later pointed the aircraft inside the FAF. Descending on the arrival; we noted that the procedure put us on a long final for the ILS to 27R; but we both got the impression that we would be #1 to the airport and slam dunked. On downwind abeam the airport we were descended to 3;000 feet and then cleared for the visual approach. I headed over toward the ILS FAF and descended toward its crossing altitude; 2;100 feet; while I evaluated the position and energy. I saw that we were in a position to join a 3-mile final in a stabilized condition. Focusing visually on the right base leg and the airport; we were at about 1;700 feet on about a three mile base. At this time ATC transmitted; "Low altitude alert; minimum vectoring altitude is 2;100 feet." Our path looked clear ahead and on final to the right; and I did not consider ATC's radar vectoring altitude to exactly apply to our operation. Still; they were trying to tell us something! I looked to the left and saw downtown; laterally closer than desired but certainly more than 2;000 feet horizontally. I shallowed the descent as much as I could without going too high to be stabilized on final. We joined the final and landed normally.By inadequately studying and briefing the airport's visual flying environment; I did a night visual approach that was safe but that (1) concerned ATC; (2) concerned my flying partner; and (3) worst of all; surprised me about our proximity to downtown because I had not identified the high buildings as a threat."

column121: The event occurred because ZZZ is working a busy airport with one Controller utilizing all three frequencies. This is a major safety of flight issue as multiple links in the safety chain were broken that day. If the sharpness of the crews from Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z had not utilized full four ear policy and patience it could have been an issue. The actions taken by the ATC operation in ZZZ are uncalled for and unsafe. If this is overlooked there could be fatal consequences in the future. There are a few local airports in the area of ZZZ that are non-towered. If the Tower Controller delayed any further for us to be handed over to Departure; we could have had a collision or RA with an unknown aircraft all due to the unsafe actions of one Controller handling a workload bound for a minimum of two personal.On the morning of date; I was in command of flight Aircraft X; ZZZ to ZZZ1. The ZZZ Tower had one Controller working all three frequencies: clearance; ground; and Tower. This day was a busy morning with Aircraft A bound for ZZZ1; Aircraft Y to ZZZ3; Aircraft Z to ZZZ4; and us to ZZZ1 all departing at roughly the same time.When we called for our clearance on the delivery frequency; we noticed there was some bleed over as the Controller was issuing takeoff clearances. We had to repeat our request for a clearance but were given it with no issues.I released the brakes and we called for push shortly after. Aircraft Y also called for push after us. In the middle of our push back the Controller called on the ground frequency to inform Aircraft A of a delay to ZZZ2 for them.  The two began to have a conversation on ground of a game plan to be made. As their conversation occurred our Ramp crew disconnected the tow bar and gave the wave off for an all clear to a taxi.I noticed Aircraft Y had pushed off gate X and we were pushed off of X+1 with our nose in the direction of travel to only exit at [intersection] with a head on collision. First Officer and I finished our 'After Start Checklist' and cleared the area to begin our taxi. I switched on our taxi and nose lights to noticed Aircraft Y did the same. With the Controller and Aircraft A conversation occurring to what was now a clearance being given with a read back to follow there was no way for me or Aircraft Y to have confirmation one was waiting for the other.There was dense fog and low visibility on the ramp that morning. Tower does not control the ramp and a courtesy call is requested. The weather was so bad we had a takeoff alternate of ZZZ5 that morning.It was a frustrating situation as Aircraft Y and I could barely make out the 2nd half of each other's aircraft; so it was a game of chicken. I tried to call over the radio and speak over the clearance being given but it did not work.Ultimately; I turned off my lights to give Aircraft Y the right of way. As we began our taxi to Runway X Aircraft Z called clearance to get their clearance to ZZZ4 and that now was being broadcast over the ground frequency adding to the safety issue that no one moving on the aircraft surface could talk to each other.The Tower issued Aircraft Y their takeoff clearance and told us we were next. After we got our takeoff clearance; we began the takeoff roll with no issues. As we continued our takeoff climb Aircraft Z called the Controller over the ground frequency. All we heard was the Controller responding over the Tower frequency meaning he was working all three frequencies still. This delayed our hand-off to departure and made us uneasy as the Tower radar could not see our path beyond a certain mileage. As we checked in with ZZZ Departure we were given an instruction to contact ZZZ3 Center as our time had been too long and radar services with ZZZ could not be utilized further.This told me the ZZZ airport Controller took too long to hand us off and impeded the Departure Controller from doing their job properly. We did not have sufficient air traffic control separation all due to the unsafe practices of the ZZZ airport and Air Traffic Control operation at the airport of ZZZ.ZZZ needs to hire another Controller! There must be at least one person working Ground and Delivery while another separate Controller works Tower. The operation in ZZZ has been compromised and it is scary to think that the unsafe actions are acceptable to those working in the ATC system.

column121: On flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 'smoke-like' smell present in both cockpit and cabin. FA (Flight Attendants) investigated to determine source; but were unable to locate anything of note. Smell dissipated and generally disappeared in cockpit; whilst simultaneously continued in the cabin and became more present. Smell when present in cockpit was identified as smelling like burn off from automobile exhaust piping when road water is splashed on the piping. Maybe even an oil burn off smell. Definitely not the same smell as deicing fluid. FAs reported the smell was similar to the burning smell of an overheated hair dryer.On continued investigation while still climbing; FAs noticed a strong smell of fuel in the aft cabin. One FA reported development of nauseous feelings and also a strong headache. As CA (Captain) I determined that continuation was a poor choice and elected to divert to ZZZ2 as it was at our approximate 4 o'clock position and was a good Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting location should fire be present.ATC notified of our intentions and diversion was begun.No indications on EICAS; no hydraulic or fuel losses. No additional identifications from the FAs except that the odors were continually present in descent and approach and taxi and were strong. Odor returned to cockpit but only slightly.  FO (First Officer) did not report noticing it again; CA noticed only slightly.ATC requested fuel remaining and souls on board. Priority handling never declared by CA; FO never heard requested priority handling status; but it is believed that we became priority handling status. Landed opposite direction in ZZZ2 and met by Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting.Landed XR; exited runway and parked on taxiway. Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting did a drive around for any abnormalities or indications of smoke or fire and found none. Taxied to gate XX with ARFF following. Taxied behind a 777 and experienced exhaust fumes. Only reason for note of this is that the exhaust fume odor was distinctly different than the odor noticed during the flight.Parked at gate. Did not start the APU having concerns that it may have been the culprit in regards to the possible odor and\or with the potential to be a source of fire and\or smoke at parking. Ground power connected and normal shutdown and parking.Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting personnel met the aircraft as jetbridge attached. Forward FA was the reporting FA for the feelings of nausea and headache and was removed from the aircraft first. As CA I assumed her position for overseeing of the passenger. FO continued to monitor radios.FA reported the fresh air provided relief; but not complete. Was released by the EMTs and also cleared by MedLink to the hotel for rest.Passengers deplaned approximately 5 minutes after door opening. Smoke like smell in the cockpit and cabin and also fuel smell in the cabin. Diversion to ZZZ2.

column121: While in cruise flight (FL370) we were cleared to cross the ZZZZZ intersection at FL330.  The FO entered the new altitude and I confirmed it.  We agreed to start down at the TOD.  ATIS indicated that we could be landing either [Runway] XXC or XXR.  I noticed the runway condition was 555 and total runway distance for Runway XXR was 7500 feet; which required a non-standard landing assessment.  I started entering the numbers in the landing app; when I decided to look back at our progress.  I immediately noticed that we had overflown the TOD.  I alerted the FO and he selected 'OPEN DESCENT!  I knew this would be insufficient and called out 'My aircraft;' he acknowledged and I attempted to make the restriction.  I quickly realized there was no chance of making the restriction; so as I stabilized the descent; I instructed the FO to inform ATC would be unable to make the restriction (we would be high).  After that I called for 'autopilot 2 and we transferred control of the aircraft back to the FO.  ATC acknowledged the transmission and we proceeded to the destination airport without further incident.  I decided not to debrief until we were at the gate; so to avoid any further incidents.In an effort to stay ahead of the; all too often; last minute approach changes and subsequent rushed approach briefings at low altitude; I as the non-flying pilot; elected to proactively run the landing numbers and review the XXR approach plate.  The obvious problem with that is; that the check and balance system for aircraft control is compromised when both pilots are not concentrating on the more immediate task at hand. It should be noted that the FO had just come from a training event to restore currency after almost 3 months off.  My FO did list that as a threat on our very first flight of the day. As such; I had been trying to complete tasks earlier than usual; not only to avoid the problems associated with operations at ZZZ1 but also so I could more closely monitor him; but in this case it backfired.According to the report home page altitude deviations are the number one reported event; so I don't really know what could effectively prevent this type of event. Possibly; the best we could hope for is to reduce the frequency.  For my part in reducing the frequency of which this event occurs; I will not address any other actions until the descent is begun and the altitude clearance is assured.

column121: Inbound to ZZZZ on ZZZZZ Star.  Taken off STAR early and cleared direct to ZZZZ1 VOR.  We were instantly 1;800 feet above the path.  Proactively used speed brakes and planned to slow and extend flaps when below 20;000 feet; but were then told to keep speed at 250 KTS.  Lowered landing gear shortly after passing ZZZZ1 to get back on profile.  Was able to regain the VNAV path just prior to ZZZZZ1 and at Vref +10 per procedure.  Flaps were at 25. Frequency was very busy and sky hazy. Very late hand off to Tower.  Localizer did not correctly ID until just prior to FAF.  FO was very busy with frequency changes; configuration changes and checklist.  Tower did not clear us to land; but instructed us to continue as an aircraft was in position on our Runway; XXR. Another aircraft was holding short of XXR waiting to cross.  At 1;000 feet I was at approach speed and called 'stable;' but was distracted by no landing clearance and aircraft on runway.  Aircraft in position was cleared for immediate takeoff; we were cleared to land; and other aircraft was given clearance to cross XXR.  Departing aircraft was slow to accelerate.  Passing 500 feet FO made 'stable' call.  Shortly after we received an aural alert indicating we did not have landing flaps selected.  Flaps indicator showed flaps at 25 degrees verses the planned and briefed of 30 degrees.  I realized I had not asked for flaps 30 and was now below 400 feet. Elected not to make a configuration change to 30 degrees below 1;000 feet per procedure.  Hesitant to go-around per procedure because I wasn't sure if the crossing aircraft had not just departed the inboard parallel Runway XXL; and the late departing XXR aircraft had just rotated.  With the very hazy sky I was concerned about a conflict and /or overtaking the other aircraft during the go-around to increase speed to Vref+10 and land with flaps 25. Landing and rollout were normal.Despite adequate and recent experience into ZZZZ; these particular controllers were hard to understand.  FO had to ask for clarification a few times in the last 1;500 feet FAF. FO had just returned from 7 months of leave; was called out on reserve; and had only flown once earlier; and 4 times in the last 7 months.  I briefed the arrival and approach thoroughly and early; but it was a Max effort with the direct clearance.  I believe he got distracted from completing the checklist when the localizer did not ID until just before the FAF.  I was distracted from not calling for final flaps with the aircraft on the runway and the hazy conditions; and the late localizer ID.Add to the note of being at Vref +10 by the ZZZZZ1 fix; to be at final landing flaps. This may have helped me if I had a goal to complete that by the fix.

column121: Prior to Final approach in ZZZ; approach vectored us very close to the final approach course with a 30 kt tailwind on base and at 4;000 ft just outside ZZZZZ for the ILS XXR; assigned 190 kts. As we intercepted the course the autopilot flew past the localizer at close to half scale deflection; as it would not correct course timely. We also had to descend and slow down to configure for final approach within 3 miles of final approach fix. As the autopilot was correcting for that we set 3;000 ft for the missed approach altitude. A CAS MISCOMP status message appeared and the altitude alerter came on would not stop ringing. When we changed navigation source to green needles; the localizer would not capture with the autopilot; therefore the glide slope would also not capture. During the navigation source change; my flight director on the first officer's side became erratic and I lost the localizer transmission. We decided to execute a missed approach due to being unstable along with the flight instrument errors. Tower assigned us a heading and altitude and we reconfigured the aircraft for the go around all while the altitude alerter was blaring. During straight and level flight; we decided to reassign the FCP to heading and altitude. Once established; we turned the autopilot on and all instruments worked correctly. The altitude alert ringer was still buzzing so we decided to silence using Data Control Unit (DCU) audio buttons to declutter the situation. After completing proper checklists; we decided to continue on with another ILS XXR and executed approach and landing normally. After shutdown the altitude alerter still continued to ring until AC power was switched from the APU GEN to EXT AC. We wrote up the problem and notified maintenance.ATC giving us tight vectors with a tailwind on base along with our equipment malfunctions. The altitude alerter sounding loudly along our flight directors being erratic caused task saturation to the captain who was PF. As PM I helped the captain de clutter the situation and to reminded him to just fly the airplane which he did well as we tracked the localizer and conducted the go around. Once we silenced the altitude alerter it became much easier to fly the aircraft and we were able to conduct the next approach successfully.Possibly asking for a slower intercept speed or lower from ATC. The equipment malfunctions lead to the approach to become unstable and that's why we conducted a go around. I could have possibly contacted tower a few seconds earlier to ask for a vector and altitude but it was quite difficult with the task saturation being as high as it was; especially with the altitude alerter loudly sounding. Overall it was a great lesson in always being able to maintain control and fly the aircraft regardless of the state of automation it is in which I thought we did a great job of despite the system malfunctions during a high work load environment.

column121: In preparation for our arrival into DEN we briefed for the CLASH 3 RNAV arrival and the ILS to 35R as this was the expected runway from our direction of arrival. We also included in our brief the threat in DEN of runway changes and how we'd handle that especially during the descent phase on the arrival. About 20 NM from the waypoint CLASH on the arrival ATC informed us to expect runway 35L. We then re-set up for that runway and re-briefed. There was still plenty of time for this and there was little time compression. One point of confusion; however; was that the CLASH 3 has a transition for RWY 35R; but doesn't for 35L; which only has a point at which to expect vectors. We spent some time studying the arrival and approach plates to ensure that was the case to make sure we weren't missing something. I asked my F/O to double check as he was the PM and I wanted to concentrate on the descent as the PF. This has always been confusing as some arrivals and approaches have transition points and some don't. There should be some consistency. This was the beginning of some of the time compression which would later result in some workload management issues.Some point after this ATC broke us off of the arrival and instructed us to descend to 9000 feet and gave us a heading. They then assigned us to RWY 35R. We related that we'd just been assigned 35L and they reiterated we were now reassigned to 35R. This resulted in a very rushed set up for 35R as we were now pretty close in to the approach environment. I asked the F/O to set it all up so that I could continue to fly. I quickly dialed in what I thought was the 35R LOC; but it turned out not to be. I could see that he was struggling and tried to help him out. In hindsight; this was a mistake in workload management because I should have let the F/O do all of the set up. I verbalized that we didn't need to re-brief for 35R as we'd already briefed it and so had a plan. Again; in hindsight; I'm not sure this was a correct call; but we literally did not have time to brief at that point.Shortly after this we were cleared the visual approach to 35R.  We were roughly 7 miles from FRONZ and discussed not descending too quickly so as not to bust the floor of the Class B airspace. At about the same time ATC asked us to slow to approach speed for traffic ahead of us for 35R. After slowing we ended up just about 2.5 miles in trail.  At this point we were apprised of traffic for 35L and received a TCAS TA because of the assigned heading we were given to intercept the LOC for 35R. We both saw the traffic and I decided to hand fly from this point on as we had an overshooting crosswind and given our heading there would have been a good chance of an overshoot of the LOC.At FRONZ I asked for gear down and flaps 15. At about this point I noticed that neither the LOC or GS were engaging but I had the runway and the PAPI and decided to continue as we had been cleared for the visual. The FO asked if I'd like him to try and dial in the correct LOC and I said yes if he had the bandwidth to do so. Soon after we passed through 1;000 feet and we both missed the call out as I think he was still trying to dial in the LOC frequency. Also we never accomplished the Landing Checklist as we never got to final flaps. We got to 500 feet and we made those call outs. At around 400 feet AFL we received a Too Low Flaps GPWS warning and my knee jerk reaction was to call for FLAP 30 once I realized we were still at FLAPS 15. I don't know if the FO ever selected them; however. I quickly realize this was the wrong call and called for us to go around and the FO called for it at about the same time. We executed the missed approach with no issues and were vectored expeditiously for a second approach and landing without further incident.The FO is not submitting a report as far as I'm aware as we had no ATC deviations or non-compliance with FARS.
column123: This is a report regarding Flight X ZZZ-DEN regarding the changes and ATC clearances we received during our descent and approach to land in DEN.When we reviewed the flight plan in ZZZ we loaded the CLASH3 STAR with runway 35R being our selected landing runway. The flight plan had 17R; but DEN was landing North so that was the only change made to the plan on our part versus what dispatch had planned.Prior to TOD the CA fully reviewed and briefed the STAR and approach that we were expecting. We were fully prepared to execute this plan. Upon checking in with a close in DEN center controller we were advised to expect runway 35L with the EBBLR transition. There was some discussion regarding the EBBLR transition by myself and the CA as we were attempting to figure out if the transition and how the transition linked up with the approach. However; we did this again prior to TOD and were able to be prepared for the new arrival transition and approach. As we descended into Denver; we were handed off to DEN APP. This controller changed our runway back to 35R. We were well into the descent at this point and fairly close to the airport. The CA instructed me to load up the new approach and as I was attempting to do so ATC took us off the arrival for vectors and speed changes. At this point we were South of DEN but still fairly close in. I was still working on getting the FMC setup when ATC vectored us due West and then turned us on to final for 35R. The vector was vey poorly planned by the controller and both the CA and I could see that we were going to blow through the localizer if we allowed the A/P to handle the intercept. The CA disengaged the A/P and made a manual turn to join the localizer. At this point we could both see that the vector had us close in behind another airplane in final. ATC requested that we slow to 160 knots. The CA asked for me to deploy the gear and the flaps to down and 15. Shortly after ATC then requested us to slow to the slowest possible speed. Both the CA and I were closely monitoring the separation between us and the preceding aircraft. At this point I noticed there was a message on the FMC scratchpad that I had not seen before and did not recognize. I don't remember exactly what the message was but it did indicate that there was a conflict between the FMC selected approach and what the VHF radios were tuned to. I was rapidly trying to get the correct frequency on the NAV radios but my JEPP app on the iPad was not responding quickly as I was attempting to zoom in to view the frequency box. At this point we were somewhere around 1;000 feet AGL. The CA announced that he had the runway and the PAPIs in sight and was going to land and just disregard the FMC He was busy attempting to slow and again we were both concerned about the separation between us the preceding aircraft. That was what are focus was on at this point. I cannot recall if either the 1;000 ft or the 500 ft call outs were made. We were both totally task saturated at this time. At some altitude below 500 ft we received a warning message 'too low-flaps'. We both looked at the flap position and realized we were still at flaps 15. The CA called for flaps 30 and I monetarily selected flaps 30 before advocating that we needed to go around. The CA also realized we had to go around at almost the same instant I was stating that we needed to go around. So we executed the go around. We did have the 10;000 ft foot missed approach altitude selected in the MCP so we were climbing to that altitude. However; while just climbing through 7;000 the tower told us to maintain 7;000. I advised tower that we were at 7;200. Tower instructed us to maintain 7;100. We descended back to 7;100 feet and flew runway heading and completed the rest of the go around profile. Tower asked us for the reason for the GA and I replied 'configuration'. They handed us off to approach and we were vectored back around for another ILS to runway 35R. We ensured everything was properly setup and landed without further incident.Some comments about this incident. Both the CA and I had discussed the threat of Denver and how they often make changes to arrivals and approaches during cruise. In fact the CA had been reading in the flight ops newsletter on his iPad about the problems we have been having with arrivals into Denver. We were both fully aware that Denver presented a threat and thought that we had planned and were prepared for our arrival. Had we been cleared as planned per our original plan we would have been fine. Even after the first change to runway 35L we had time to plan and brief. It was only after the final switch back to 35R that we both began to become task saturated with the speed changes; the off route vectors; the FMC programming; the NAV radios; the poor vector to join final; and finally the separation between us and the preceding aircraft and the speed changes made while on final in regards to that aircraft. The amount of items needed to be accomplished while this was occurring in the terminal area was long and complex. We both became so overcome that we must have failed to accomplish the landing checklist; which would have had both of us realizing that we were not in the landing configuration.We made errors along the way; failing to get some of the call outs accomplished; FMC programming; and NAV radio frequency selection among some of the errors. However; many of these errors were driven by the nature of the changes being made by ATC in regards to arrival vectors; speed changes; runway and approach changes among other demands being made by ATC in a very time compressed period while flying within (or near) the terminal area.One more note about the runway changes in Denver. I know Denver and am aware of its threat even on departure. So while we were getting ready to depart and head to ZZZ2 I asked the ramp controller which runway was in use for the ZZZZZ SID. He stated XXR. Yet; when we received our push clearance 15-20 minutes later he told us to expect runway XY. I don't know if he was given bad information by the ATC tower or what happened; but yet again here we are in a high workload situation having to make changes to the FMC and request new TO data.Because of our short turn time in Denver the CA decided to debrief the entire arrival event into Denver while in cruise flying back to ZZZ2. We spent a good 30-40 minutes discussing the flight. Threat and errors were discussed; we used the briefing cards and identified what had occurred on the flight. I am not going to make excuses for the errors that we made; even if they occurred during a task saturated situation. However; a couple of my observations from this event were that we had talked about Denver ATC being a threat. We thought that we had addressed this threat by a good solid brief for the originally planned arrival; even after the change to the 35L arrival; we had time to plan and brief. We were ready; but ATC in Denver threw us some many changes and curve balls that we both were task saturated to the point leading to an undesired aircraft state. Fortunately; both the CA and I followed our training and SOP. safely executed a missed approach; and subsequently landed safely and uneventfully on the next approach.

column121: While waiting for the airplane to be towed to the departure gate; I ate a heavy breakfast and did not consume any coffee as this was an Air Carrier X operation and I anticipated coffee being readily available on the plane. I forgot to select the NAV mode on guidance panel and we continued on the previous heading for 3 more minutes.  I snapped to attention ATC reissued the Direct SUNED clearance and after a moment of confusion as to why the clearance was reissued; I realized that the guidance panel was still set to HDG mode. Driven by adrenaline; I remained mentally aroused and vigilant for the remainder of the flight.Cause - PF's Postprandial lassitude caused by failure to ingest a suitable amount of caffeine following heavy breakfast.  PM inattention/distraction was also a factor.Ensure personal availability of postprandial drowsiness countermeasures (aka Coffee) and remember to verify changes on flight mode annunciator.

column121: The incident took place at ZZZZ on runway XX; where aircraft must back taxi to use full length. The CA (Captain) and I had just deadheaded down; with our first flying leg of the trip being from ZZZZ to ZZZ. I was feeling refreshed as I had napped for about 2 hours on the [deadhead] down. We had 1.5 hours on the ground; so did not feel rushed; even though it was my first time to ZZZZ. Boarding; preflight; briefing; clearance; pushback; start and taxi to hold short of Rwy XX were uneventful. The CA briefed language as a threat; but the clearance and ground control went smoothly. Initially we held short at taxiway E. Following a departure by another AC we were cleared to back taxi down to Runway XX approach end; and lineup and wait. While in our turn around; an aircraft checked in on final for our runway; I visually identified that aircraft and said aloud that he looked to be on a 6 mile final. Tower told that aircraft to continue.Once aligned with the centerline; I confirmed with the Captain that he was ready to depart; then told Tower Aircraft X in position; ready for takeoff'. Tower responded that we were cleared for takeoff runway XX; and to contact departure when airborne. I replied that we were cleared for takeoff; runway XX; and echoed the departure frequency we were just given.The Captain and I confirmed with each other we were both ready to go and he pushed up the throttles. As we both were watching the engines spool up; we began to roll forward down the runway. Tower then said something to the effect of "Aircraft X; please do not takeoff; there is an aircraft...' As I started to look up; my first thought was about the aircraft on final. The CA and I both looked at each other; confused about the nonstandard radio call. Tower sounded a bit flustered; and then I saw 2 strobe lights at the far end of the runway. I said 'Reject' aloud; then answered tower "Aircraft X rejecting takeoff.' The CA executed the rejected takeoff; but at only 40 knots or so; was really just bringing throttles to idle stopping the aircraft. I called 'Remain seated; remain seated' on the PA.At that point I started to see an aircraft that went with those strobe lights and a white twin engine civilian airplane lifted off our runway. Somehow this aircraft had gotten onto or been cleared onto RWY XX for an intersection takeoff. There had been Spanish being spoken on the frequency but I did not connect that discussion with an aircraft on our runway. The same frequency is used for clearance; pushback; ground; and tower control.As we stopped...perhaps 500-1000 ft. down the runway; tower then told us we were cleared for Takeoff again. We replied negative that we would need to taxi clear or do a 180 turn and go to the approach end. Tower then told the aircraft on final to go around while we taxied. The CA called for the Rejected takeoff checklist; which we ran. We used the card first then QRH back cover. The CA also used the PA to briefly explain what had just happened. We quickly discussed our options; and decided that we could do a 180; and rerun the before takeoff checklist. Subsequent lineup; and takeoff were uneventful."

column121: I was the pilot monitoring and my First Officer was the pilot flying on Aircraft X from ZZZ1 to ZZZ.  We were rather high and fast at 6;000 feet with 250 knots when ATC cleared us for a visual approach for [Runway] XXL (backed up by RNAV XXL).  Approach clearance included the altitude restriction to cross ZZZ2 VOR at or above 2;500 feet which is normal when landing south at ZZZ.  However; in our effort to lose excess altitude and airspeed quickly we got busy; and that created a distraction in the cockpit.  The result was our crossing the VOR at around 2;200 feet (RNAV FAF altitude).During our post flight de-brief; the First Officer told me that he was not aware of the safety alert memo on the chart page; which cautions pilots on being high and fast when landing south.  He also told me that he was not sure of the location of ZZZ2 VOR on his navigational display.  None of that was communicated while in flight.  My being very familiar with operating in and out of ZZZ; and the past experience of working well with this particular First Officer; led me to assume that he was well aware of the uniqueness of the local procedures.  I should know better than to make assumptions about my crew's awareness.  What I should have done was bring that alert memo to his attention when he did not include that in his briefing.  I should have realized that the First Officer's recent flight experience might have been lacking due to COVID pandemic induced schedule reductions.  Again; a thorough briefing without my assuming First Officer's knowledge and awareness could have prevented the altitude deviation.  I will be careful going forward.
column123: We were vectored off of the ZZZZZ arrival (landing south) for the visual [Runway] XXL. At this point; we were still holding 250 KIAS at 4;000 feet. We were given a heading to intercept and a clearance for the visual approach with the restriction to 'cross the VOR above 2;500 feet.' Although we had the aircraft stabilized by 1;500 feet AGL; we may have missed the crossing restriction by approximately 300 feet. During my approach briefing; I failed to notice the safety alert box located on the chart page. When we received the crossing restriction in the clearance; I struggled to find the VOR on the approach plate (RNAV XXL). First; I did not know which 'VOR' the clearance was referencing. Second; the ZZZ VOR is not charted on the RNAV XXL approach plate. This caused a brief moment of confusion allowing me to get 'behind' the aircraft. Instead of arming NAV mode; I engaged APPR mode. The Captain objected and NAV mode engaged. Realizing that we were fast; high and becoming task saturated with automation; I elected to disconnect the aircraft and fly the approach manually. We used gear and flaps to reduce airspeed before I lowered the nose to put the aircraft onto a glide path. We intercepted the glide path from above and managed to establish a stabilized approach by approximately 2;200 feet AGL.  However; in my assumption that we were high on the approach anyway; I did not verify that we crossed the VOR at 2;500ft. The Captain made mention of this after the flight ended in the debrief. He believes that we may have actually crossed the VOR at 2;200 feet (300 feet low).I realize that my failure to thoroughly review and brief all necessary approach plates resulted in missing critical information that would have helped us avoid the threat of this unusual crossing restriction.
