column121: Prior to initiating descent to ZZZZ1; the flight crew contacted ZZZZ Center and advised that we were unable to accept RNP-1 (Required Navigation Performance) arrival procedures. At this point; Center instructed the flight crew to fly an RNP-1 arrival despite having been informed of the incapability and the flight crew reiterated the fact they were unable to accept the arrival. Instead; the flight crew requested to fly direct to ZZZZZ waypoint for the start of the RNP RWY (Runway) XX approach. However; Center ignored this request and instructed the flight crew to fly direct to ZZZZ1 VOR and expect the VOR-A approach (Jeppesen Plate [Page]). When the crew once again requested to fly direct to ZZZZZ for the RNP RWY XX; Center repeated the instruction to fly direct to ZZZZ1 and expect the VOR-A approach without further acknowledgement or explanation of denial. The flight crew speculated that Center's refusal to assign the RNP approach was due to misinterpretation of the flight crew's inability to accept the RNP arrival; and efforts to clarify this case were also ignored by Center. The Captain (Pilot Monitoring) selected the VOR-A approach in the MCDU (Multi-Purpose Control Display Unit) and verified the route information while the First Officer (Pilot Flying) briefed the approach plate. At this time; both crew members observed what appeared to be inconsistencies between the MCDU approach database and the Jeppesen approach chart; specifically that the waypoint on Chart X did not match the waypoint shown in the MCDU routing; nor did the MCDU approach procedure indicate the required procedure turn under routing [FLP page] or Procedure Turn Info page [NAV - Page 2 - Patterns - Procedure Turn]. As the workload for the flight crew increased due to the inconsistency between chart and MCDU database; Center's refusal to assign a more effective approach; continuing descent towards mountainous terrain; and multiple segmented and non-standard clearances from Center that threatened to interrupt critical flight deck operations (notably the approach briefing); the flight crew elected to fly the VOR-A approach under raw data (green needles). All elements of the planned approach thus far mentioned became void after the flight crew received the hand-off to Approach Control who instructed them to fly direct to the airfield and complete a visual left-hand traffic pattern from overhead the runway.This flight crew highly recommends that an investigation be conducted into inconsistencies observed between the Jeppesen approach plate for the ZZZZ1 VOR-A Approach [Chart] and the MCDU database for the EJET fleet; namely the incorrectly labeled waypoint identified as ZZZZZ1 on the chart. This flight crew also highly recommends that effective communications be made between [Company] Flight Operations and the [Country] Air Traffic Control agency to ensure better understanding of which procedures [Company] flights are able to conduct and which procedures they are not; specifically the differences between RNP-1 'Arrivals' and RNP Approaches.

I also feel misinformation or agenda also play a role on differences regarding relative issues.Keep the current Pilot protocol which works well and imposes minimal restrictions regarding operational safety.  Clarify Flight Attendant protocols so they do not conflict with the cockpit.   To each individual this pandemic is relative and emotional. Passing through 5;000 feet we called the 'airport insight' and received the clearance for the visual approach for Runway 28. By the time we were abeam the airport flap 1 was down and altitude was 2;400 feet descending to 2;200 feet which was final approach segment altitude. Even though I was fully aware of the presence of obstacle (1;687 feet) on the path of our downwind I was confident that 500 feet margin and few thousand feet right of the course would give us good margin for safety. As we were getting close to the tower crane 'terrain' aural message came and after 2-3 second later 'terrain! pull up!' message came. I applied immediate max power and established pitch between 15-20. The message lasted few seconds and we climbed about 2;700 feet. After the conflict was resolved I intercepted the final course and follow the PAPI to the runway as normal operation.When we have received the visual clearance about 20 miles away I bugged the altitude down to 2;200 feet assuming within the 10 mile radius to the airport there cannot be anything that can pose threat to our path. Even though I was aware of the Tower; I didn't mention it during my briefing and considered it a big threat. When the Captain brought me an attention about the Tower once we were getting closer to it and asking me to turn inside the final approach point I delayed his suggestion wanting to intercept the final course outside the FAP. I could have been clear to ask him his intention or worries as we are nearing the obstacle and get the concurrence from both of us that 500 feet is enough or not.1. Better understanding of EGPWS logic could have given me the conservative altitude margins. 2. Detailed briefing; I could have planned better plan by flying higher or going around the tower instead of over flying it. 3. Rushing; I could have gone further out and fly higher to intercept instead of tightening my base turn to join right at the FAP.

column121: In ZZZ we attempted to start number two engine using APU air and it spooled up abnormally slowly; and I noticed that the EGT seemed to lag. At 45% N2 the start stagnated and decayed until a 2.5% N2 decrease and Engine Fail indication on the ECAM. We stopped the start; then following guidance in our paperwork; we started number one (which also stagnated a little bit but then started normally) and then attempted a second start on number two using cross-bleed from the number one engine. We allowed the engine to spool up to 25.7% N2; then added fuel. At starter cutout; the engine hung again; dropping to about 43.2% N2 and hanging there before slowly spooling up to about 43.8% N2 when it timed out for the start and Engine Fail was indicated on ECAM again. Our Quick Reference Handbook said we could attempt a second start after the first hung start; but that maintenance action was required if the second start failed. At that point we requested a tug and BTB to our parking space. This is where Maintenance Control got involved. At first they suggested that we defer the APU bleed; however it was obvious to me that the air was not the problem (we used a separate source for each start); so I told him the APU bleed deferral was not sufficient. Then he suggested that a problem with the Integrated Drive Generator might be causing the hung start and suggested we defer that; and I agreed it could be tried. As part of the maintenance action during start the Inetgrated Drive Generator was disconnected and deferred; and the Airworthiness Release in the log book was signed off; then we continued getting the jet started and were on our way. During the flight the APU was running as required by the deferral; and at 36;000 ft. it automatically shut down. I attempted to start the APU; and on the second try; it started. I requested and descended to a lower altitude of 30;000 ft. and the APU operated normally for the rest of the flight. If I had not been able to start it; I would have had to advise ATC and divert. I wrote up the APU under a P code for momentary or transitory malfunction. In ZZZ1; maintenance checked the APU for any failure codes; did the repetitive inspection for oil quantity for the Integrated Drive Generator deferral; and signed off the APU. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed the situation and agreed that the APU was not malfunctioning and may have had a momentary problem with operating at high altitude. We accepted the jet for the leg to ZZZ2. With a fresh Airworthiness Release in the log book; we started the number one engine first; then started number two using cross-bleed at the request of maintenance. The number two engine came close to exceeding time limits; but did eventually spool up. We were filed for 33;000 ft.; and at that altitude the APU did the same thing--it shut down--and we were able to get it started again on the second try. We requested and descended to 29;000 ft. for the remainder of the flight. Again; the APU operated normally from there on; and again; I wrote it up with a P code for the shut down. I also made a comment in the logbook about the number two engine start; even though our flight paperwork said that comments for a successful start were not needed. There I made a note that the EGT from fuel introduction to the point where the start stagnated; then started to spool up; seemed abnormally low and was at least 50 degrees cooler at 45% N2 than the other engine. The stagnated start was evident from fuel introduction until after started cutout when it became apparent that the engine was not ready to continue the start on its own. The Integrated Drive Generator has nothing to do with the EGT during start. I suspect something else is going on here; perhaps a Electronic Engine Control problem with the fuel mixture at high altitude; or a sensor malfunction. On further reflection; I feel that the deferral of the Integrated Drive Generator was inappropriate for the problem we had; and I should not have accepted it. It created a problem where we could have been forced to request priority handling and divert. It is likely that whatever is wrong with our engine starts does not pose a safety of flight risk once we get the engine going; so it makes no sense to do a deferral that could compromise safety. Until this is figured out; the guidance needs to be specific and it needs to go out to everyone in the maintenance and crew pipelines and it should be operations friendly. My recommendation is that everything in the fuel system be checked in case it is causing the starting problem for cold engines at high altitude. I think that the bleed system is less likely to be the issue because of the low EGT I saw during all four start attempts on that engine. I also recommend that maintenance be able to attempt at least one more start before the aircraft is taken out of service; and that crew get more guidance concerning the problem. 'Maintenance action' is not enough to let a Captain know what to expect or what to accept. I also have felt for a long time that our systems manual has been scrubbed of a lot of detail about systems with which we do not directly interact; so we are less able to make informed decisions and instead have to rely on experience. That will not always save us from making the wrong call. Everyone in this situation acted in good faith; and I am not writing this report to cast any doubt on anyone. I only want to point out a safety issue that we can avoid in the future.

column121: For the ILS Runway 04R at ZZZ; performance numbers were run for a Flaps 30 landing with a good stopping margin at Autobrakes 3. ATIS winds were calling approximately 070/13 - no gusts. Upon switching to Tower at ZZZZZ on the localizer course and tracking the glideslope; Tower cleared us to land with winds now gusting to 20. As PF (Pilot Flying); I elected to add 4 knots to the Vtarget and as an added Safety measure at ZZZ; I selected Autobrakes MAX to compensate for a slightly increased approach speed. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) attempted to quickly re-run the performance data; but the gusts were not yet accounted for in the METAR. Rather than going heads down any longer inside 1;000 feet AGL; we agreed a 4-5 knot addition to VTarget and using Autobrakes MAX would be more than sufficient to account for the gust factor.At approximately 500 feet AGL; we received a GPWS Too Low Flaps Alert. The PM immediately called for the go-around and it was initiated. A quick scan of the flap handle and I realized that I had neglected to call for Flaps 30 from a Flaps 15 setting; and the Before Landing Checklist was not run. We were quickly vectored around for another uneventful ILS. The minor distraction of adding a gust factor and changing the Autobrakes setting sent me out of a normal approach configuration sequence and we ended up both missing the final flap setting and subsequent checklist.With the normal ZZZ procedure of not contacting (and often not switching to) Tower until reaching the fix at about a 5-mile final; it's possible for us to miss out on cues to changing weather on the ground. We were number 3 or 4 in a sequence of landings on 04R. Had we switched to Tower five or more miles sooner; we may have caught the gusting winds earlier and had more time to type in the adjusted winds and send away for the performance numbers prior to 1;000 feet AGL. This was another series of events combined with mild fatigue that led to poor task prioritization on our parts.
column123: The short version is that we got 'Too Low; Flaps' at 500 feet because we were at Flaps 15. We went around. Planned winds were 070/7. Tower winds were 070/12G20. column121: While in line for takeoff on Taxiway for XXR; we received a notification from the flight attendants that the cabin was filling up with smoke which was coupled with a foul odor akin to burning rubber. We smelled the odor at the same time the flight attendants notified us of the smoke. I asked them if it was thick enough to block view of the back of the aircraft and if they thought we needed to evacuate right away. They answered no to both questions. I then told them that we would be moving to a cargo ramp to run a QRH and if they thought at any point we would need to evacuate while moving to call me back and we would stop immediately. I also informed them that the next time we stopped would be the last time we would move without calling them and that once stopped; if they felt the need to evacuate; they were to do it. We taxied to the cargo ramp just south of taxiway after alerting ATC that we were [requesting priority handling] and would be pulling off to the side to run a QRH and to have the fire trucks standby. We ran the entirety of the smoke fire fumes QRH; which had us deactivate the PACs (Air Conditioning Packs) and close the bleed valves. We elected to not drop pass O2 or go on O2 ourselves as we were not having any adverse reactions; but just dealing with an unpleasant smell in the flight deck. We called the flight attendants at this time and asked about the passengers' condition and they stated that everyone was fine. The smoke slowly dissipated throughout the rest of the event. At this point; we decided to go back to the gate as the smoke was no longer producing from the vents and the passengers were not complaining about any issues when asked. We cancelled [priority handling] but requested that crash rescue follow us to the gate. Once arriving at the gate with the aircraft shut down and the flight deck door open and main cabin door; we had one woman reportedly having bronchitis coughing to a large extent. She was the first off. I was not aware she had an adverse reaction until pulling into the gate. We deplaned everyone as quickly as possible and had Maintenance confirm that PAC 2 was the culprit. To my knowledge; all passengers refused medical attention. We later got another aircraft and had all passengers board.The probable cause was something happened with the Right PAC as we were single engine no APU taxiing to XXR with Engine 2 running.

column121: TCAS RA on arrival into ZZZ [airport]. Assigned descent to 7;000 feet and vectors to final by ZZZ Approach. We reached 7;000 feet and noted approach was extremely busy where the Controller was being stepped on seemingly more than half of her transmissions. While level at 7;000 feet the TCAS noted a proximate target converging from 1 o'clock; 400 feet below. We attempted to contact Approach but there was zero opportunity to get a word in due to the sheer amount of communication on frequency. I advised the Captain PF to 'get ready' while we attempted to locate the aircraft visually. A few seconds later the TCAS noted traffic and ordered a very shallow climb. I announced to ZZZ Approach that we were responding to an RA; but I believe I was blocked; the frequency still jammed with constant communication. A very short time later the controller issued traffic to us and I again advised 'Climbing on RA.' Controller replied 'Roger' I believe and the event was over shortly after. We returned to 7;000 feet and were vectored for the visual; but the controller still had to vector us around multiple VFR targets on our way to the runway. Most significantly we were cleared for the visual approach; but were restricted to flying and intercepting between 5 and 7 NM from the airport due to area traffic. This caused a perceived limitation that pilots are not used to. The CA/PF then overflew the Localizer slightly attempting to maintain these limitations. The aircraft was clearly stable by 1000 feet and we continued in to land; but this was following an incident due to the same cause.Cause was due to the intense level of traffic in ZZZ Approach's airspace. I spoke with a contact at ZZZ [Approach] later who noted the Controller had 15 active aircraft not including the VFR targets attempting to get clearance from the closed airspace; Practice IFR traffic; and VFR flight following requests. The Controller was doing an excellent job and maintained a very professional demeanor throughout. There was just no reasonable way for Controller to maintain communications with the volume of aircraft. I am not sure; but this could have been a result of reduced staffing due to COVID. Maybe there was an East and West ZZZ [Approach] sector available; but no staffing to accommodate. My suggestions would be to either split ZZZ Approach or to draw a new arrival for ZZZ airport to reduce the amount of communications and possible routes needed for the controllers.

column121: Flew ZONNA1 arrival to TUS. I was PF (Pilot Flying) and did the arrival briefing prior to descent which included terrain hazards and the MSA. Both pilots had terrain selected. Approach control gave us a clearance to turn right to 270 and descend to 10;000' for sequencing. Soon after this clearance we entered IMC. Passing north and abeam Mt Lemmon at about 10;300'; we got an EGPWS TERRAIN PULL UP warning. I executed the EGPWS Recovery Action. Almost immediately we went VMC. After passing the MSA of 10;700 and visually verifying terrain clearance; I resumed normal flight; leveled at 11;000' and informed ATC that we had responded to a GPWS terrain warning. They acknowledged and gave us a descent to 9000'. Remainder of flight was uneventful.Either the Terrain system gave us a false alert or we were given a clearance to descend below the radar minimum altitude. We never got any indication on the Terrain display. STAR page showed us north of Mt Lemmon and the terrain depicted around it. While we had good terrain awareness; I should have queried Approach about an IMC descent below the Sector MSA.I recommend a Radar Minimum Altitudes chart be included in the Jeppesen pages for TUS.

column121: ATC turned us onto the approach while still at 4;000. Told us to 'maintain 3;000 till established cleared ILS [Runway] XXL. FO (First Officer) put in 3;000 in the altitude selector and I acknowledged it. Once established; instead of selecting 2;700 feet for the FAF altitude he rolled the altitude selector to 3;300 and started a slow descent. Stated he was going to just control the altitude himself. I thought that was strange; but let him do it figuring it was just a technique he liked to do.As we approached 2;700 feet; he was still descending at ~700 FPM; so I realized he was going to blow through the altitude. I told him he needed to stop descending and return to the FAF altitude until we intercepted the GS. The first time I said this he seemed confused and didn't really do much. I said more sternly that we needed to climb back to the proper altitude. This time he initiated a climb back to the proper altitude and we were still stabilized and fully configured by 1;000 feet AGL. ATC did issue us a low altitude alert as we were climbing back to the proper altitude and we got a single 'Glideslope' callout from the aircraft.The cause was the FO's improper use of the altitude selector and VS (Vertical Speed) mode. Contributing was me allowing him to do the method he did instead of asking him to just put the FAF altitude in the altitude selector till GS intercept.I should have insisted that the FO put the FAF altitude in the altitude selector; especially in IMC. I also told him afterword's that he could have just stayed at 3;000 once established and intercepted the GS from there since at that point we were already close to GS intercept.
column123: Cleared ILS [Runway] XXL; we were given an intercept heading and told to maintain 3;000 feet. The Controller kept us close and fairly high before clearing us for the approach. We were at 4;000 feet when cleared. Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring); First Officer was PF (Pilot Flying). Once established; PF started down with vertical speed to capture glide slope by 2;700 feet at ZZZZZ. PF moved altitude knob up to 3;300 feet from 3;000 feet instead of to 2;700 feet causing us to go below published altitude by almost 500 feet. Was immediately corrected and aircraft was stabilized. Given a close proximity intercept; task saturation was high with intercepting; radio communications; and configuring aircraft. Should have cross checked better and stated intentions more clearly (PF to PM).If crew starts to feel rushed or task saturation is high; ask for longer final or a more stable intercept from ATC. Never let cross checking suffer due to task saturation; should always come first. PM should state approach intention more clearly while getting established. Don't have tunnel vision (Example Focusing on getting configured and not having correct altitude set).

column121: Operating flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After landing on Runway XX; exited on Taxiway A and turned left on Taxiway C; and believing that Tower had actually cleared us to taxi to the gate; we started to slowly taxi; when Tower called us and asked that we call Ground. We called Ground and he stated 'You started to taxi without calling us; and crossed Runway XX; which is an active runway'. We had barely started to taxi on C. We had read the NOTAMs; and in fact; Runway XX was 'NOTAMed CLOSED'; so it could not be an 'Active' at all. Regardless; we asked Ground for taxi clearance to the gate; and received clearance to the gate via 'C.' We did not want to argue with the Ground Controller; but we do know that Runway XX is Closed at ZZZ1; so it's not Active in any way. We asked the Ground Controller if we should 'expect any paperwork'; and he said 'no'. I do not believe we did anything wrong; but it's better to be safe and proactive; and learn from our possible mistakes.We had flown into ZZZ1 previously (a few days before) and due to controller shortages or consolidation of ATC positions (During COVID-19 times); the Tower normally gives us the taxi instruction after we cleared the landing runway. This time; we cleared the runway and thought we had heard the Tower tell us to 'taxi to the gate' (as they have been doing recently). We started to slowly taxi on Taxiway C and that's when Tower asked us to 'call ground for taxi;' something they had not done in the past 3-6 times we had landed there recently. So; probably I was expecting the same ATC procedures to happen; but regardless; in the future; will come to a stop on the taxiway and not move until further taxi clearance is received.I would suggest to avoid being complacent; and instead of expecting the same type of ATC handling from small airports as we may be getting every day during COVID-19 (combined controller positions; where there is perhaps combined Tower and Ground; or even Approach/Tower/Ground Controller); and instead treat it just like a busy airport.

column121: I returned to work after a 3 month absence. I am still qualified on the module. I was assigned as the trainer to Mechanic Y. I was training him on the stator case assembly. The procedure that I was taught; and which had been in use as long as I can remember; was to slide the case and vane assembly; so that approximately one third of it overhung the table surface. Then the bolts were tightened from below with a ratchet with a socket and long extension; repositioning the case and vane assembly as necessary until all bolts were tightened. At the time of the incident; I was not in the work area; having gone to the restroom.Support the case with a hoist and sling before tightening the bolts. This should be added to the job card.
column123: One week after return from 3 months off and being the first time working on this unit as a trainee.On Graveyard shift I was working on the module and order # XXXX. Inspection will be called to inspect the unit.I would add to the job card to support the case with a hoist before tightening the bolts. Or developing a fixture that would allow to reach the bolts from the bottom without having to move part of the case off the edge of the table.

column121: I was performing a functional test of the stall protection computer. On step XX; the task tells you to put the aircraft in the weight off wheels configuration. On the first page of the task for putting the aircraft in the weight off wheel configuration you are told to pull and tag Circuit Breakers (CB): CB P-1; A12; A13; A14; G14; & CB P-1 lower U7. On the second page to pull and tag CB P-1 lower T7; T8; T9; CB P2; N6; H8; CB P2 lower S1; V5 and CB P-5; B10.I pulled the circuit breaker on the first page but failed to pull the circuit breakers on the second page of the task. On the next step on the functional test of the stall protection computer you are told to set the air data test set to 90 kts and the altitude to 18;000 feet. During this step is when we noticed smoke coming from the left pitot probe. I ran out to check the pitot probe and saw that I melted the pitot probe test head to the pitot probe. I quickly removed heat from the pitot probe.To pay more attention to the Aircraft Maintenance Manual and to double check all the correct circuit breakers are pulled.
column123: While performing a functional check of stall protection system we were required to put aircraft in weight off wheels and put aircraft at 18;000 feet and 90 kts using pitot static test set. column121: I was deadheading on Aircraft X. I identified myself to the A Flight Attendant (FA) (as I always do) as a safety and security asset.The flight was nearly full.  During boarding a man who I later learned was Mr. X approached my seat.  He was wearing a camo gaiter around his neck which was partially covering his mouth but was not covering his nose. As he approached; I identified myself as a crew member and politely asked him to pull his mask up over his nose.  He complied but said that I should pinch my mask tight over my nose.  I didn't quite hear what he said so I queried him.  He said; 'You should pinch down on your nose to close the gap at the top of your mask.'   My mask was an NP95 which had no gaps anywhere around my face.  It was my sense that the man was being sarcastic and antagonistic.  I said nothing further to him.I advised the FA A what happened before we pushed back.  She told me that the man had boarded without his face covered and was told to cover his face.  Thus he had pulled his face covering off his face between the time he boarded (when he was told to put it on) and the time he approached me; which was no more than thirty seconds. He clearly had no intention of complying with the mask policy.  FA A asked me to brief the Captain about the incident and asked if I would talk to the CSR agent whom she wanted to speak with Mr. X. I agreed.  Before departure I walked into the jet bridge and spoke with FA A and the CSR.  I briefly explained what I observed and what he said to me then I went back onto the airplane and took my seat.  A short time later I observed Mr. X walk back down the aisle past me.Sometime during the flight FA A advised me that Mr. X had been [violating other regulations].  She advised me that Mr. X demanded to know the crews names (including mine) but that she did not give him any names. She was clearly concerned about this and I could see how his actions were distracting to the flight crew and were thus interfering with their duties.  She told me that she was going to have CS meet the aircraft and asked me to stay as a witness.  FA A as well as the rest of the inflight crew were nothing but polite and professional the entire flight; when I observed her dealing with Mr. X or otherwise.After leaving the aircraft I was standing in the jet bridge and spoke with a CS Supervisor.  Mr. X walked by me and said in an aggressive and hostile tone; 'I want your name.'  I told him that I could not give it to him and that I could not speak with him about this matter.  He again demanded my name and moved closer to me.  I backed up.  He then raised his camera and said; 'I'm taking your picture.'  I stated; 'Do not take my picture.'  He said; I'm taking your picture.'  I quickly turned around and walked around the jet bridge corner toward the aircraft door.   I do not know if he took my photograph or not but felt that his forcing his camera in my face was one of belligerence; hostility; and aggression.  I felt threatened.  All of this simply because he was asked to properly wear his mask.  After the CSR Supervisor and Mr. X walked into the terminal; I remained in the jet bridge as I did not want to encounter Mr. X again.When the CSR Supervisor walked back onto the jet bridge; I explained to her that I could not have my photograph taken and suggested that if he loitered around the terminal waiting for me that she please call law enforcement.  I asked her if she felt he was being hostile and or belligerent.  She agreed that he was.  After some time; Mr. X left the area; and I departed the terminal.Based on his behavior and actions I would strongly urge that Mr. X is not allowed to fly on our airline in the future.

column121: It wasn't supposed to be a very long leg or a long day. The plan was to fly from ZZZ to ZZZ1; grab a quick snack and go to ZZZ2 for the overnight and good food. But; that wasn't what happened.  Snow flurries forced us into unplanned deicing. Bad alternates required reworking and refueling. In the middle of deicing; a sudden snow squall sent visibility plummeting and negating any holdover times. New takeoff alternates then had to be amended onto the paperwork; and re-validating required new paperwork. To describe our departure out of ZZZ as a struggle would be an understatement. But; ever so slowly and methodically; we did eventually depart to ZZZ1. It was on arrival that we were notified that our overnight had changed and to contact scheduling on the ground. So; you can imagine that when we landed in ZZZ1; we were mentally bruised; hungry; tired; and on edge. The landing was normal; as was the taxi to our planned gate. What confused us is what we saw upon turning to face south; looking at [Gate X]. There was nothing. No rampers; or wands or even lights. It was a completely empty and dark. I set the parking brake and asked my FO (First Officer) to send another in range report and commented that we should probably call ZZZ1 OPS and see if they had changed our gate. FO dutifully called OPS on the number two radio so I dialed the north ramp frequency into radio one to monitor. At that exact moment the ACARS message returned as my FO was repeating what OPS had just said; gate change to [Gate Y]! I released the parking brake and began a slow turn to the right when I realized I wasn't at an outstation in the middle of nowhere or on an uncontrolled ramp. I had lost all situational awareness and was in the middle of ZZZ1 moving without permission! I immediately stopped the aircraft and called North Ramp with the gate change. He replied yea there was a gate change and 'did i just do a 180?' I don't recall saying much before he asked 'and are you still moving???' I immediately replied we were not moving. At that point I was told I should never; ever do that and that he had numerous aircraft with beacons on trying to push. I should have apologized right then but instead fumbled though the gate change and having the pushing aircraft in sight. I still can't believe I would make such stupid mistake. I can't believe I didn't apologize. I was just beat up and wanting desperately to just take a five minute brake. Instead I let my guard and awareness down which led me to make a very stupid move.

column121: We departed on time for a XX minute flight. Climbing through 10;000 feet I chimed the flight attendants and we continued our climb to 21;000 feet. Center was telling me to expect bad rides all the way to our destination. So when we leveled off at 21;000 feet. I made an announcement stating that the ride was going to be rough and that I would keep the seat belt sign of the entire flight. I also asked the flight attendants to remain seated for the duration of the flight as well or so I thought. The ride was not good. Continuous light occasionally moderate turbulence. The arrival is challenging on a good day and today was no exception. We were dealing with a complex arrival; turbulence; icing and multiple changes to speed and altitude. We were cleared to descend via the arrival with no speed restrictions with about a 90 knot tailwind.We would be early. Around the time that we started our descent I noticed that someone was trying to use the door code to gain access to the cockpit. I immediately declined it and made sure door was locked. The Pilot Flying and I both thought that was strange so I tried calling back to a Flight Attendant to see what was going on. That was the first indication something was wrong. When I turned on the speaker for the cabin I could hear an audible cycling noise. When I tried to chime the flight attendants I couldn't hear the chime and I could not hear any voices on the interphone. I tried to make a quick announcement but nothing was coming out back in the cabin. As the Pilot Flying and I were extremely busy managing the descent and approach we heard a knock at the door and could faintly hear a voice. Pilot Flying turned around and saw a note on the ground that said INTERPHONE INOP.I wanted to get up and grab the note to try and write something back but we were too busy. A few minutes passed. The cockpit door lock code was entered again and I denied it a second time. I tried to yell as loud as I could that we got the message. I think they must have heard that time because they stopped knocking on the door. We landed and began our taxi to the gate. After clearing the active runways I had Pilot Flying call maintenance and inform them that our Cabin Interphone and Public Address system was inoperative. We taxied to the gate and shutdown. After the shutdown checklist was complete and before the forward door was opened I got up to check on the A Flight Attendant and see if everything was OK. He was visibly upset. After the passengers got off the other two Flight Attendant's joined us up in first class to discuss what had happened. A Flight Attendant said that it was the scariest flight of his life. He said that after we had hit a rough patch of turbulence the cabin lights in the plane started to cycle on and off. They were still doing it after I went back to talk to them. He then had tried to call me to see if everything was OK but couldn't reach me. He thought that maybe we had lost pressurization and that we might have been incapacitated. He tried the door code to maybe get a peek inside to see if we were OK. He left a note under the door in hopes that we would grab it and write back. Only after the last time that he tried the door lock and I denied it did he hear me yell through the door. The other two flight attendants were also upset that they couldn't communicate with me. I spent at least 15 minutes with them trying to explain why I couldn't respond to them even though I wanted to.Trying to unlock the cockpit door without my authorization put me on high alert. This is not something I expected. If this had been a different flight with more time I would have taken their note and responded to it and sent it back. That would have been the best way. I tried yelling through the door; but it is loud in the cockpit and only on the second time did they hear me. If we had lost pressurization the masks in the back would have dropped and they would have felt it in their ears. The first time I denied his access to the cockpit door he should have known we were OK. I cannot just open the cockpit door without knowing who is behind it. My first priority is to fly the aircraft. I just didn't have enough time to respond to them the way they wanted me to.I tried to address all of their concerns and I did understand that they were upset. I wrote up the Public Address system as well as the Interphone system with their input to give the mechanics all they needed to fix the system. Maintenance came on board and reset the system. I tested the PA and both forward and aft intercoms with the Flight Attendants and in front of maintenance to make sure everything worked. Maintenance signed off the system and we than headed back. After our initial conversation about what had transpired I thought all Flight Attendants were OK just a little rattled but good enough to continue. If I had known they still had reservations about what had happened I would have immediately responded to them. My crew always comes first.
column123: During our descent on the arrival we heard a knock on the cockpit door. column121: My first attempt at writing this portion did not save so I will attempt it again. We had an A321 sharklet. Every portion of the beginning of the flight leg from gate departure; takeoff and climb up to the fume event was normal and routine. At sometime above 10;000 ft. we got a call from our #1 FA (Flight Attendant) telling us that the FAs in Economy Class more towards the rear of the aircraft were smelling a sweat odor and a more robust glue type odor. I believe from my prospective that the odor came from the back from the wings black wards because we did not smell anything in the flight deck and no one smelled anything in first class; #1 FA or forward section of the cabin behind 1st class section. Captain began trouble shooting the problem with the QRH guidelines and the FAs that was smelling the odors. One of the FAs was feeling ill from the fume which was strong in the area they were working. Passenger in that area smelled the odors as well. Captain asked if she can continue or do we need to get back to the gate in ZZZ so she can seek medical attention. She was not sure if she wanted to continue on toward ZZZZ1 or return. Captain asked the #1 FA to monitor the FA's condition and if she worsened we will return to ZZZ. While we were discussing the QRH fume trouble shooting pages and making plans to return to ZZZ or another airport that may be closer to our position if we continued to fly farther away from ZZZ; the #1 FA called and told us the FA that was feeling ill was on O2 and was not getting better. So we notified ATC that we will be returning to ZZZ which was the best option to land. We [were given priority handling] to expedite our return to ZZZ and so the FA can get the medical attention she needed. As we began to descend into ZZZ I remember it was below FL180 and through landing that the odors began to infiltrate the flight deck and the #1 FA and passengers began smelling it too. We donned our O2 masks. It was a sweaty smell and it also had an Elmer's glue order to us. The odors continued until we arrived to the gate. The FA that was really ill went to the hospital and the remaining flight crew continued with us to ZZZZ1 with a replacement FA.I don't know of any causal factors that would cause a fume event other than fixing the problem of the source that caused the fumes from escaping and preventing and future leaks from going into the cabin.The only thing that would prevent this from happening would be a complete redesign of the airplane systems that keeps the cabin ventilation isolated from any possible fume leaking into the cabin.

column121: We were waiting to take off. The aircraft that took off ahead of us reported hitting birds on take off. The controller asked if they hit the birds directly over the runway; the crew confirmed it was. We were next for takeoff when the controller asked if we had heard the report from the aircraft ahead. We said we did. Tower then delivered a caution about possible FOD (Foreign Object Debris) and birds on the runway and cleared us for takeoff. We refused the clearance and asked that the runway be inspected. We were then informed that it would take a long time for an inspection; we said we will wait. This seemed to aggravate the controller. Tower continued to give takeoff clearances until eventually no one wanted to go until the runway was inspected. This seemed to expedite the runway getting inspected. Once it was deemed safe and free from FOD; takeoffs resumed.I then reached out to an airport authority and their ATC group. They informed me that they have an agreement between the ATC and the Airport Authority about such events. If at their airport that same report was made on takeoff they stated the runway would have been closed for an inspection. They also stated it takes less than 5 minutes At DFW I waited longer than that due to refusing the takeoff clearance.I then took the question to the APA National Safety Committee and asked what they knew about procedure when this happens. Coincidentally; on that call was another pilot that had the same thing happened to them at a different airport. As we have been researching this we are finding there is no standardization from airport to airport on this. Some airports have written agreements between ATC and Airport Authorities and others don't. Does this infer that certain airports take safety more seriously than another? It is factual that the Captain will always have final authority. But shouldn't ATC procedures across the system be uniform with regard to concerns with the runway condition? To give a takeoff clearance with no attempt to inspect the runway in order to keep traffic moving seems at odds with a culture of safety.

column121: Taxing from the device pad for departure we came very close to coming in contact with Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y had been given clearance to taxi to the runway while we were still finishing up de-ice and neither the Captain or myself as First Officer gave it much thought. When we finished the de-ice process I called for taxi and we were given clearance to taxi. The Runway Visual Range was being reported at the time of 1;000 ft. so the visibility was obviously a contributing factor in the described events. As we were on Taxiway A approaching an intersection; I began to notice some lights on the right hand side of the airplane. I assumed that I was seeing hangar lights as they did not appear to be moving. Looking back this was due to the fact that ourselves and Aircraft Y had roughly the same ground speed and therefore the lights were staying in the same position on my window.As we got closer the Captain and I both realized at about the same time that what we were seeing was Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y must have seen us about the same time because we both came to a stop. When we stopped on the slick taxiway we were probably no more then 20 or 30 ft. away from Aircraft Y. We began to taxi away and as we did I asked ground to verify that we were in fact cleared to taxi to the runway. They stated that we were. Aircraft Y then asked the same thing and ground replied that they as well were cleared to taxi to the same runway. Due to the 1;000 ft. Runway Visual Range I know that Tower could not see where either of us were. I think that the normal low visual procedures of reporting when passing certain points would have saved this from happening. I think that Ground thought that Aircraft Y was already at the end of the runway when we were cleared for taxi and for some reason Aircraft Y was delayed.
column123: We were departing. ATIS prevailing visibility was 1/4 mile in freezing fog. After start we went to device pad 1 and completed Type I and Type IV deicing. Ground gave us taxi instructions and to hold short the ILS critical area. Taxi was uneventful until reaching an intersection. Aircraft Y had been cleared to taxi to the same runway and we nearly met at the intersection. We both applied brakes. Aircraft Y told Ground they would 'give way to...' us. After starting to taxi we called Ground to confirm our taxi instructions. Aircraft Y did the same. We were both cleared all the way to Runway 12. Aircraft Y was cleared to taxi before us and either taxied slow or delayed their start. Ground could have confirmed their position before clearing us to taxi.

column121: After takeoff at acceleration altitude I called for 'flaps 0; climb checks; pitch mode.' The PM (Pilot Monitoring) began the duties; however at the same time we were told to immediately turn right and level off at 3;000 feet as there was an aircraft that was not communicating with Tower headed straight for us. This diverted our attention from the task at hand. I suspect the PM omitted retracting the flaps accidentally and I failed to notice. Once we were clear of the traffic we were handed off to another frequency on which we were told to look for yet another aircraft in close proximity. By the time we were clear we were through 10;000 feet and due to the distractions we forgot to complete the climb check. I initially began accelerating and reached about 265 knots before I decided to slow to complete the second part of the ice test. Once the test was complete (at around 18;000 feet) I began accelerating and again reached about 265 knots before we realized the flaps were still set to 9. We slowed; retracted the flaps; contacted Maintenance and continued the flight without further incident.No real suggestions. It was human error on my part. I should have been more vigilant and will be in the future.

column121: In our initial climb to 6;000 feet we were instructed by Departure to turn off course and given a fix to fly to. I confirmed the fix with the CA (Captain) and pressed Nav Mode on the FMS. I looked over to my PFD to set the new altitude assigned by Departure and the CA looked away at the same time. Shortly thereafter; Departure called and asked us if we were turning on course. We both looked up and realized that the Nav mode had not captured the course. I immediately turned the heading bug towards the course line on the display; while the CA notified the Controller that we were correcting and turning on course.While compensating for winds and flying via the heading bug; we started to analyze the problem. Shortly after changing the AP to the CA's side; we were able to correct the Nav issue; as the AP was functioning properly on the CA's side; I continued as the pilot flying. About 45 minutes out; the CA left the flight deck to use the LAV. As he returned; he noticed that we had about 8 status messages that popped up sometime after he had left the flight deck. I was engaged with a short conversation with the FA (Flight Attendant) and did not notice the display of messages until he returned. The status messages were flight control related; noting flight spoilers; rudder; etc. The CA referred to the QRH for landing data as a precautionary measure; in the event of a total system failure to those systems. The CA Then notified ATC of our potential systems status and requested deleting the LAHSO restrictions. ATC was unable to comply.Later; as we were given an intercept angle to intercept the final approach course; I selected the NAV button and was waiting for the intercept. We had a [heavy aircraft] on our left and we were paying close attention to that traffic; when we noticed that the aircraft had blown through the center line and was deviating right. The CA then asked me what was going on and while trying to process the information; I replied; 'I have no idea.' At that time Tower called to query our actions; It was as if the aircraft had a mind of its own and before I was able to kick off the autopilot; the CA then asked for the flight controls. We landed without incident and all flight control systems were operational throughout the landing phase; as all the spoilers had deployed. The AP had remained on the CA's side throughout the entire approach.Hindsight; I told the CA; that the one course of action we could have taken at the onset of discovering that the AP/Nav was not recognizing my side; we should have changed roles and allowed him to be the Pilot Flying. With the unexpected behavior of the FMS during the critical phase of flight; I was in total agreement with the CA's actions and decisions; I believe his actions were appropriate and timely while operating in the essence of safety for the passengers and crew.

column121: I checked in with the gate agent prior to my flight to ZZZZ.  I don't recall if any passengers were boarded but there were no passengers that I remember waiting to check in because it was still pretty early.  As I walked down the jet bridge I noticed a Flight Attendant walking the opposite direction.  I had not met her prior as I had not been to the aircraft yet.  She told me she was trying to get better cellular reception so she could complete her COVID-19 form which is required for entry into ZZZZ.  When I boarded the aircraft; I met the other two FAs.  At no time did I notice any passengers boarding or on our aircraft.  After checking the aircraft maintenance log; flight documents; etc. I briefed the A FA.  I only briefed the A FA as passengers were now being boarded.  I assumed the other two flight attendants were on board.  I was completely unaware that we didn't have minimum crew while boarding.  Approximately 10-15 minutes prior to departure; the A1 FA informed me that she was informed that we had boarded without minimum crew.  I think the COVID-19 online form (for ZZZZ) was the reason that caused this problem.  I fly this trip nearly every week and it's generally always a bit of a scramble at the last minute to get the form completed by all crew members prior to departure.  In addition it is a very difficult form to electronically fill out for the first time.  I believe the FA was only trying her best to complete the form prior to boarding. Perhaps a reminder to both cockpit and cabin crew that a COVID-19 declaration form is required for entry into ZZZZ.  And that the form takes a while to complete as it NOT intuitive and can take a few attempts to complete it and requires sufficient WiFi or cellular signal.

column121: On Date aircraft XXX had fumes/smoke in the cockpit smell noticed by the flight crew.The event occurred due to a razor blade that was left inside CBP1 possibly during a visit to ZZZ for the ADS-B modification in the middle of month of 2019 and I could have possibly left it there during the installation of breaker CBP1-XX during the mod. Due to the length of time between when possibly leaving a razor blade and when it was discovered I cannot recall whether or not I used a razor blade in the area. But; typically; when I do wiring work I don't use razor blades to cut tape or remove wiring insulation. As we usually have the equipment to remove fiberglass tape (a wire spoon and flush cutters or just peeling it off by hand;) and wiring insulation (standard wire strippers and the twisted pair stripping tool). Reflecting on the experience I would hope that even during the crunch time of the push to finish the ADS-B modifications on all our aircraft before the deadline that I would have continued to practice strict FOD control.My suggestion is to not use lose razor blades when doing work on wires unless absolutely necessary; and to practice strict FOD control and to perform detailed FOD inspections before every panel close-up.

column121: During the DINGO 5 arrival into TUS; after waypoint MAVVA; I continued on the charted 075 degree heading passing through the Runway 11L localizer course; not complying with the textual instruction to intercept the I-TUS localizer course. ATC gave me vectors back around to re-intercept the localizer course; and a normal landing was made.The cause of the event was a failure to cross-check the textual instructions with what is displayed on the chart. Contributing factors were as follows: 1) A 'Descend Via' clearance was not issued. ATC instructed to 'Descend and maintain 8;000 feet; and EXPECT a visual approach.' I misinterpreted that to mean he would provide vectors to the final approach course; or clear me for a visual approach passing MAVVA.  2) I found the verbiage on the chart confusing where it states 'Runway 11L EXPECT approach clearance'. I interpreted that to mean once established on the 075 heading from MAVVA; not upon intercepting the localizer; as normally you would not intercept a localizer without ATC clearance or prior to accepting a visual approach.To avoid a recurrence of this event; a thorough briefing covering all noted and textual information should be conducted and cross checked prior to every landing. While my briefing did cover all of the information on the plan-view of the arrival; I missed a crucial piece of information solely located in the textual description that was not well depicted nor defined on the plan-view. It would have been helpful if ATC had offered us a visual approach earlier; directed us to intercept the localized after MAVVA and THEN expect approach clearance; or have the instruction to Intercept I-TUS localizer clearly printed on the plan view. It is worthy to note; the ATC controller stated 'Yeah; you're not the first airliner to do this' both over the frequency and on the telephone while speaking with him after landing. This leads me to believe that this could be a common mistake that could be corrected easily with a revised; emphasized; note on the arrival chart.

column121: I was First Officer and pilot monitoring for a reposition flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. When I arrived to the airplane; the Captain was already there with multiple maintenance technicians working through a dual inoperative GPS situation. The consensus was to defer both GPS units; along with the associated MEL items. After processing our 9 MELs during our pre-flight discussion we waited approximately two hours for a flight plan to be filed due to the issue with ADS-B being inoperative.During the after-start checklist; the CONT CAB ZONE TEMP fault appeared on Master Caution recall. We complied with the QRH and MEL and contacted Maintenance Control for deferral under the 'flight crew placard' option. The Captain and I discussed the phrase in the QRH; 'if the light extinguishes when Master Caution System is reset; no further action is required' - and he noted that this does not alleviate us from the need to defer the item per the MEL XX-XXY. Along the same time; the Captain noted that the 'dispatch alert' box was unchecked; so after the deferral was complete we resumed normal operations.After takeoff we experienced two additional master recall lights - 'Anti-Skid Inop' and the 'Reverser' on the overhead panel.Shortly after we leveled off at cruise altitude the dispatcher asked if we had added a new deferred item after pushback. We responded that we had; that it was XX-XXY. He advised us to fill out a report; despite the 'dispatch alert' box not being checked.The reposition flights after long-term storage lend themselves to multiple maintenance related issues and could be planned ahead to be operated by Functional Check Flight pilots.The filing of our flight plan took nearly two hours. Not knowing the exact cause of the issue; it would be helpful for future flights to review the process for filing flights with inoperative GPS and ADS-B to minimize future delays.
column123: Aircraft X was a reposition flight for aircraft (tail) in storage several months.  The aircraft was dispatched with multiple MELs.  We waited over two hours for Dispatch to be able to get ATC to accept a flight plan into the system for a clearance.A Control Cab 'Zone Temp' light illuminated during Master Cation recall during the after-start checklist.  QRH procedures were followed and Maintenance control was contacted for a crew MEL (XX-XXY) before departure despite the misleading 'No further action required' guidance in the QRH.Two more master caution lights were encountered after takeoff (Master caution 'anti-skid and reverser.')Dispatch sent an ACARs message after level off advising us to submit a report for not getting an amended release for XX-XXY before departure.  We responded that a Dispatch alert is not required for XX-XXY.  Dispatch responded 'They give us a heads up anyway.'  We did not believe we violated any maintenance/dispatch procedures but were led to believe we had.Reposition flights from long term storage are a severely irregular operation and should be conducted by the Functional Check Flight department.

column121: While on visual approach to COS [Runway] 35L; crew both identified a very large building under construction with crane offset between 1.7 to 2 miles from the runway threshold. At approximately 1.5 miles from threshold; received EGPWS (Electronic Ground Proximity Warning) 'Obstacle; Pull Up!' warning. Aircraft was stable and on visual glide path as verified by FMS 3 degree visual glide path indicator and also visually with Runway 35L PAPI. Sink rate at time of incident was 500 ft. per minute. As the building was either directly underneath or just behind aircraft; no other obstacles were noted and aircraft was stable and on glide path; PIC (Pilot-in-Command) decided this was an erroneous warning and elected to continue flight. Landing was uneventful. During debrief; both crew members agreed that the message was erroneous and must be an anomaly caused by the new construction and a go-around at that time would be futile. If the weather was not CAVU (Ceiling and Visibility Unlimited) an immediate go-around would have been performed. There is a current NOTAM (01/037) regarding a crane at this location but the crane was offset from the flight path and at 300 ft. AGL. An issue exists with the EGPWS system and this new building construction that will trigger false warnings and may cause aircraft to go-around unnecessarily.

As the Captain started to correct back to the PAPIs we received a low alt alert from Tower; along with a glide slope warning from EGPWS. The Tower saw us correcting during the call however and noted disregard. As we were able to re established on glide path and were stable before 500 ft. we continued the approach to land. Not sure why the flight director disconnected from the glide slope and defaulted to pitch hold; and if was something we did while configuring; or if it was a fault of the plane or ground equipment.I was distracted by the running of the checklist and did not see the entities deviation from glide path; more why the autopilot changed modes. column123: ILS [Runway] 16R into Seattle; visual conditions; LOC and GS captured with autopilot engaged. After aircraft configuration complete I felt like we were low. ATC was informing us about low altitude alert; then immediately said disregard. I regained glide-slope utilizing PAPI.Not sure why the GS disconnected; if it was something we did wrong or if it was a fluke or something to do with the system. I talked to the Captain taking the airplane about the event and suggested to use the ILS. Lesson learned; at all times monitor glide path and lat/vertical modes. Stopped the aircraft and made a very 'To the point' PA that any non-compliance with Flight Attendant instructions; particularly pertaining to facial coverings; would have 'un-favorable' consequences. I had already made it clear that facial coverings were required while on-board during my 'welcome aboard' PA. Conferred with FAs that my second PA was successful; and we continued taxi and takeoff. Once established in cruise; the FAs informed me that they were having problems with FC passengers willfully being non-compliant regarding wearing a facial covering after being advised as such multiple times by at least 2 different FAs. My FAs had even switched working positions in order to try to de-escalate the situation and convince the passengers to comply. I commenced communication with Dispatch and relayed the situation with advisement to contact customer representatives. Shortly thereafter; due not only to non-mask wearing; but also; disruptive behavior by passengers requested to be re-seated in Main Cabin. I further relayed this information to Dispatch. It was at this point the FAs gave the notification of passenger misconduct warning. Shortly thereafter passenger started harassing my FAs with constant cornering them in the FC galley and demanding trivial items. At this point; even after a tremendous amount of patience; de-escalation attempts and warnings by the FAs; and with building harassment and aggressiveness being demonstrated by passengers; I notified Dispatch that we would be diverting to ZZZ1. We landed at ZZZ1 non-eventfully; without being overweight and without declaring an emergency. Passengers were removed from the aircraft. We departed ZZZ1 and arrived in ZZZZ uneventfully. Please allow me to acknowledge my FAs for their display of 'Consummate Professionalism' during this flight. They were tireless in their attempts to de-escalate the situation in hopes of precluding a diversion. I would also like to acknowledge the support of Dispatch and company as reflective of the number of communications that were made prior to our diversion. And last; but certainly not least; I would like to acknowledge the expert airmanship demonstrated by my First Officer during our extremely busy diversion as well as throughout the rest of a very long day. Should you need additional information from me regarding this diversion; please don't hesitate to contact me.

column121: I was the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X from ZZZ2-ZZZ1. I flew the RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach with rain and wind in the vicinity. I attempted to configure early but a strong tailwind made it challenging. I encountered a wind gust which caused me to counter increasing airspeed by pitching up and slightly reduce power to maintain airspeed and continue configuring. This resulted in a position higher than anticipated. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) noticed this also and we articulated that. About that time; ATC directed a go-around. We executed the missed approach and climbed to 3;000 [feet] on vectors for another approach.Noting the conditions; I configured early for the second RNAV RNP XX approach. Rain and wind were still predominant throughout the approach but fewer gust excursions and we remained stable throughout the approach all the way to minimums. At minimums; we both had the approach lights and runway environment in sight and I continued the approach. As I turned final aligning with Runway XX; I lost sight of the runway environment due to the weather. The PM called go around and I initiated go around procedures. We climbed to 3;000 feet on vectors as directed by ATC. We communicated with one another and ensured we were both in the green; we had ample fuel; and agreed to attempt a third approach. On the third RNAV RNP XX approach; I configured early again and remained stable throughout the approach. The wind was still a factor though and required careful monitoring and aircraft correction to maintain a stable approach. Fully configured and in the vicinity of arriving at minimums; ATC advised a wind shift on the field of 330 degrees at 26 knots of wind. ATC asked for our intentions. Due to airline limitations on Maximum Tailwind Component for Landing; the PM told ATC we could not land and we would go-around. ZZZ1 Tower handed us off to ZZZ Departure and they advised us that they 'turned the airfield around' and they would give us vectors for the ILS RWY XY approach and we would be 'number 1' to the field. Again; the Captain and I communicated that we were both in the green; we noted that we had ample fuel; and we prepared for an ILS approach to Runway XY.After intercepting the localizer for the ILS to Runway XY; I configured fully and continued down the glideslope from the final approach fix. It was raining outside and was windy but we remained stable. Shortly prior to 1;000 feet AGL; it grew increasingly difficult to maintain a stable approach. I told the PM that I didn't feel comfortable; the weather was worsening; and it was likely that we would not be stable at 1;000 feet. We agreed and elected to go-around. Just as I began the go around procedure; we encountered a Wind Shear Warning and I proceeded with the Wind Shear escape maneuver. We exited the conditions quickly and transitioned to ATC's directives. We quickly agreed to divert to ZZZ3 and the PM informed ATC of our intention to divert. We climbed to 3;000 feet and flew vectors to ZZZ3.We flew the ILS RWY XYC approach and landed safely at ZZZ3 and taxied to the gate. We shut down the aircraft with approximately 7.4k pounds of fuel remaining. During the deplaning process; the Captain coordinated with the Maintenance and Dispatch and agreed to continue on to ZZZ1 as the weather cleared the area. We added fuel departing with 11.8k pounds of fuel. The Captain flew as the PF and I was the PM for the return flight to ZZZ1. The Captain maintained appropriate communication throughout the event. He communicated with the passengers explaining as best as possible what occurred and what we were doing to ensure their safety while doing our best to land at our intended destination. He kept the flight attendants apprised of the situation after each approach and we discussed each approach; verified we were both in the green; and maintained situational awareness at all times.
column123: Flew RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach. FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying) and was configuring the aircraft early. He was at gear down; flaps 15; and we encountered a wind gust that drove the airspeed indication almost to redline. The FO raised nose slightly and reduced power to slow the airspeed in order to continue configuring the aircraft. As this occurred; aircraft got a little high. As PM; I noticed this and was in process of informing FO when ATC said that we looked a little high and to just go around. We executed the missed approach as directed by ATC and climbed on a heading to 3;000 ft. to vector for another approach.On the second RNAV RNP XX; FO configured the aircraft early and shot approach to minimums. At minimums; approach lights and runway lights were visible; but as we turned to final approach; visibility was lost.  I called go-around; and FO initiated go-around. We climbed on a heading to 3;000 feet. We communicated with each other that we were both in the green; had plenty of fuel; and prepared for another approach.On the third RNAV RNP XX; the FO had fully configured the aircraft; when ATC advised that the wind had shifted out of the north at 330 degrees and we had 26 knots of wind at our tail. ATC asked our intentions; I told them that we could not land with those winds and that we were going around. At that point; ATC handed us off to departure; and departure immediately advised us that they had turned the airport around and could give us an immediate left downwind to be number 1; shooting ILS Runway XY. FO and I communicated with each other that we were both in the green; had plenty of fuel; and prepared for an approach using the new runway.On attempt to Runway XY; we intercepted localizer and G/S. We had continual high winds indicating to me that the aircraft would not be able to remain stable throughout approach and landing. As PIC; I called for a go-around. FO communicated to me his agreement; and I immediately notified Tower of our intention to divert to ZZZ3. FO initiated the miss. As he did; we encountered a brief Wind Shear Warning. FO finished cleaning aircraft up and we diverted to ZZZ3 without incident.We were vectored to ZZZ3 and landed on Runway XYC and taxied to the gate with 7.4 pounds of fuel. I called Dispatch and she said we had plenty of fuel to get to ZZZ1 but as a precaution due to the frontal weather passage; she added more fuel and brought us up to 11.8 pounds. After the front passage; I flew the aircraft as PF uneventfully to ZZZ1. During all of the approaches and the divert I kept the flight attendants up to date and communicated with the passengers at all times. We exercised good situational awareness and followed SOPs during the entire flight.

column121: Aircraft X had a dual engine wash on the night of Date. Maintenance Technician 1 and I performed the run up after engine wash; followed Job Card XXX-XX-XX. Taxi aircraft onto taxiway for run up to 60%; 60% run was not done at the blast fence as paperwork doesn't specify location. The 700 has a different Job Card time requirement and seems to have less issues with 'smell/odor'. Cause of flight crew 'smell/odor' discovery may be out of Maintenance Technician's control as engines and packs have been run longer and at different altitudes/temperatures/parameters. Have the Job Card for the 700/800/MAX mirror each other so all aircraft and all technicians are performing job the same way to avoid  gate return/air returns/out of service aircraft.
column123: Aircraft X was taken out of service in ZZZ1 for oil smell after it landed there from ZZZ after having performed an engine compressor wash. Flight crew reported it. My co-worker and I believe we followed the Job Card and hit the times and parameters that it asks for. Maintenance Technician 2 and myself did not smell anything; this could be due to becoming acclimated. The company pointed out that we needed to be at the blast fence for the 60% N1. I was unaware of this. The task card does not specify to do so. As it only requires a very short time at 60% we set brakes during taxi to run the engine up. We also did an engine compressor wash on another 800 aircraft the same shift the exact same way. Only Aircraft X was taken out of service. This leads me to think that maybe something else may have caused the oil smell. Also after talking to other employees about this; I hear there have been multiple similar situation of 700 series aircraft going out of service following engine compressor washes. So much so that the company has changed the Job Card for the 700 series engine compressor washes. They run the engine at 60% N1 much longer. Why the 800 does not mirror the 700 Job Card is unknown.

column121: The event occurred because Greenville-Spartanburg (GSP) is working a busy airport with one controller utilizing all three frequencies. This is a major safety of flight issue as multiple links in the safety chain were broken that day. If the sharpness of the crews from Air Carrier X and Air Carrier Y had not utilized full four ear policy and patience it could have been an issue. The actions taken by the ATC operation in GSP are uncalled for and unsafe. If this is overlooked there could be fatal consequences in the future. There are a few local airports in the area of Greenville-Spartanburg that are non-towered. If the Tower Controller delayed any further for us to be handed over to Departure; we could have had a collision or RA with an unknown aircraft all due to the unsafe actions of one controller handling a workload bound for a minimum of two personal.I was in command of Aircraft X. The Greenville Tower had one controller working all three frequencies: clearance; ground; and tower. This was a busy morning with Air Carrier Z; Air Carrier X; Air Carrier A; and us to ZZZ all departing at roughly the same time. When we called for our clearance on the delivery frequency; we noticed there was some bleed over as the controller was issuing take-off clearances. We had to repeat our request for a clearance but were given it with no issues.  I released the brakes and we called for push shortly after. Air Carrier X also called for push after us. In the middle of our push back the controller called on the ground frequency to inform Air Carrier Z of a delay for them. The two began to have a conversation on ground of a game plan to be made. As their conversation occurred our ramp crew disconnected the tow bar and gave the wave off for an all clear to a taxi. I noticed Air Carrier X had pushed off gate and we were pushed off with our nose in the direction of travel to only exit with a head on collision. We finished our 'After Start Checklist' and cleared the area to begin our taxi. I switched on our taxi and nose lights and noticed Air Carrier X did the same. With the controller and Air Carrier Z conversation occurring to what was now a clearance being given with a read back to follow there was no way for me or Air Carrier X to have confirmation one was waiting for the other. There was dense fog and low visibility on the ramp that morning. Tower does not control the ramp and a courtesy call is requested. The weather was so bad we had a take-off alternate of ZZZ1 that morning. It was a frustrating situation as Air Carrier X and I could barely make out the 2nd half of each other's aircraft; so it was a game of chicken. I tried to call over the radio and speak over the clearance being given but it did not work. Ultimately; I turned off my lights to give Air Carrier X the right of way. As we began our taxi to Runway 4 Air Carrier A called clearance to get their clearance to Houston (IAH) and that now was being broadcast over the ground frequency adding to the safety issue that no one moving on the aircraft surface could talk to each other. The Tower issued Air Carrier X their take-off clearance and told us we were next. After we got our take off clearance; we began the take-off roll with no issues. As we continued our take-off climb Carrier called the controller over the ground frequency. All we heard was the controller responding over the tower frequency meaning he was working all three frequencies still. This delayed our hand off to Departure and made us uneasy as the tower radar could not see our path beyond a certain mileage. As we checked in with GSP Departure we were given an instruction to contact Center as our time had been too long and radar services with GSP could not be utilized further.This told me the GSP airport controller took too long to hand us off and impeded the Departure Controller from doing their job properly. We did not have sufficient air traffic control separation all due to the unsafe practices of the GSP airport and Air Traffic Control operation at the airport of GSP. GSP needs to hire another controller! There must be at least one person working Ground and Delivery while another separate controller works Tower. The operation in GSP has been compromised and it is scary to think that the unsafe actions are acceptable to those working in the ATC system. If this issue were to happen again; I'm worried it could turn out like the Tenerife airport disaster with KLM and Pan Am but scraping metal on the ramp or taxing into each other.
